steps.overview: This step sets up a safe AWS account. You will lock the root user with MFA, create a separate identity for daily work, add a budget alert so you never get a surprise bill, and learn how AWS global infrastructure is organised. Root user rules, IAM best practice, Budgets and Regions/AZs/edge locations are tested heavily in CLF-C02 and appear again in every Associate and Professional exam.
objectives: Create an AWS account and secure the root user with MFA
Set up IAM Identity Center (or an IAM admin user) and use it instead of root for all daily work
Configure an AWS Budgets cost alert with email notifications and explain the Free Tier model
Distinguish Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations and choose a Region for a workload
Identify which tasks truly need the root user

concepts.explanation: The identity created with the email address used to open the account. It has complete, unrestricted access, and IAM policies cannot limit it inside its own account. Use it only for the few tasks that need it, such as changing account settings, changing the support plan, closing the account or restoring IAM access. Never create access keys for root.

A second factor on top of the password. Options are passkeys or security keys (FIDO2), virtual authenticator apps, and hardware TOTP tokens. AWS now enforces MFA for root users, and you can register more than one MFA device per user for backup. Exam answers about 'securing the root account' almost always include enabling MFA.

The AWS-recommended way for people to sign in. It works with AWS Organizations, gives users a single access portal, and issues short-term credentials. You assign permission sets (for example AdministratorAccess) to users or groups for specific accounts. It replaces long-lived IAM user passwords and access keys for human users.

An IAM user is a long-term identity inside one account, with a password and optional access keys. It is acceptable for a simple lab account but not the preferred pattern for people at scale. Grant permissions through groups and policies, and give only the access needed (least privilege). Prefer IAM roles for applications and AWS services.

A service that tracks cost, usage, Reserved Instance or Savings Plans coverage against a limit you set. Alerts can fire on actual spend or forecasted spend crossing a threshold, and they notify by email or Amazon SNS. Budget actions can go further, for example by applying an IAM policy or a Service Control Policy (SCP) to stop new spend. Use Cost Explorer to analyse past spend and Budgets to alert on future spend.

For accounts created from 15 July 2025, new customers get a credit-based free plan: sign-up credits plus extra credits for exploring services, valid for a limited period. Some 'always free' offers continue on top, such as monthly AWS Lambda requests. Usage beyond the credits or the free plan period is billed only if you move to a paid plan, but lab resources can still burn credits. Older accounts stay on the legacy 12-month Free Tier. Always check the current Free Tier page.

A Region is a separate geographic area, such as ap-south-1 (Mumbai) or ap-south-2 (Hyderabad). A Region contains multiple Availability Zones (AZs). Each AZ is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, joined to the other AZs by low-latency links. Deploy across multiple AZs for high availability and across Regions for disaster recovery.

Points of presence, many more than there are Regions, used by Amazon CloudFront, Route 53 and AWS Global Accelerator to serve users with low latency. Edge locations cache content and answer DNS queries. They do not run your EC2 instances. Local Zones and Wavelength Zones are different things: they extend compute close to users.

keyFacts: Root user best practice: enable MFA, delete or never create root access keys, use root only for root-only tasks, and keep the root email and phone details secure.
IAM policies cannot restrict the root user in a standalone account; only SCPs in AWS Organizations can limit root in member accounts.
IAM is a global service; IAM Identity Center is enabled in one home Region and requires AWS Organizations.
IAM users cannot see billing data until root turns on 'IAM user and role access to Billing information' in Account settings.
AWS Budgets can alert on actual or forecasted cost; each budget supports multiple thresholds, delivered to email or SNS subscribers.
Billing data is not real time; budget evaluation runs a few times a day, so an alert can arrive hours after the spend happens.
Choose a Region by four factors: data residency and compliance, latency to users, service availability, and price.
Each Region has multiple isolated AZs (new Regions launch with at least three); AZ names like ap-south-1a are mapped differently per account, and AZ IDs (aps1-az1) are consistent.
Shared responsibility: AWS secures the cloud (facilities, hardware, global infrastructure); you secure what is in the cloud (identities, MFA, data, configuration).

example.caption: Create a USD 5 monthly cost budget with 80% actual and 100% forecasted email alerts using the AWS CLI (run as your admin user, not root)
example.code:
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)

cat > budget.json <<'EOF'
{
  "BudgetName": "monthly-5-usd",
  "BudgetLimit": {"Amount": "5", "Unit": "USD"},
  "TimeUnit": "MONTHLY",
  "BudgetType": "COST"
}
EOF

cat > notifications.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"Notification": {"NotificationType": "ACTUAL", "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN",
    "Threshold": 80, "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"},
   "Subscribers": [{"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "you@example.com"}]},
  {"Notification": {"NotificationType": "FORECASTED", "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN",
    "Threshold": 100, "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"},
   "Subscribers": [{"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "you@example.com"}]}
]
EOF

aws budgets create-budget \
  --account-id "$ACCOUNT_ID" \
  --budget file://budget.json \
  --notifications-with-subscribers file://notifications.json

aws budgets describe-budgets --account-id "$ACCOUNT_ID" --query 'Budgets[].BudgetName'

pitfalls: Using the root user 'just this once' for daily tasks, or creating root access keys. On the exam, any answer that uses root for routine work is wrong.
Assuming a budget stops spending. A plain budget only alerts; you need budget actions, or you must delete the resources yourself.
Confusing AZs with edge locations. CloudFront caches at edge locations, but EC2, RDS and subnets live in AZs.
Forgetting to enable IAM access to billing, so the admin user sees 'access denied' on the Billing and Budgets pages.
Leaving lab resources running, such as NAT gateways, idle EC2 instances, Elastic IPs or RDS instances. These quietly consume Free Tier credits or create charges.
Mixing up Cost Explorer (analyse past and current spend) with AWS Budgets (alert on thresholds) and the Pricing Calculator (estimate before you build).

workflow.title: Secure a new AWS account in one sitting

steps.label: Create the account
steps.detail: Sign up with a dedicated email address and a payment method, then choose the free or paid plan and a Support plan (Basic is free).

steps.label: Lock down the root user
steps.detail: Sign in as root, register an MFA device (preferably a passkey or security key plus a backup), and confirm that no root access keys exist.

steps.label: Enable billing access for IAM
steps.detail: In Account settings, turn on IAM user and role access to Billing information so non-root identities can manage Budgets.

steps.label: Create a daily-use admin identity
steps.detail: Enable IAM Identity Center with an AdministratorAccess permission set, or create an IAM user in an Admins group, and turn on MFA for it.

steps.label: Sign out of root, sign in as admin
steps.detail: Use the Identity Center access portal URL or the account sign-in URL, and from now on never sign in as root for routine work.

steps.label: Set the USD 5 budget alert
steps.detail: In AWS Budgets, create a monthly cost budget of USD 5 with actual and forecasted email alerts, and confirm the alert email arrives.

steps.label: Pick your home Region
steps.detail: Select a nearby Region such as ap-south-1 (Mumbai) in the console, and note its AZ IDs for later labs.

project.title: aws-safe-setup
project.summary: This project makes a new AWS account safe for study. It uses Terraform to create a USD 5 monthly budget with email alerts and a least-privilege 'DailyWork' permission set in IAM Identity Center, and a check script confirms that you are not root, that root MFA is on, and that the budget exists. README.md covers the one-time root steps done in the console, versions.tf and variables.tf set the provider and inputs, budget.tf is the cost guardrail, identity_center.tf is the non-root daily login, aws-config.example is the CLI SSO setup, and check-setup.sh is the checkpoint.
project.run:
cp config/aws-config.example ~/.aws/config   # then edit start URL and account ID
aws sso login --profile mc-admin
export AWS_PROFILE=mc-admin
cd infra && terraform init
terraform apply -var="alert_email=you@example.com" -var="sso_user_name=learner"
cd .. && bash scripts/check-setup.sh

files.code:
# aws-safe-setup (Step 1: Set up safely)

Goal: get a USD 5 budget alert, then use a non-root user from now on.

## A. One-time root steps (console only, never create root access keys)
1. Create the AWS account. Sign in as the root user (the account email).
2. Account menu > Security credentials > assign an MFA device to root
   (a passkey, a security key or an authenticator app).
3. Account menu > Account > turn on "IAM user and role access to Billing
   information". Without this, non-root users cannot see costs or budgets.
4. Pick your Region (this sample uses ap-south-1, Mumbai). Open
   IAM Identity Center and choose Enable. This Region becomes its home Region.
5. In Identity Center, create user `learner`, create the permission set
   `AdministratorAccess` and assign it to `learner` on this account.
6. Accept the email invite, set a password, register MFA, and note the
   AWS access portal URL (https://d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start).
7. Sign out of root. Lock the root MFA and password away.

## B. Daily work (non-root, done with this project)
- Copy `config/aws-config.example` to `~/.aws/config` and edit it.
- `aws sso login --profile mc-admin` (short-lived credentials, no keys on disk).
- Run Terraform in `infra/`. It creates:
  - `budget.tf`: a USD 5 monthly cost budget with email alerts.
  - `identity_center.tf`: a `DailyWork` permission set (PowerUserAccess)
    assigned to `learner`. Use it for labs and keep admin for IAM changes.
- Run `scripts/check-setup.sh` to pass the checkpoint.

## Key ideas for the exam
- Root user: full access that cannot be restricted by IAM. Use it only for
  root-only tasks, such as closing the account or changing the support plan.
- IAM Identity Center is the recommended way for people to sign in. An IAM
  user with long-term access keys is the older option.
- Least privilege: grant only what the task needs. This is why DailyWork
  uses PowerUserAccess and not full admin.
- AWS Budgets only alerts you. It does not stop spending unless you add
  budget actions. Free Tier offers and limits change, so check the Free Tier
  page and the Billing console.
- A Region contains several isolated Availability Zones (AZs). Edge
  locations serve CloudFront and Route 53 traffic close to users.

# USD 5 monthly COST budget. It alerts you but does not stop resources.
resource "aws_budgets_budget" "monthly_cost" {
  name         = "masterclass-monthly-usd-${var.budget_limit_usd}"
  budget_type  = "COST"
  limit_amount = var.budget_limit_usd
  limit_unit   = "USD"
  time_unit    = "MONTHLY"

  # Alert 1: actual spend has passed 80% of the limit (about USD 4)
  notification {
    comparison_operator        = "GREATER_THAN"
    threshold                  = 80
    threshold_type             = "PERCENTAGE"
    notification_type          = "ACTUAL"
    subscriber_email_addresses = [var.alert_email]
  }

  # Alert 2: the forecast says you will pass 100% this month
  notification {
    comparison_operator        = "GREATER_THAN"
    threshold                  = 100
    threshold_type             = "PERCENTAGE"
    notification_type          = "FORECASTED"
    subscriber_email_addresses = [var.alert_email]
  }

  # Alert 3: actual spend has passed the full limit, so act now
  notification {
    comparison_operator        = "GREATER_THAN"
    threshold                  = 100
    threshold_type             = "PERCENTAGE"
    notification_type          = "ACTUAL"
    subscriber_email_addresses = [var.alert_email]
  }
}

# Copy to ~/.aws/config, then replace the start URL and the account ID.
# Sign in with: aws sso login --profile mc-admin
# No long-term access keys are stored. SSO gives temporary credentials.

[sso-session masterclass]
# Your AWS access portal URL (shown in the Identity Center console)
sso_start_url = https://d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start
# Home Region of Identity Center
sso_region = ap-south-1
sso_registration_scopes = sso:account:access

# Admin: use it only for IAM changes and for running this Terraform
[profile mc-admin]
sso_session = masterclass
sso_account_id = 111122223333
sso_role_name = AdministratorAccess
region = ap-south-1
output = json

# Daily labs: PowerUserAccess (least privilege), created by identity_center.tf
[profile mc-daily]
sso_session = masterclass
sso_account_id = 111122223333
sso_role_name = DailyWork
region = ap-south-1
output = json

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Checkpoint for Step 1. Run it with the admin SSO profile.
set -euo pipefail
export AWS_PROFILE="${AWS_PROFILE:-mc-admin}"
REGION="${REGION:-ap-south-1}"

echo "1) Who am I?"
ARN=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text)
echo "   $ARN"
if [[ "$ARN" == *":root" ]]; then
  echo "   FAIL: you are using the root user. Stop and sign in with SSO."; exit 1
fi
echo "   OK: non-root identity (an assumed role from Identity Center)"

echo "2) Is root MFA on?"
MFA=$(aws iam get-account-summary --query 'SummaryMap.AccountMFAEnabled' --output text)
if [[ "$MFA" != "1" ]]; then
  echo "   FAIL: root MFA is not enabled"; exit 1
fi
echo "   OK: root MFA enabled"

echo "3) Does the budget exist?"
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
aws budgets describe-budgets --account-id "$ACCOUNT_ID" \
  --query 'Budgets[].[BudgetName,BudgetLimit.Amount,BudgetLimit.Unit]' --output table

echo "4) Availability Zones in $REGION (one Region, several isolated AZs)"
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region "$REGION" \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId,State]' --output table

echo "All checks passed. From now on, use: aws sso login --profile mc-daily"

revision.examFocus: This step maps to CLF-C02 Domain 2 (Security and Compliance: shared responsibility, root user, IAM, MFA), Domain 3 (global infrastructure: Regions, AZs, edge locations) and Domain 4 (Billing, Pricing, and Support: Budgets, Cost Explorer, Pricing Calculator, Free Tier). The same ideas come back in SAA-C03 under Design Secure Architectures and Design Cost-Optimized Architectures. Questions are short scenarios that ask for the 'most secure' or 'best practice' identity choice, the right cost tool, or the right infrastructure unit for availability or latency.

compare.difference: Identity Center gives people single sign-on with short-lived credentials across many accounts in AWS Organizations. An IAM user has long-term credentials that live inside one account.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when the question mentions a workforce, multiple accounts, SSO, an external identity provider, or 'temporary credentials for people'.
compare.chooseB: Pick it only for a single standalone account with no Organizations, or for a legacy tool that truly needs long-term access keys (and even then prefer roles).

compare.difference: Budgets watches a threshold and notifies you, or runs a budget action. Cost Explorer is for viewing and analysing spend trends. It does not alert on thresholds.
compare.chooseA: Pick Budgets for 'notify when cost or usage exceeds or is forecast to exceed X'.
compare.chooseB: Pick Cost Explorer for 'analyse', 'visualise', 'which service drove last month's bill', or 'view RI and Savings Plans recommendations'.

compare.difference: The Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of an architecture before anything is built. Budgets tracks real spend after resources run.
compare.chooseA: Pick the Calculator for 'estimate', 'before migrating', or 'compare the cost of a proposed design'.
compare.chooseB: Pick Budgets once resources exist and you need guardrail alerts.

compare.difference: AZs host compute, databases and subnets for high availability inside a Region. Edge locations cache and serve content close to users through CloudFront, and also serve Route 53 and some Global Accelerator and Shield traffic.
compare.chooseA: Pick AZs for 'highly available', 'fault tolerant', 'Multi-AZ', 'survive a data centre failure'.
compare.chooseB: Pick edge locations or CloudFront for 'lowest latency for global users', 'cache static content', 'deliver content worldwide'.

compare.difference: An SCP sets the maximum permissions for a whole member account, including its root user, and grants nothing by itself. An IAM policy grants or denies permissions to a user, group or role inside one account and cannot restrict root.
compare.chooseA: Pick an SCP for 'prevent every principal in member accounts, including root, from doing X' or 'restrict Regions across the organisation'.
compare.chooseB: Pick an IAM policy for 'give this developer or role permission to do X'.

cues.cue: Most secure way to protect the account owner credentials
cues.pick: Enable MFA on the root user, remove root access keys, and lock it away
cues.why: This is AWS's stated root best practice, and any option that uses root for daily work is wrong.

cues.cue: Task that can only be done by the root user
cues.pick: Root user (for example: close the account, change the account email or root password, change the support plan, restore an admin who has locked themselves out)
cues.why: These few tasks are root-only, so they are the only valid time to sign in as root.

cues.cue: Employees need one login for several AWS accounts
cues.pick: IAM Identity Center with AWS Organizations
cues.why: It provides central SSO and temporary role credentials across accounts.

cues.cue: Notify when spend is forecast to exceed a limit
cues.pick: AWS Budgets with a forecasted threshold to email or SNS
cues.why: Only Budgets alerts on thresholds, and the forecasted type warns before the money is actually spent.

cues.cue: Automatically stop further spend when a budget is breached
cues.pick: Budget actions (apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop EC2/RDS instances)
cues.why: A plain budget only sends alerts. Actions are the built-in way to respond.

cues.cue: Unexpected spike in spend without a fixed threshold
cues.pick: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
cues.why: It uses machine learning to flag unusual spend patterns, whereas Budgets needs a value you set in advance.

cues.cue: Data must stay in India for regulation
cues.pick: Choose an India Region (ap-south-1 Mumbai or ap-south-2 Hyderabad)
cues.why: Compliance and data residency are decided at Region level, and data does not leave a Region unless you move it.

cues.cue: Refer to the same physical AZ across two accounts
cues.pick: AZ ID (for example aps1-az1), not the AZ name
cues.why: AZ names are mapped randomly per account, but AZ IDs are the same in every account.

scenario.situation: A three-person startup in Pune opened an AWS account last month. The founder signs in with the account email for all work, and has created access keys on that identity for a deployment script. The team wants to keep using one account for now. They want an email warning before the monthly bill crosses USD 50. Which combination of actions follows AWS best practice?
reasoning: Eliminate any option that keeps the founder working as root or keeps the root access keys. Root is for root-only tasks, and root keys should be deleted.

Enable MFA on root, delete the root access keys, and create a non-root admin identity. For one standalone account this is an IAM admin user, or IAM Identity Center if they enable Organizations. Give the script its own least-privilege identity, ideally a role.
For the warning, eliminate Cost Explorer (analysis only) and the Pricing Calculator (pre-build estimates only). Choose an AWS Budgets cost budget with a forecasted threshold and an email subscriber.
Check the hidden step: root must turn on IAM user and role access to Billing information, or the new admin cannot see or manage the budget.
scenario.answer: Secure root with MFA and delete its keys, move daily work to a non-root admin, and give the script a separate least-privilege identity. Create an AWS Budgets cost budget with a forecasted alert at USD 50 to email, after enabling IAM access to billing.

memoryAids: Root = 'MFA, no keys, rarely seen': lock it, strip its keys, use it only for root-only tasks.
Cost tools by time: Calculator = BEFORE you build, Explorer = AFTER you spend (look back), Budgets = WARNING at a line, Anomaly Detection = SURPRISE spikes.
Choosing a Region, 'CLSP': Compliance, Latency, Services available, Price.
cheatSheet: Any answer that uses the root user for routine admin is wrong. Root is only for root-only tasks.
Root best practice: strong password, MFA, no access keys, protected contact email and phone.
Only SCPs, not IAM policies, can limit the root user, and only in member accounts of an organisation.
With AWS Organizations, IAM Identity Center is the preferred way for people to sign in. It gives temporary credentials and SSO.
Least privilege: start with minimum permissions and add more only as needed. Use roles for apps and services, not shared users.
Budgets can alert on actual or forecasted spend, with several thresholds, to email or SNS. Budget actions are needed to enforce limits.
Billing data lags by hours. Set alerts below your true limit and delete lab resources the same day.
Common silent costs: NAT gateways, idle EC2, unattached or idle public IPv4 addresses and Elastic IPs, RDS instances, EBS volumes and snapshots.
A Region contains multiple isolated AZs. Use multiple AZs for high availability and multiple Regions for disaster recovery or data residency.
Edge locations exist for CloudFront caching and Route 53, not for running EC2, RDS or subnets.
Shared responsibility: AWS secures the cloud itself; you secure identities, MFA, data, encryption choices and configuration.
IAM is global. A user created once works in all Regions, unlike Region-scoped resources such as EC2.
selfCheck: I can list at least four root-only tasks and explain why everything else should use a non-root identity.
I can choose between IAM Identity Center, an IAM user and an IAM role for a given scenario, and justify the choice.
I can pick the right tool among Budgets, budget actions, Cost Explorer, Cost Anomaly Detection and the Pricing Calculator from the question wording.
I can explain why my admin user might get 'access denied' on Billing and fix it.
I can tell whether a requirement needs multiple AZs, multiple Regions or edge locations, and choose a Region using compliance, latency, services and price.
I have set a USD 5 budget alert, signed in as a non-root user, and have not used root since.

objective.question: You have just created a new AWS account for learning. Which action should you take first to protect the account?
options: Launch a test EC2 instance to confirm the account works
Change the default Region to ap-south-1
Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the root user
Create access keys for the root user so you can use the AWS CLI
objective.explanation: The root user has full, unrestricted access, so protecting it with MFA is the first security step. Root access keys should never be created, and launching resources or changing Regions does nothing for security.

objective.question: A startup uses AWS Organizations and expects to grow to several AWS accounts. Developers need daily console and CLI access with short-lived credentials and one sign-in for all accounts. What should the administrator set up?
options: IAM Identity Center with permission sets assigned to users and groups
The root user with MFA, shared among the developers
A shared IAM admin user whose password is stored in a team password manager
One IAM user per developer in every account
objective.explanation: IAM Identity Center gives central sign-in across Organizations accounts, uses permission sets, and issues temporary credentials. Separate IAM users per account do not scale, and shared users or a shared root break accountability and least privilege.

objective.question: An IAM user has the AdministratorAccess policy attached but sees an access denied message on the Billing and Cost Management pages. What is the most likely cause?
options: The user is signed in to the wrong Region
The account has not enabled AWS Budgets yet
The root user has not turned on 'IAM user and role access to Billing information' in Account settings
IAM users can never view billing data
objective.explanation: Billing access for IAM identities works only after the root user activates this setting, in addition to the IAM permissions. Billing is not tied to a Region, and Budgets is not a prerequisite.

objective.question: A security team wants to stop the root user of member accounts in AWS Organizations from deleting CloudTrail trails. Which control can do this?
options: An IAM permissions boundary on the root user
A resource-based policy on the CloudTrail trail
A service control policy (SCP) attached to the member accounts or their OU
An IAM identity-based policy attached to the root user
objective.explanation: SCPs set the maximum permissions for a member account, including its root user. IAM policies and permissions boundaries cannot be attached to or restrict the root user.

objective.question: You set a budget alert at USD 5. You launch an expensive resource in the morning, but the alert email arrives in the evening. Why?
options: The alert was sent to the wrong Region
Email notifications are slower than SNS by design
Billing data is not real time, and budgets are evaluated only a few times a day
AWS Budgets only sends emails once a week
objective.explanation: Cost data takes time to process, and budget evaluation runs periodically, so alerts can arrive hours after the spend. Budgets are not weekly-only and are not Region-specific.

objective.question: A learner wants a warning before the monthly bill actually reaches USD 5, based on the current spending trend. Which budget setting should they use?
options: A forecasted cost threshold
A Reserved Instance utilization budget
A Savings Plans coverage budget
An actual cost threshold at 100%
objective.explanation: A forecasted threshold alerts when AWS predicts that month-end cost will cross the limit. An actual threshold fires only after the cost is incurred, and the RI and Savings Plans budgets track commitment use, not total spend.

objective.question: Which of these tasks can be done only by the root user?
options: Creating an AWS Budgets alert
Launching an EC2 instance in a new Region
Closing the AWS account
Creating an IAM role for EC2
objective.explanation: Closing the account is a root-only task. Roles, budgets and EC2 instances can all be managed by IAM identities that have the right permissions.

objective.question: A security review shows that the root user of an account has an active access key that was used by a script last year. What is the best action?
options: Attach a deny policy to the root access key
Keep the key but enable MFA on the root user
Delete the root access key and move the script to an IAM role or a least-privilege identity
Rotate the root access key every 90 days
objective.explanation: AWS best practice is to have no root access keys at all, so delete the key and give the script its own limited credentials. Rotating the key still leaves full-power keys in place, IAM policies cannot restrict root, and MFA does not protect access keys used by the CLI.

objective.question: Two teams in different AWS accounts agree to deploy into ap-south-1a so they share the same physical Availability Zone. Later they find their resources are in different zones. What should they use instead?
options: Edge location names
Local Zone names
AZ IDs such as aps1-az1
The Region code ap-south-1
objective.explanation: AZ names are mapped differently in each account, but AZ IDs point to the same physical zone in every account. The Region code does not identify a zone, and edge locations and Local Zones are different infrastructure.

objective.question: Which AWS service mainly uses edge locations to deliver content with low latency to users?
options: AWS IAM
Amazon EBS
Amazon RDS
Amazon CloudFront
objective.explanation: CloudFront caches content at edge locations close to users, as do services like Route 53 and Global Accelerator. RDS and EBS run inside Regions and AZs, and IAM is a global identity service.

objective.question: An Indian bank must keep customer data within India because of regulation. It is choosing an AWS Region. Which factor must be decided first?
options: The Region with the most AWS services
The Region closest to the developers' office
Data residency and compliance requirements
The Region with the lowest price
objective.explanation: Compliance and data residency are hard constraints, so they limit the options before latency, service availability and price are compared. A cheaper or feature-rich Region outside India would fail the legal requirement.

objective.question: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which task is the customer's responsibility?
options: Replacing failed hardware in an Availability Zone
Enabling MFA and managing IAM permissions
Maintaining the global network between Regions
Physical security of AWS data centres
objective.explanation: Customers are responsible for security in the cloud, including identities, MFA, data and configuration. Facilities, hardware and global infrastructure are AWS's responsibility.

objective.question: A team wants budget alerts sent to several email addresses and also to an automated workflow that posts to a chat tool. What should they configure in AWS Budgets?
options: An Amazon SNS topic as a subscriber, with the workflow subscribed to the topic
A CloudFront distribution for notifications
An IAM policy that forwards billing data
Only an email subscriber, because Budgets supports nothing else
objective.explanation: Budgets can notify email subscribers and Amazon SNS topics, and other systems can subscribe to the SNS topic. CloudFront and IAM policies do not deliver budget notifications.

objective.question: A learner on the AWS Free Tier receives a charge after launching an EC2 instance for a lab. What is the most likely reason?
options: The instance type or usage was outside Free Tier eligibility or limits
EC2 is never covered by the Free Tier
Free Tier is available only in the us-east-1 Region
The Free Tier applies only to IAM users, not root
objective.explanation: Free Tier covers only specific services, sizes and usage levels, so a non-eligible instance type or extra usage is billed. It is not limited to one Region and has nothing to do with root versus IAM users.

objective.question: You open the IAM console to create an admin user and notice the Region selector shows 'Global'. What does this mean?
options: IAM is a global service, so users and policies apply across all Regions in the account
IAM works only in us-east-1
You must enable IAM Identity Center before using IAM
IAM users must be created separately in each Region
objective.explanation: IAM is global, so identities and policies are not tied to a Region. IAM does not need Identity Center, and you do not create users per Region.

objective.question: An administrator attaches this policy to an IAM group for all human IAM users. What is the effect for a user who signs in to the console with only a password?
options: The policy grants the user permission to manage MFA devices and does nothing else.
Every action except the listed MFA-setup actions is denied until the user signs in with MFA.
The policy has no effect because a Deny statement cannot use NotAction.
The user is blocked from signing in to the console until an MFA device is registered.
objective.explanation: The Deny applies to all actions not in NotAction whenever MFA is absent, so the user can only set up MFA. The user can still sign in; the policy does not grant anything, and NotAction with Deny is valid syntax.

objective.question: A developer runs this command after signing in with 'aws sso login'. What does the output tell you?
options: Priya is using the root user of account 111122223333.
The CLI profile is misconfigured because an IAM user ARN should appear.
Priya is signed in as an IAM user named priya with a long-term access key.
Priya is using temporary credentials from an IAM Identity Center permission set role in account 111122223333.
objective.explanation: The 'assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_...' ARN shows a role that IAM Identity Center created from a permission set, which issues short-lived credentials. An IAM user ARN would start with 'arn:aws:iam::...:user/', and root would end in ':root'.

objective.question: A company wants development EC2 instances to be stopped automatically when the development account's monthly cost passes 90% of its budget, without anyone acting on an email. Which solution meets this need with the least effort?
options: Turn on Free Tier usage alerts in Billing preferences.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks to stop instances.
Configure an AWS Budgets action on the budget that stops the selected EC2 instances at the threshold.
Create a Cost Explorer report and review it daily.
objective.explanation: AWS Budgets actions can run automatically at a threshold, such as stopping EC2 or RDS instances or applying an IAM policy or SCP. Cost Explorer and Trusted Advisor only report, and Free Tier alerts only notify.

objective.question: A team's spending changes a lot from month to month, so fixed budget thresholds create many false alarms. They want to be told about unusual spending spikes in a specific service without setting a fixed amount. What should they use?
options: AWS Pricing Calculator
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
A CloudWatch billing alarm at a fixed amount
An AWS Budgets cost budget with a forecasted threshold
objective.explanation: Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to learn normal spending patterns and alerts on unusual changes, with no fixed amount to set. Budgets and billing alarms need fixed thresholds, and the Pricing Calculator only estimates costs before you build.

objective.question: The root user of a learning account has one virtual MFA device on the owner's phone. The owner is worried about being locked out if the phone is lost. What is the best preventive step?
options: Register a second MFA device, such as a hardware security key, on the root user.
Share the root password with a colleague as a backup.
Create root access keys and store them as a backup login method.
Remove MFA from the root user and rely on a strong password.
objective.explanation: AWS lets you register more than one MFA device on the root user, so a second device removes the single point of failure. Removing MFA, creating root access keys or sharing credentials all weaken security.

objective.question: A security team wants the most phishing-resistant MFA option for administrators who sign in to the AWS console. Which should they choose?
options: SMS text-message codes
A strong password rotated every 30 days
A FIDO2 security key or passkey
A virtual authenticator app that shows a six-digit code
objective.explanation: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys bind the login to the real site's origin, so a fake login page cannot reuse them. Six-digit codes can be typed into a phishing site, AWS does not offer SMS MFA for IAM users, and a password is not a second factor.

objective.question: An IAM user has these two identity-based policies attached. Which statement describes what the user can do?
options: Nothing, because conflicting policies cancel each other out.
Only ec2:TerminateInstances, because the more specific statement wins.
Everything except terminating EC2 instances, because an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow.
Everything, because Policy A allows all actions and the broader Allow wins.
objective.explanation: In IAM policy evaluation, an explicit Deny overrides any Allow. The policies do not cancel out, and being more specific does not matter.

objective.question: An administrator with full permissions wants to deploy into the Asia Pacific (Hyderabad) Region, ap-south-2. CLI calls to that Region fail, and the Region appears greyed out in the console. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hyderabad is an edge location, not a Region, so it cannot host resources.
The Free Tier blocks access to Regions outside ap-south-1.
The administrator needs a separate IAM user created inside ap-south-2.
ap-south-2 is an opt-in Region that must first be enabled for the account in Account settings.
objective.explanation: Regions launched after March 2019, including Hyderabad, are disabled by default and must be enabled per account. IAM is global, so no per-Region user is needed; ap-south-2 is a full Region, and the Free Tier does not block Regions.

objective.question: A company runs a web application for Indian users in ap-south-1. The application must keep running if one data centre fails, and latency between the application tiers must stay low. Which design meets this need?
options: Run the application across at least two Availability Zones in ap-south-1 behind a load balancer.
Run one copy in ap-south-1 and a second copy in a Region in Europe.
Run the application in ap-south-1 and serve it through CloudFront edge locations only.
Run all instances in one Availability Zone and take daily snapshots.
objective.explanation: AZs in a Region are physically separate but linked by low-latency networking, so a multi-AZ design survives a data centre failure. A single AZ is a single point of failure, CloudFront caches content but does not run the app, and a European Region adds latency and may break data-residency needs.

objective.question: A new hire is added to the 'Developers' group in IAM Identity Center. She signs in to the AWS access portal successfully, but no AWS accounts are listed. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Developers group has not been assigned to any AWS account with a permission set
She must enable MFA on the root user of each member account first
The access portal shows accounts only after 24 hours
Her IAM user in the member account has no password
objective.explanation: The portal lists only the accounts where the user or her group has an assignment, meaning a permission set linked to that account. Identity Center does not use IAM users in member accounts, and there is no 24-hour wait or root MFA dependency.

objective.question: You have just created a new AWS account. Which order of steps is safest?
options: Sign in as root, enable root MFA, activate IAM access to billing, create an admin identity, create a budget, sign out of root and use the admin identity
Create an IAM admin user, create a budget, enable root MFA in a month when the account is in use
Sign in as root, create a budget, launch lab resources as root, then create an IAM user
Create root access keys, set up the AWS CLI, enable MFA, create a budget
objective.explanation: Protect root first with MFA, allow IAM identities to see billing, create the daily-use identity, set cost alerts, then stop using root. The other orders create root keys, delay MFA or use root for routine work.

objective.question: A learner created a monthly cost budget with a limit of USD 5 and this notification. They expected an email when actual spend passed USD 5, but they got one when spend was only about USD 0.25. What is the mistake?
options: ComparisonOperator should be EQUAL_TO
Email subscribers always receive the first alert early as a test
ThresholdType PERCENTAGE means 5% of USD 5; they should use Threshold 100 with PERCENTAGE, or Threshold 5 with ABSOLUTE_VALUE
NotificationType should be FORECASTED
objective.explanation: With PERCENTAGE, the threshold is a percentage of the budget amount, so 5 means 5% of USD 5, which is USD 0.25. Changing to FORECASTED or EQUAL_TO does not fix the unit error, and there is no automatic test alert.

objective.question: Before building a three-tier web app, a team lead must give management a monthly cost figure for EC2, RDS and a load balancer in ap-south-1. Nothing has been deployed yet. Which tool fits best?
options: AWS Budgets
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
AWS Pricing Calculator
AWS Cost Explorer
objective.explanation: The Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of an architecture before you build it. Cost Explorer analyses spend that already exists, Budgets alerts on thresholds, and Anomaly Detection flags unusual spend that already happened.

objective.question: A learner's bill last month was USD 12, but they expected near zero. They want to see which service caused the cost and on which days it grew. What should they use?
options: An AWS Budgets forecasted alert
The IAM credential report
AWS Cost Explorer, grouped by service with daily granularity
AWS Pricing Calculator with daily view
objective.explanation: Cost Explorer analyses past and current spend and can group it by service and show it day by day. The Pricing Calculator only estimates, a budget alert only warns about thresholds, and the credential report is about IAM credentials.

objective.question: After a lab, a learner terminated all EC2 instances in ap-south-1. A few days later the bill still shows a small hourly charge for public IPv4 addresses in that Region. What is the most likely cause?
options: An Elastic IP address is still allocated to the account but no longer associated with a running instance
The IAM admin user is billed per hour
CloudFront edge locations charge for idle IPs
Terminated instances are billed for 7 more days
objective.explanation: An allocated Elastic IP keeps generating a public IPv4 charge until you release it, even after the instance is gone. Terminated instances stop billing for compute, and IAM users have no cost.

objective.question: A reporting app's role has this policy. Calls to s3:GetObject on 'reports-bucket/2026/jan.csv' fail with AccessDenied. There are no other policies involved. What is the fix?
options: Add "Principal": "*" to the statement
Change the Region of the policy to ap-south-1
Change the Resource to arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*
Change the Action to s3:*
objective.explanation: GetObject acts on objects, so the resource must be the object ARN pattern 'bucket/*', not the bucket ARN. Using s3:* breaks least privilege, identity-based policies do not take a Principal, and IAM policies have no Region.

objective.question: An architect proposes: 'To cut latency for users in Delhi, we will launch our EC2 app servers in the AWS edge location in Delhi.' What is wrong with this plan?
options: EC2 cannot run in edge locations; use an AWS Local Zone for compute close to users, or CloudFront to cache content at the edge
Edge locations exist only in the US
EC2 can run at edge locations only through the root user
Nothing; edge locations run EC2 at lower prices
objective.explanation: Edge locations serve services such as CloudFront and Route 53, not EC2. For low-latency compute near a city you use a Local Zone where one is available, and for content you cache with CloudFront.

objective.question: A budget action was set to attach a deny policy to a developer role when actual cost passes 100%. The threshold has been crossed, but the policy is not attached and the action shows that it is waiting. What is the most likely cause?
options: The action was configured to require manual approval, so someone must approve it
Budget actions can only stop EC2 instances, not apply IAM policies
The root user must be signed in for any budget action to run
Budget actions only run on the first day of each month
objective.explanation: A budget action can run automatically or wait for approval; in approval mode it stays pending until someone approves it. Budget actions can apply IAM policies and SCPs or target EC2 and RDS instances, and they do not need root.

objective.question: A learner created a new AWS account in 2026 and chose the free account plan. What happens when the plan's credits are used up or the plan period ends?
options: All resources keep running for free for another 12 months
Only the root user can keep using the account
The account is closed unless the learner upgrades to a paid plan; the free plan itself does not charge them
AWS automatically switches to on-demand billing and charges the card
objective.explanation: Under the free account plan, usage is covered by credits, and when the credits or plan period run out, the account is closed unless you upgrade to the paid plan. AWS does not silently move you to paid billing on the free plan.

objective.question: An administrator is enabling IAM Identity Center for the first time. Which order is correct?
options: Enable Identity Center, choose the identity source, create users and groups, create permission sets, assign groups and permission sets to accounts, users sign in through the access portal
Assign accounts to users, enable Identity Center, create a root access key for the portal
Create IAM users in every account, then enable Identity Center to link them
Create permission sets, enable Identity Center, assign users, choose the identity source
objective.explanation: You must enable the service and choose where identities live before creating users, then define permission sets and assign them to accounts. Identity Center does not link existing IAM users, and it never needs root access keys.

objective.question: A newly created IAM admin user tries to sign in on the AWS sign-in page by choosing 'Root user' and typing her user name. Sign-in fails. What should she do?
options: Choose IAM user sign-in and enter the account ID or alias, or open the account-specific sign-in URL, then enter her IAM user name and password
Reset the root user's MFA device
Wait for the IAM user to replicate to all Regions
Ask for the root password instead
objective.explanation: Root sign-in uses the account email address; IAM users sign in with the account ID or alias plus their user name. IAM is global, so there is no replication wait.

objective.question: In a member account, an admin sees a role named 'AWSReservedSSO_DeveloperAccess_…' and wants to add S3 read access for all developers. What is the right way to do it?
options: Update the DeveloperAccess permission set in IAM Identity Center so the change is provisioned to every assigned account
Attach the policy to the root user of the member account
Create an IAM user per developer with S3 read access
Edit the AWSReservedSSO role in IAM directly in each account
objective.explanation: Identity Center creates and manages these roles from the permission set; you change the permission set and it reprovisions the roles. Direct edits to the reserved roles are not supported and can be overwritten, and IAM users or root are the wrong tools.

objective.question: A design document says: 'Create one subnet that spans ap-south-1a and ap-south-1b, and put both web servers in it for high availability.' What is the mistake?
options: A subnet lives in exactly one Availability Zone; create a subnet in each AZ and place one server in each
Web servers cannot run in ap-south-1b
High availability requires two Regions, not two AZs
Subnets must span all AZs in the Region
objective.explanation: A VPC spans a Region, but each subnet belongs to a single AZ. Spreading servers across subnets in two AZs is the standard way to survive one AZ failing.

objective.question: A gaming company in India runs a multiplayer game server on UDP in ap-south-1. Players connect from many countries. They need static entry IP addresses and traffic routed over the AWS global network from the nearest edge location. Which service fits best?
options: An extra Availability Zone
AWS Budgets
AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon CloudFront
objective.explanation: Global Accelerator gives static anycast IPs and carries TCP and UDP traffic from edge locations over the AWS network to your Regional endpoints. CloudFront is mainly for caching and delivering HTTP(S) content, so it does not fit raw UDP game traffic.

objective.question: An admin gave a developer role broad permissions during setup. Now she wants to cut the role down to only the actions it actually used over the last 90 days. Which AWS feature helps most directly?
options: IAM Access Analyzer policy generation based on CloudTrail activity, together with last-accessed information
AWS Budgets actions
CloudFront access logs
AWS Pricing Calculator
objective.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from the actions recorded in CloudTrail, and last-accessed data shows unused services. This is the practical route to least privilege; the other tools are about cost or content delivery.

subjective.question: Why should you stop using the root user for daily work after setting up an AWS account?
subjective.answer: The root user has complete, unrestricted access to everything in the account, including billing, account closure and changing the root email. In a standalone account, no IAM policy can limit it. If its password or keys leak, an attacker owns the account with no guardrail. Daily work also creates more chances for the credentials to leak, for example on a shared laptop. So the practice is: secure root with a strong password and MFA, never create root access keys, and use root only for root-only tasks like closing the account or restoring IAM permissions. For daily work I use an IAM Identity Center user or an IAM admin user, and later move to least-privilege roles. This also gives clear CloudTrail records of who did what.
keyPoints: Root has unrestricted access and cannot be limited by IAM policies in a standalone account
Leaked root credentials mean full account takeover
Use root only for root-only tasks
Use Identity Center or IAM identities for daily work for accountability

subjective.question: List the steps you would take to secure the root user of a new AWS account.
subjective.answer: First, I set a long, unique password stored in a password manager. Second, I enable MFA on the root user, ideally a phishing-resistant FIDO security key, with a backup device registered. Third, I check that no root access keys exist; if any do, I delete them. Fourth, I make sure the root email address is a monitored mailbox, ideally a group alias rather than one person's inbox, and that the phone number and alternate contacts for billing, operations and security are correct. Fifth, I create an admin identity for daily work and sign out of root. Finally, I note the root-only tasks so root is used only for those. In an Organization, I would also add SCPs to limit root in member accounts.
keyPoints: Strong unique password and MFA, with a backup MFA device
No root access keys
Secure, monitored root email and correct contact details
Create a daily admin identity and stop using root
Use SCPs for member accounts in an Organization

subjective.question: Compare IAM Identity Center and IAM users for human access. When would you pick each?
subjective.answer: IAM users are identities inside one account with long-term credentials: a password and optional access keys. They are simple for a single learning account but do not scale, because each account needs its own users, and long-term keys are a leak risk. IAM Identity Center is the recommended way for people to access AWS. It is enabled in one home Region, works with AWS Organizations, and gives one sign-in portal across many accounts. Access is defined with permission sets, and users get temporary credentials for the console and CLI. It can use its own directory or connect to an external identity provider like Microsoft Entra ID or Okta. I would pick Identity Center for any team or multi-account setup, and an IAM user only for a quick solo lab or a case where Identity Center is not possible.
keyPoints: IAM users have long-term credentials in a single account
Identity Center gives central sign-in and temporary credentials
Identity Center uses permission sets and works with AWS Organizations
Identity Center can connect to external identity providers
Prefer Identity Center for teams and multi-account setups

subjective.question: Explain the principle of least privilege with a practical AWS example.
subjective.answer: Least privilege means giving an identity only the permissions it needs for its task, and nothing more. This limits damage if credentials leak or someone makes a mistake. For example, a developer who only uploads files to one S3 bucket should get a policy allowing s3:PutObject and s3:GetObject on that bucket's ARN, not AmazonS3FullAccess and certainly not AdministratorAccess. In practice, I start with AWS managed policies while learning, then tighten them. Tools like IAM Access Analyzer can generate policies from CloudTrail activity and show unused permissions, and last-accessed information helps remove permissions nobody uses. I also prefer roles with temporary credentials over long-term access keys. On day one an admin user is fine for a personal lab, but it should not be the long-term pattern in a team.
keyPoints: Grant only the permissions needed for the task
Scope actions and resources tightly, for example one bucket ARN
Refine broad managed policies over time
Use Access Analyzer and last-accessed data to remove unused permissions
Prefer roles and temporary credentials

subjective.question: Walk through how you would set up a USD 5 budget alert for a learning account, and which thresholds you would choose.
subjective.answer: I open Billing and Cost Management, go to Budgets and create a cost budget with a monthly period and a fixed amount of USD 5. I then add more than one alert threshold. For example, one actual cost alert at 50 percent so I hear early, one actual alert at 100 percent, and one forecasted alert at 100 percent so I get warned if the month is trending over USD 5. I add my email as a subscriber and, if I want automation, an SNS topic. I also turn on Free Tier usage alerts in billing preferences. Because budgets are evaluated only a few times a day, I keep the thresholds low. After saving, I check that the budget appears and the notification emails are confirmed.
keyPoints: Create a monthly cost budget of USD 5
Use several thresholds, both actual and forecasted
Notify by email and optionally SNS
Keep thresholds low because alerts are delayed
Also enable Free Tier usage alerts

subjective.question: A budget alert is not a hard spending limit. Explain why, and how you would protect yourself from a large surprise bill.
subjective.answer: AWS Budgets watches costs and notifies you; by default it does not stop resources. Billing data is also not real time, and budgets are evaluated only a few times a day, so an alert can arrive hours after the spend. An expensive resource can keep running in that gap. To protect myself, I set low thresholds and a forecasted alert so I am warned early. I can configure budget actions, for example applying a restrictive IAM policy or SCP or stopping specific EC2 or RDS instances when a threshold is crossed. I also delete lab resources right after use, check Cost Explorer and the Billing dashboard regularly, stick to Free Tier eligible sizes, and use least-privilege identities so nobody can launch large resources by accident.
keyPoints: Budgets notify; they do not stop spend by default
Billing data and budget evaluation are delayed
Use low and forecasted thresholds
Budget actions can apply policies or stop some resources
Clean up lab resources and check costs regularly

subjective.question: What four factors do you consider when choosing an AWS Region? Apply them to an app for users mainly in India.
subjective.answer: The four factors are compliance and data residency, latency to users, service availability, and price. Compliance comes first because it is a hard rule. If Indian regulation or a customer contract needs data to stay in India, I must pick an Indian Region: Asia Pacific (Mumbai), ap-south-1, or Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), ap-south-2. Next is latency. Users in India get the lowest latency from an Indian Region. Third, I check that every service I need is available in that Region, because new services and features do not launch everywhere at once. Mumbai is older and usually has wider service coverage. Last, I compare prices, since they vary by Region. If no residency rule exists, I could weigh a cheaper Region, but latency for Indian users would usually make Mumbai or Hyderabad the right choice.
keyPoints: Compliance and data residency first, as a hard constraint
Latency to end users
Service and feature availability differs by Region
Price differs by Region
Mumbai (ap-south-1) and Hyderabad (ap-south-2) for Indian users

subjective.question: Explain the difference between a Region, an Availability Zone and an edge location.
subjective.answer: A Region is a separate geographic area, such as ap-south-1 in Mumbai. Regions are isolated from each other, and you choose where your resources and data live. Each Region has multiple Availability Zones. An AZ is one or more discrete data centres with its own power, cooling and networking, physically separated from other AZs but linked by low-latency networks. New Regions launch with at least three AZs. You spread resources across AZs for high availability, so one AZ failure does not take down your app. Edge locations are a separate, much larger set of sites in many cities. They do not host your EC2 instances; they are used by services like CloudFront for caching, Route 53 for DNS, and Global Accelerator to bring traffic closer to users and cut latency.
keyPoints: Region is an isolated geographic area you choose for resources
AZs are isolated data centre groups inside a Region
Multi-AZ design gives high availability
Edge locations serve CloudFront, Route 53 and Global Accelerator
Edge locations are more numerous and closer to users

subjective.question: What is the difference between an AZ name and an AZ ID, and why does it matter?
subjective.answer: An AZ name looks like ap-south-1a. AWS maps these names to physical zones independently for each account, so ap-south-1a in my account may be a different physical zone from ap-south-1a in yours. This spreads load across zones. An AZ ID looks like aps1-az1 and always refers to the same physical zone in every account. It matters when work involves more than one account. For example, if a shared service runs in one account and consumers run in another, using the same AZ ID keeps traffic in one physical zone, which reduces latency and cross-AZ data transfer cost. It also matters for resilience planning, when you want to be sure two accounts are really in different zones. You can see AZ IDs in the EC2 console or with the describe-availability-zones API.
keyPoints: AZ names are mapped per account
AZ IDs are consistent across accounts
Use AZ IDs when coordinating between accounts
Affects latency, data transfer cost and resilience planning

subjective.question: Apply the shared responsibility model to the setup tasks in this week. What does AWS handle and what do you handle?
subjective.answer: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: the physical data centres, hardware, the network between Regions and AZs, and the software that runs services like IAM itself. I am responsible for security in the cloud. For this week's setup, that means everything about my account's identities and configuration. I must enable MFA on the root user, keep the root email secure, and avoid root access keys. I must create a non-root identity for daily work and give it sensible permissions. I must set up budgets to watch my own spending. I must choose a Region that meets my data rules. If my root password leaks because I reused it, that is my failure, not AWS's. AWS gives the tools, like MFA, IAM and Budgets, but I must turn them on and use them correctly.
keyPoints: AWS secures facilities, hardware and global infrastructure
Customer secures identities, MFA, data and configuration
Root security and IAM setup are the customer's job
AWS provides tools; the customer must configure them

subjective.question: Your finance colleague has an IAM user but cannot see the bill. Explain what needs to change and why.
subjective.answer: By default, billing pages are restricted. Even an IAM user with full permissions cannot see them until the root user enables 'IAM user and role access to Billing information' in the Account settings. This is a root-only task. It exists so the account owner decides whether anyone besides root can see costs. After root enables it, the IAM identity still needs IAM permissions for billing, for example the AWS managed Billing job-function policy for full billing work, or a read-only policy if the colleague should only view. Following least privilege, a finance person who only reviews costs should get read-only billing and Cost Explorer access, not admin. In a multi-account setup, it is usually better to give finance access through IAM Identity Center with a billing permission set in the management account.
keyPoints: Root must enable IAM user and role access to Billing information
This is a root-only task
IAM permissions for billing are still required
Give read-only billing access where possible
Use an Identity Center permission set in multi-account setups

subjective.question: Can you restrict what the root user does? Explain for a standalone account and for an account in AWS Organizations.
subjective.answer: In a standalone account, no. IAM policies, permissions boundaries and roles cannot be attached to the root user, so it always has full access. The only protection is to secure it well with MFA, no access keys, a secure email, and rare use. In AWS Organizations it is different for member accounts. Service control policies set the maximum permissions for every principal in a member account, and that includes the member account's root user. For example, an SCP can deny deleting CloudTrail trails or leaving the Organization, and even root in that member account cannot do it. SCPs do not affect the management account, so the management account's root must be guarded very carefully. AWS also offers centralized root access management for member accounts, so organizations can remove root credentials from member accounts.
keyPoints: IAM policies cannot restrict root in a standalone account
SCPs limit all principals in member accounts, including root
SCPs do not apply to the management account
Secure the management account root with extra care
Central root access management can remove member root credentials

subjective.question: What are common ways learners get unexpected bills while on the AWS Free Tier, and how do you avoid them?
subjective.answer: The Free Tier covers only certain services, sizes and usage amounts, and some offers have time limits. Common mistakes are launching an instance type that is not Free Tier eligible, leaving resources running after a lab, and forgetting things that bill on their own, like NAT gateways, Elastic IP addresses not attached to a running instance, EBS volumes and snapshots left after deleting an instance, or load balancers. Another mistake is launching resources in a Region you do not normally check, then forgetting them. To avoid this, I read the Free Tier details for each service before using it, set a low budget with actual and forecasted alerts, turn on Free Tier usage alerts, tag lab resources, and delete everything after each lab. I also check the Billing dashboard and Cost Explorer weekly, filtering by service and Region.
keyPoints: Free Tier covers specific services, sizes and limits only
Non-eligible instance types and leftover resources cause charges
Watch NAT gateways, unused Elastic IPs, EBS and snapshots
Check all Regions for forgotten resources
Use budgets, Free Tier alerts and cleanup after labs

subjective.question: You get an email saying your root password was changed, but you did not do it. What do you do?
subjective.answer: I treat it as a security incident and act fast. First, I try to sign in as root and reset the password using the root email. If I cannot, I contact AWS Support through the account recovery process. Once I am back in, I change the root password, check and re-register MFA devices, and delete any root access keys. I verify the root email, phone number and alternate contacts have not been changed. Then I review IAM for new users, roles, access keys or policies I did not create, and remove them. I use CloudTrail and the Billing dashboard to look for unknown activity, especially new EC2 instances in unusual Regions. I rotate credentials for all IAM users. Finally, I fix the cause, for example password reuse, and confirm MFA is in place.
keyPoints: Regain root access and reset the password, using AWS Support if needed
Check MFA, delete root access keys, verify contact details
Remove unknown IAM users, keys and roles
Review CloudTrail and billing for unauthorized resources in all Regions
Rotate credentials and fix the root cause

subjective.question: Design a safe starting setup for a small team of five developers who are new to AWS and will soon need separate dev and prod accounts.
subjective.answer: I would create the first account as the management account and enable AWS Organizations. I secure its root user with MFA, no access keys and a group email, and never use it for workloads. I create separate member accounts for dev and prod so mistakes in dev cannot touch prod. I enable IAM Identity Center in a chosen home Region, for example ap-south-1, create a group for developers, and assign permission sets: wider access in dev, read-only or limited deploy access in prod. Everyone signs in through the access portal with MFA and temporary credentials, so there are no IAM users with long-term keys. I add SCPs to block risky actions like disabling CloudTrail or using unapproved Regions. I set budgets per account with actual and forecasted alerts to a team email and SNS. Finally, I turn on CloudTrail across the organization.
keyPoints: Organizations with a protected management account
Separate dev and prod member accounts
IAM Identity Center with groups and permission sets, MFA and temporary credentials
SCPs as guardrails, including Region restrictions
Budgets per account and organization-wide CloudTrail

subjective.question: Explain what this policy does, why it uses BoolIfExists instead of Bool, and what a new user experiences on first sign-in.
subjective.answer: This statement forces MFA. It denies every action except the few needed to register an MFA device whenever the request was not authenticated with MFA. A new user can sign in with a password, but almost everything shows access denied. They can only create and enable their MFA device. After they sign out and sign in again with MFA, the condition no longer matches, and their normal Allow policies take effect. BoolIfExists matters because requests signed with long-term access keys do not include the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent key at all. With BoolIfExists, a missing key is treated as a match, so the Deny also blocks plain access-key calls without MFA. With Bool, a missing key would not match, and those calls would slip through. The user would need to call sts:GetSessionToken with an MFA code to use the CLI.
keyPoints: Denies all actions except MFA self-setup when MFA is absent
Normal Allow policies work only after an MFA sign-in
BoolIfExists catches requests where the key is missing, such as access-key calls
An explicit Deny overrides any Allow

subjective.question: Show how you configure the AWS CLI to use IAM Identity Center, and how you prove you are not using the root user or a long-term key.

code.code:
aws configure sso
# SSO session name: masterclass
# SSO start URL: https://d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start
# SSO region: ap-south-1
# choose account and permission set, profile name: dev

aws sso login --profile dev
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile dev

subjective.answer: I run 'aws configure sso' and enter the session name, the AWS access portal start URL and the Region where Identity Center is enabled. The CLI opens a browser, I sign in with my Identity Center user and MFA, and I pick the account and permission set. The CLI saves this as a named profile in ~/.aws/config. No secret key is written to ~/.aws/credentials. Each day I run 'aws sso login --profile dev' to get fresh short-lived credentials. To check who I am, I run 'aws sts get-caller-identity'. The ARN should look like 'arn:aws:sts::<account>:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_<PermissionSet>_.../<myname>'. If it ended in ':root', I would be using root. If it showed ':user/...', I would be using an IAM user with long-term keys. Both of those mean something needs fixing.
keyPoints: aws configure sso creates a named profile with no stored secret keys
aws sso login refreshes short-lived credentials
get-caller-identity shows the identity actually in use
An assumed-role AWSReservedSSO ARN confirms Identity Center access

subjective.question: What are AWS Budgets actions? Describe when you would use one instead of a plain alert, and what risks you must plan for.
subjective.answer: A Budgets action is an automatic response that runs when a budget threshold is crossed. It can apply an IAM policy, apply a service control policy in AWS Organizations, or stop selected EC2 or RDS instances. You can let it run automatically or require approval first. I use an action when a human reply to an email would be too slow or unreliable. A good example is a sandbox or training account where students forget to stop instances. At 100% of budget, an action could stop the instances, or attach a policy that denies launching new resources. The risks are real. Actions can stop workloads someone still needs, so I never point them at production without approval. Budget data refreshes a few times a day, so actions react late. Stopping instances does not stop costs from EBS volumes, snapshots or Elastic IPs. Budgets also needs an execution role with the right permissions.
keyPoints: Actions apply IAM policies or SCPs, or stop EC2/RDS instances
Use them where human response is too slow, such as sandbox or training accounts
Can run automatically or after approval
Budget data is delayed, and storage costs continue after instances stop

subjective.question: A user has AdministratorAccess through one group and a second policy that denies s3:DeleteBucket. Explain step by step how IAM decides whether a DeleteBucket request is allowed.
subjective.answer: IAM starts from an implicit deny: nothing is allowed unless something allows it. It then gathers every policy that applies to the request. For a single account, that means identity-based policies, resource-based policies, any permissions boundary and, in Organizations, SCPs. Step one: if any applicable policy has an explicit Deny that matches the action and resource, the request is denied immediately. Here the second policy denies s3:DeleteBucket, so evaluation stops and the request fails. AdministratorAccess does not matter. Step two applies only when there is no explicit deny. Then there must be an Allow, and guardrails such as SCPs and boundaries must also permit the action. Otherwise the implicit deny stays in place. In practice, this means you can give broad admin rights and still protect critical actions with targeted Deny statements. The deny cannot be overridden by adding more Allows.
keyPoints: Default is implicit deny
An explicit Deny anywhere overrides all Allows
An Allow is needed, and SCPs and boundaries must also permit the action
Targeted Deny statements protect critical actions even for admins

subjective.question: Using IAM Identity Center, design permission sets for a small company with developers, one finance person and one cloud admin across dev and prod accounts.
subjective.answer: I create groups in Identity Center, not individual assignments: Developers, Finance and CloudAdmins. I then create permission sets and assign each group to the accounts it needs. Developers get a PowerUserAccess-style permission set in the dev account, so they can build freely without managing IAM. In prod they get only ReadOnlyAccess, and deployments go through a pipeline. Finance gets a billing permission set based on the Billing job-function policy, assigned to the management account, so they see costs across the organization. IAM access to billing must be activated for this to work. CloudAdmins get AdministratorAccess in all accounts, with a short session duration, and they use it only when needed. I enforce MFA for everyone in Identity Center. I keep root users unused, with MFA set, and I review assignments every quarter. Each permission set grants the smallest access that still lets the person do their job.
keyPoints: Assign permission sets to groups, not to individuals
Different access per account: broad in dev, read-only in prod
Finance gets billing access, and IAM access to billing must be enabled
MFA enforced, short sessions for admin, regular reviews

subjective.question: A colleague says, 'I deployed in Hyderabad but my EC2 instances from Mumbai are not showing, and the Hyderabad Region was missing at first.' Explain both issues.
subjective.answer: There are two separate issues. First, the console and CLI always work in one Region at a time. EC2 instances are regional resources, and each one sits in an Availability Zone. Instances in ap-south-1 (Mumbai) do not appear when the Region selector is set to ap-south-2 (Hyderabad). You switch Regions, or use a tool that looks across Regions, such as Resource Explorer or Cost Explorer. Only a few services, such as IAM, are global. Second, Hyderabad was missing because it is an opt-in Region. Regions launched after March 2019 are disabled by default. Someone with the right permissions must enable it in Account settings, and enabling can take some time. Opt-in is a safety and compliance feature, because it stops people from using Regions you did not approve. For a learner, it is also a reminder: always check the Region before you look for resources or think something has been deleted.
keyPoints: Console and CLI views are per Region
EC2 is regional and zonal; IAM is global
ap-south-2 is an opt-in Region that must be enabled
Always check the Region selector before troubleshooting

subjective.question: Classify IAM, Amazon S3 buckets and EC2 instances as global, regional or zonal, and explain how this affects designing for an Availability Zone failure.
subjective.answer: IAM is global. Users, roles and policies apply in every Region, which is why the IAM console shows 'Global'. S3 buckets are regional. You choose a Region when you create the bucket, and S3 stores data redundantly across multiple AZs in that Region, so one AZ failure does not lose the data. EC2 instances and EBS volumes are zonal, because each lives in exactly one Availability Zone. If that AZ has a problem, the instance and its volume are affected. So for resilience, I run EC2 in an Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs behind a load balancer. I keep state in multi-AZ services, such as S3, RDS Multi-AZ or DynamoDB, and not on a single instance's disk. I do not need to copy IAM per Region. To survive a full Region failure, I would replicate data to a second Region, but that adds cost and must respect data-residency rules.
keyPoints: IAM is global, S3 is regional, EC2 and EBS are zonal
Zonal resources fail with their AZ
Spread compute across at least two AZs behind a load balancer
Keep state in multi-AZ services; going multi-Region has cost and compliance trade-offs

subjective.question: Why are long-term IAM access keys risky, and what would you use instead for a laptop, an EC2 application and a quick CLI task?
subjective.answer: Long-term access keys never expire unless you rotate or delete them. They often leak through Git commits, shared scripts or copied config files, and anyone who holds the key has its permissions until someone notices. Bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes, and crypto-mining bills are a common result. Instead, on a laptop I use IAM Identity Center with 'aws configure sso', which gives short-lived credentials after an MFA sign-in. For an application on EC2, I attach an IAM role through an instance profile. The instance gets rotating temporary credentials from the metadata service, and no key is stored on disk. For a quick CLI task, I use AWS CloudShell in the console. It runs with my signed-in identity and needs no keys. If a key is truly unavoidable, for example for a third-party tool, I give it least privilege, rotate it, watch its last-used date and never put it in code.
keyPoints: Long-term keys do not expire and leak easily
Laptop: Identity Center short-lived credentials
EC2: IAM role through an instance profile
Quick tasks: CloudShell; if a key is unavoidable, use least privilege and rotation

subjective.question: Compare AWS Budgets, AWS Cost Anomaly Detection and Free Tier usage alerts. How would you combine them for a learner's account?
subjective.answer: AWS Budgets lets me set a fixed amount, such as USD 5, and get alerts on actual or forecasted spend. I can also add actions. It is predictable but only as good as the threshold I choose. Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to learn my normal spending pattern. It alerts me on unusual spikes by service or account, with no fixed amount needed, so it catches problems a high budget would miss. Free Tier usage alerts, turned on in Billing preferences, warn me when I am close to the free limits of a service, before charges start. For a learner, I would use all three. I would set a USD 5 monthly cost budget with alerts at about 50% and 100% actual and 80% forecasted. I would create a cost monitor with daily or immediate alerts by email, and keep Free Tier alerts on. None of these is a hard cap, so I would still delete resources after every lab.
keyPoints: Budgets: fixed thresholds on actual or forecasted spend, optional actions
Cost Anomaly Detection: ML-based alerts on unusual spend
Free Tier alerts warn before free limits are passed
None is a hard cap, so clean up resources after each lab

subjective.question: Case study: A college gives 60 students AWS access for a cloud course. Requirements: no student uses a root user, each student's spend is capped at around USD 10, students cannot see each other's work, and labs must stay in Indian Regions. Design the setup.
subjective.answer: I would use AWS Organizations with one management account owned by the college IT team. Each student gets their own member account, so work and bills are separated. Students sign in through IAM Identity Center with a limited permission set, so nobody needs root, and root users in member accounts are never shared. For Regions, I would attach an SCP that denies actions outside ap-south-1 and ap-south-2, with exceptions for global services such as IAM. I would also use an SCP to deny large instance types. For cost, each account gets an AWS Budget at USD 10 with alerts at 50%, 80% and a forecasted alert.
