It offers static IPs per AZ, ultra-low latency and very high throughput. A Gateway Load Balancer inserts third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls. Set the ASG health check type to ELB so instances that fail the load balancer's health checks get replaced.

An Auto Scaling group launches instances from a launch template across multiple AZs and keeps capacity between min and max. Target tracking is the default choice, for example average CPU at 50%. Scheduled scaling suits known peaks, and predictive scaling suits recurring patterns. Purchase options to combine: On-Demand, Savings Plans/Reserved for steady baseline, and Spot for fault-tolerant, interruptible work.

The classes are Standard, Intelligent-Tiering (for unknown access patterns), Standard-IA, One Zone-IA (data you can re-create), Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle rules transition objects between classes or expire them, and IA and Glacier classes have minimum storage-duration charges. S3 is designed for 11 nines of durability.

EBS is block storage attached to an instance in a single AZ: gp3 for general use, io2 for high IOPS, st1/sc1 HDD for throughput or cold data. Instance store is ephemeral. EFS is managed NFS for Linux, mountable across AZs by many instances. FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB with Active Directory. FSx for Lustre is for HPC and ML and integrates with S3. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS also exist for those specific file systems.

concepts.term: RDS Multi-AZ vs read replicas vs Aurora
concepts.explanation: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ for automatic failover. It is for availability, not read scaling. Read replicas use asynchronous replication to scale reads and can be cross-Region for DR. Aurora stores 6 copies of data across 3 AZs, supports up to 15 low-latency replicas and offers Aurora Global Database for cross-Region DR. Aurora Serverless v2 suits variable load.

DynamoDB is a serverless key-value store with single-digit-millisecond latency. It offers on-demand or provisioned capacity, global tables for multi-Region active-active, DAX for microsecond read caching, and Streams for change events. ElastiCache (Redis OSS/Valkey or Memcached) caches database query results or session state to cut read load and latency. Redis/Valkey supports replication, persistence and Multi-AZ, and Memcached does not.

SQS is a pull-based queue. Standard queues give at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, and FIFO queues give ordering and exactly-once processing. SNS is push pub/sub; SNS-to-multiple-SQS is the fan-out pattern. EventBridge routes events by rules, including SaaS and scheduled events. Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows with retries. DR strategies in order of rising cost and falling RTO/RPO: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active.

keyFacts: SAA-C03: 65 questions (50 scored, 15 unscored), 130 minutes, USD 150, pass mark 720/1000.
Gateway VPC endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB and have no hourly charge. All other services use interface endpoints (PrivateLink).
Security groups are stateful and allow-only. NACLs are stateless, support allow and deny, and are evaluated lowest rule number first.
A NAT gateway is zonal and lives in a public subnet. Use one per AZ for HA. A NAT gateway cannot be used by resources outside its VPC through peering.
Lambda maximum timeout is 15 minutes. For longer or multi-step jobs, use Step Functions, ECS/Fargate or Batch.
SQS default visibility timeout is 30 seconds (max 12 hours). Message retention defaults to 4 days (max 14 days). Use a dead-letter queue for poison messages.
S3 minimum storage durations: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA 30 days, Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval 90 days, Deep Archive 180 days.
RDS Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication (HA). Read replicas use asynchronous replication (read scaling and cross-Region DR). Aurora keeps 6 copies across 3 AZs and supports up to 15 replicas.
DynamoDB maximum item size is 400 KB. Store large objects in S3 and keep a pointer in DynamoDB.
Decision rule: 'least operational overhead' usually points to a managed or serverless option (Fargate, Lambda, Aurora Serverless, DynamoDB) over self-managed EC2.

example.caption: Hands-on: three-tier app (ALB → Auto Scaling EC2 → RDS Multi-AZ) with AWS CLI, then teardown. Assumes a VPC with 2 public and 2 private subnets, NAT gateways and security groups already exist.
example.code:
# Data tier: Multi-AZ RDS in private subnets
aws rds create-db-subnet-group --db-subnet-group-name app-db --db-subnet-group-description private --subnet-ids $PRIV_A $PRIV_B
aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier app-db --engine mysql --db-instance-class db.t3.micro --allocated-storage 20 --master-username admin --manage-master-user-password --multi-az --db-subnet-group-name app-db --vpc-security-group-ids $DB_SG --no-publicly-accessible

# Web tier: ALB in public subnets
ALB_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name app-alb --subnets $PUB_A $PUB_B --security-groups $ALB_SG --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)
TG_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-target-group --name app-tg --protocol HTTP --port 80 --vpc-id $VPC --health-check-path /health --query 'TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn' --output text)
aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN --protocol HTTP --port 80 --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$TG_ARN

# App tier: Auto Scaling group in private subnets
aws ec2 create-launch-template --launch-template-name app-lt --launch-template-data "{\"ImageId\":\"$AMI\",\"InstanceType\":\"t3.micro\",\"SecurityGroupIds\":[\"$APP_SG\"],\"UserData\":\"$USERDATA_B64\"}"
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name app-asg --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=app-lt --min-size 2 --max-size 4 --desired-capacity 2 --vpc-zone-identifier "$PRIV_A,$PRIV_B" --target-group-arns $TG_ARN --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 300
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name app-asg --policy-name cpu50 --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling --target-tracking-configuration '{"PredefinedMetricSpecification":{"PredefinedMetricType":"ASGAverageCPUUtilization"},"TargetValue":50}'

# Teardown (reverse order) - stop all billing
aws autoscaling delete-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name app-asg --force-delete
aws elbv2 delete-load-balancer --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN
sleep 60; aws elbv2 delete-target-group --target-group-arn $TG_ARN
aws ec2 delete-launch-template --launch-template-name app-lt
aws rds delete-db-instance --db-instance-identifier app-db --skip-final-snapshot
aws ec2 delete-nat-gateway --nat-gateway-id $NAT_A   # then release its Elastic IP

pitfalls: Confusing RDS Multi-AZ with read replicas. The Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads, so 'scale reads' means read replicas or Aurora replicas.
Choosing a NAT gateway for private S3 or DynamoDB access. A gateway endpoint is cheaper and keeps traffic on the AWS network.
Forgetting that NACLs are stateless. Blocked ephemeral return ports (1024-65535) break connections that the security groups allow.
Picking SNS when messages must be buffered and processed later, or SQS when many subscribers each need a copy. Use SNS fan-out to multiple SQS queues when you need both.
Leaving NAT gateways, Elastic IPs, RDS instances or final snapshots running after the lab. These keep billing even when idle. Check AWS Cost Explorer the next day.
Over-engineering. When a question asks for lowest cost and the RTO is hours, backup and restore beats warm standby or multi-site.

workflow.title: How a request flows through the three-tier lab, and how to build it

steps.label: Design VPC across two AZs
steps.detail: Create public subnets for the ALB and NAT gateways, and private subnets for EC2 and RDS, each with the correct route table.

steps.label: Chain security groups by tier
steps.detail: Allow 80/443 from the internet to the ALB SG, the app port from the ALB SG to the app SG, and 3306 from the app SG to the DB SG.

steps.label: Launch RDS Multi-AZ privately
steps.detail: Place the database in a private DB subnet group with Multi-AZ enabled, and store credentials in Secrets Manager.

steps.label: Create ALB and target group
steps.detail: The internet-facing ALB receives the request and forwards it to healthy targets based on the /health check.

steps.label: Attach Auto Scaling group
steps.detail: The launch template and ASG spread instances across private subnets, use ELB health checks, and scale on target-tracking CPU.

steps.label: Test failover and scaling
steps.detail: Reboot RDS with failover, terminate an instance, and load-test to confirm the app stays available.

steps.label: Tear down in reverse
steps.detail: Delete the ASG, ALB, target group, RDS, NAT gateways and Elastic IPs, then confirm zero spend in billing.

project.title: three-tier-alb-asg-rds
project.summary: Terraform builds a three-tier app in ap-south-1: an internet-facing ALB in public subnets, an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances in private app subnets, and a Multi-AZ RDS PostgreSQL database in isolated DB subnets, all torn down with one command. main.tf holds the provider, variables and outputs; network.tf covers subnets, route tables, the NAT gateway and the S3 endpoint; security.tf shows chained security groups and a stateless NACL; compute.tf covers the ALB and Auto Scaling; database.tf covers RDS Multi-AZ; app/user_data.sh is the app tier code.
project.run:
cd infra
terraform init
terraform apply -auto-approve
curl http://$(terraform output -raw alb_dns_name)/
terraform destroy -auto-approve

files.code:
# three-tier-alb-asg-rds (SAA-C03 hands-on)

Internet -> ALB (public subnets, 2 AZs) -> EC2 Auto Scaling group (private app subnets)
-> RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ (private DB subnets, no internet route).

## Prerequisites
- Terraform 1.6 or later. AWS CLI credentials for a sandbox account.
- Default region is ap-south-1 (Mumbai). To change it: `-var region=...`.

## Run
```
cd infra
terraform init
terraform apply -auto-approve      # RDS Multi-AZ takes about 10-15 min
curl http://$(terraform output -raw alb_dns_name)/
```
Repeat the curl a few times. The `host` value changes because the ALB spreads requests across instances.
`db_reachable: true` proves the app SG -> DB SG chain works.

## Try these (exam scenarios)
- Terminate one EC2 instance. The ASG replaces it, and ELB health checks stop routing to it.
- Reboot the DB with failover: `aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier three-tier-db --force-failover`.
  The endpoint DNS name stays the same. Only the IP behind it moves to the standby.

## What each file teaches
| File | Exam topic |
|---|---|
| network.tf | Public vs private subnets, route tables, NAT gateway, S3 gateway endpoint |
| security.tf | Security groups (stateful) vs NACLs (stateless, need ephemeral ports) |
| compute.tf | ALB, target group health checks, launch template, target tracking scaling |
| database.tf | RDS Multi-AZ (HA standby) - not a read replica (that is for read scaling) |

## Cost and teardown
The NAT gateway, the ALB and RDS Multi-AZ are all billed by the hour. Destroy the stack the same day:
```
terraform destroy -auto-approve
```
This lab uses a single NAT gateway to save cost. In production, use one NAT gateway per AZ for high availability.

# A DB subnet group needs subnets in at least two AZs (required for Multi-AZ)
resource "aws_db_subnet_group" "main" {
  name       = "${var.project}-db-subnets"
  subnet_ids = aws_subnet.db[*].id
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  identifier     = "${var.project}-db"
  engine         = "postgres"
  engine_version = "16" # major version; RDS picks the current default minor version
  instance_class = "db.t4g.micro"

  allocated_storage = 20
  storage_type      = "gp3"
  storage_encrypted = true

  db_name                     = "appdb"
  username                    = "appadmin"
  manage_master_user_password = true # RDS creates and rotates the password in Secrets Manager

  # Multi-AZ = a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover.
  # It is for high availability, not read scaling (use read replicas or Aurora for that).
  multi_az = true

  db_subnet_group_name   = aws_db_subnet_group.main.name
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.db.id]
  publicly_accessible    = false

  backup_retention_period = 1 # automated backups enable point-in-time restore (the backup-and-restore DR strategy)

  # Lab-only settings so that terraform destroy finishes cleanly
  skip_final_snapshot = true
  deletion_protection = false
  apply_immediately   = true
}

#!/bin/bash
# Rendered by Terraform templatefile(): db_host and app_port are filled in at launch.
set -euo pipefail
mkdir -p /opt/app

cat > /opt/app/app.py <<'PYEOF'
import json, os, socket
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

DB_HOST = os.environ["DB_HOST"]
DB_PORT = 5432
APP_PORT = int(os.environ["APP_PORT"])

def db_reachable():
    # TCP check proves the route table, NACL and SG chain from app to DB
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((DB_HOST, DB_PORT), timeout=2):
            return True
    except OSError:
        return False

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path == "/health":
            body = {"status": "ok"}  # ALB health check; kept independent of the DB
        else:
            body = {"host": socket.gethostname(), "db_host": DB_HOST,
                    "db_reachable": db_reachable()}
        data = json.dumps(body).encode()
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", APP_PORT), Handler).serve_forever()
PYEOF

cat > /etc/systemd/system/app.service <<SVCEOF
[Unit]
Description=Three-tier demo app
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Environment=DB_HOST=${db_host}
Environment=APP_PORT=${app_port}
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/app/app.py
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
SVCEOF

systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now app.service # starts now and restarts on reboot

revision.examFocus: This step maps to all four SAA-C03 domains: Design Secure Architectures (30%), Design Resilient Architectures (26%), Design High-Performing Architectures (24%) and Design Cost-Optimized Architectures (20%). Most questions are scenarios with two plausible answers. The winner is decided by one qualifier such as 'least operational overhead', 'most cost-effective', 'without traffic over the internet' or a stated RTO/RPO. Read the last sentence of the question first, then match the requirement to the service.

compare.difference: ALB works at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) with path, host and header routing, and integrates with AWS WAF. NLB works at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS), gives very low latency, and can have a static IP or Elastic IP per AZ.
compare.chooseA: Pick ALB for web apps, microservices routed by URL path or hostname, Lambda targets, or when WAF protection is required.
compare.chooseB: Pick NLB when the question needs static or whitelisted IPs, non-HTTP protocols, millions of requests per second, or a PrivateLink endpoint service in front of your app.

compare.difference: A gateway endpoint is a route-table target and works only for S3 and DynamoDB, with no hourly fee. An interface endpoint is an ENI with a private IP in your subnet, has hourly and data charges, and can be reached from on-premises over VPN or Direct Connect.
compare.chooseA: Pick gateway when EC2 in a private subnet in the same VPC needs S3 or DynamoDB access at lowest cost.
compare.chooseB: Pick interface for any other AWS service (SQS, Secrets Manager, KMS, ECR and so on), or when on-premises clients must reach S3 privately through a private IP.

compare.b: Amazon FSx (for Windows File Server / for Lustre)
compare.difference: EFS is a managed NFS file system for Linux that scales automatically and can be mounted across AZs. FSx for Windows gives SMB with Active Directory integration. FSx for Lustre gives high-performance parallel storage for HPC and ML and can link to S3.
compare.chooseA: Pick EFS when many Linux EC2 instances, containers or Lambda functions need a shared POSIX file system.
compare.chooseB: Pick FSx for Windows for Windows apps, SMB or AD-based permissions. Pick FSx for Lustre for HPC, ML training or 'process S3 data at high throughput'.

compare.difference: Pilot light keeps only core data replicated (for example, the database) with compute switched off or not created. Warm standby runs a smaller but fully working copy of the whole stack that can take traffic at once and then scale up.
compare.chooseA: Pick pilot light when RTO is tens of minutes and cost must stay low but faster than backup and restore.
compare.chooseB: Pick warm standby when RTO is minutes and the business accepts paying for always-on scaled-down capacity. Pick multi-site active/active only when near-zero RTO is demanded.

compare.difference: EventBridge routes events with content-based rules and receives events from AWS services, SaaS partners and schedules. SNS is a simple, high-throughput pub/sub push to subscribers, with optional filter policies.
compare.chooseA: Pick EventBridge for reacting to AWS service events, scheduled jobs, SaaS integration, or rich routing to many target types.
compare.chooseB: Pick SNS for fan-out to SQS queues, email, SMS or mobile push, and for 'notify many subscribers at once'.

cues.cue: Process each message exactly once, in order
cues.pick: SQS FIFO queue (with message group IDs)
cues.why: Standard queues give at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering. Only FIFO guarantees order and deduplication.

cues.cue: Unknown or changing access pattern for S3 objects
cues.pick: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
cues.why: It moves objects between tiers automatically with no retrieval fees, so you do not need to guess lifecycle rules.

cues.cue: Microsecond read latency on DynamoDB with no code rewrite
cues.pick: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
cues.why: DAX is an API-compatible in-memory cache for DynamoDB. ElastiCache needs application caching logic.

cues.cue: Store session state so any instance behind the load balancer can serve the user
cues.pick: ElastiCache (Redis OSS/Valkey) or DynamoDB
cues.why: External session storage makes EC2 stateless, so Auto Scaling can add or remove instances freely. Sticky sessions are the weaker answer.

cues.cue: Cross-Region database DR with RPO of about a second and fast failover
cues.pick: Aurora Global Database
cues.why: It uses storage-level replication to secondary Regions and allows promotion within about a minute. That beats a manual cross-Region read replica setup.

cues.cue: Fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work at lowest cost
cues.pick: EC2 Spot Instances (often in a mixed-instances Auto Scaling group or AWS Batch)
cues.why: Spot gives the deepest discount. A 2-minute interruption notice is acceptable when jobs can retry.

cues.cue: Scale workers based on how much work is waiting
cues.pick: Auto Scaling target tracking on SQS backlog per instance
cues.why: Queue depth divided by running instances reflects real load better than CPU for queue consumers.

cues.cue: Restrict S3 bucket access to traffic from one VPC only
cues.pick: Bucket policy with aws:SourceVpce (or aws:SourceVpc) condition plus a gateway endpoint
cues.why: The endpoint keeps traffic private, and the bucket policy enforces that no other path is allowed.

scenario.situation: An e-commerce company runs a web tier on EC2 behind an ALB. The web tier calls an order-processing tier on EC2 directly over HTTP. During sale events the processing tier is overwhelmed, requests time out and orders are lost. The company wants orders to be stored durably and processed even during spikes, with the least operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?
reasoning: Identify the real problem: tight coupling. The producer depends on the consumer being available and fast, so the fix is a buffer between the tiers.
Eliminate 'use larger instances for the processing tier'. It does not remove coupling and still fails on a big enough spike.
Eliminate SNS. It pushes messages and does not hold them for later processing, so a busy subscriber can still miss work unless a queue sits behind it.
Eliminate Kinesis Data Streams. It can buffer, but shard management and replay semantics add overhead the question does not need. Ordering and replay were not asked for.
Choose SQS standard: the web tier sends orders to the queue, processing instances poll it, a dead-letter queue catches poison messages, and an Auto Scaling group scales on backlog per instance.
scenario.answer: Put an Amazon SQS queue between the tiers and scale the processing Auto Scaling group on queue backlog. SQS durably buffers orders, is fully managed, and lets consumers process at their own pace.

memoryAids: DR ladder, cheapest to fastest: 'Back up, Pilot, Warm, Multi' (BPWM). Hours RTO goes left, seconds RTO goes right. Match the stated RTO/RPO, never one step more.
SG = 'Stateful Guard' (remembers the reply, allow only, attached to the instance). NACL = 'No Automatic Comeback Lane' (stateless, subnet level, numbered rules, first match wins).
Queue vs topic: 'SQS Stores, SNS Shouts.' Need both buffering and many copies? Shout into many stores (SNS → multiple SQS).
cheatSheet: Domain weights: Secure 30%, Resilient 26%, High-Performing 24%, Cost-Optimized 20%. Unscored questions are not marked, so treat every question seriously.
Public subnet means its route table has a route to an internet gateway. A private subnet reaches out only through a NAT gateway or endpoints.
To block one bad IP address, use a NACL deny rule. Security groups cannot deny.
ALB for HTTP routing and WAF. NLB for static IP, TCP/UDP and extreme performance. Gateway Load Balancer for third-party firewall appliances.
Need fixed anycast IPs or faster global TCP/UDP? Global Accelerator. Need cached static or dynamic content at the edge? CloudFront.
EBS is single-AZ block storage for one instance (io2 for highest IOPS, gp3 for tunable IOPS at low cost). Instance store is fastest but data is lost when the instance stops.
For shared Linux files, use EFS. For Windows/SMB/AD, use FSx for Windows. For HPC on S3 data, use FSx for Lustre.
Lifecycle tip: transition cold data to IA or Glacier tiers only when it will stay long enough. Otherwise minimum-duration charges cancel the savings.
Unpredictable relational load with minimal admin: Aurora Serverless v2. Key-value at any scale, serverless: DynamoDB (on-demand capacity for spiky traffic).
Long-running or multi-step workflow with retries and branching: Step Functions, not Lambda chaining.
Encryption at rest on an existing unencrypted RDS instance: snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption, restore from it.
Before you sit the exam, confirm the lab teardown: delete the ALB, Auto Scaling group, RDS (decide on the final snapshot), NAT gateway and Elastic IPs, then check Cost Explorer.
selfCheck: I can draw a VPC with public and private subnets in two AZs and explain every route-table entry, including the NAT gateway and gateway endpoint routes.
I can pick between Multi-AZ, read replicas, Aurora replicas and Aurora Global Database from a requirement for HA, read scaling or cross-Region DR.
I can choose the right decoupling service (SQS standard/FIFO, SNS, EventBridge, Step Functions, Kinesis) and justify it in one sentence.
I can map a given RTO/RPO and budget to backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby or multi-site without over-engineering.
I can choose the S3 storage class, EBS volume type or file system (EFS/FSx) from access pattern, OS and performance clues.
I have built and fully torn down the ALB → Auto Scaling EC2 → RDS Multi-AZ lab, and I score above 80% on two full practice exams with time left over.

objective.question: EC2 instances in a private subnet must read objects from an S3 bucket in the same Region. The subnet has no NAT gateway. The company wants the lowest-cost solution that keeps traffic off the internet. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Deploy a NAT gateway in a public subnet and route 0.0.0.0/0 to it
Attach an internet gateway and give the instances Elastic IP addresses
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and add it to the private subnet's route table
Create an interface VPC endpoint for S3 and update the security group
objective.explanation: Gateway endpoints exist for S3 and DynamoDB, use route table entries and have no hourly charge, so they are the cheapest private path. An interface endpoint works but costs per hour and per GB, and NAT or an internet gateway sends traffic toward the internet path at extra cost.

objective.question: A web server in a public subnet allows inbound TCP 443 in both its security group and the subnet's network ACL. The NACL outbound rules allow only TCP 443. Clients cannot complete HTTPS connections. What is the most likely cause?
options: The internet gateway must be attached to the subnet, not the VPC
NACL rules are evaluated highest number first, so the allow rule is ignored
The NACL is stateless and must allow outbound traffic to the client's ephemeral ports
Security groups block return traffic unless an outbound rule is added
objective.explanation: NACLs are stateless, so response traffic to client ephemeral ports (for example 1024-65535) needs an explicit outbound allow. Security groups are stateful, internet gateways attach to the VPC, and NACLs evaluate the lowest rule number first.

objective.question: A company runs private EC2 instances in three Availability Zones. All of them use a single NAT gateway in AZ-a for outbound internet access. The architect must remove this single point of failure. What should be done?
options: Replace the NAT gateway with a gateway VPC endpoint
Place the NAT gateway in a private subnet in each AZ
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each AZ and point each AZ's private route table to its local NAT gateway
Enable Multi-AZ on the existing NAT gateway
objective.explanation: A NAT gateway is zonal and must sit in a public subnet, so HA means one per AZ with per-AZ route tables; this also avoids cross-AZ data charges. There is no Multi-AZ setting for NAT gateways, and a gateway endpoint only reaches S3 or DynamoDB.

objective.question: A nightly job processes files and runs for about 40 minutes. It has several dependent steps and needs retries on failure. The team wants the least operational overhead. Which solution fits best?
options: Orchestrate the steps with AWS Step Functions, running long steps as Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate
Chain Lambda functions by having each one invoke the next synchronously
Run a cron job on a self-managed EC2 instance
Run the whole job in one AWS Lambda function with the timeout set to 60 minutes
objective.explanation: Lambda's maximum timeout is 15 minutes, so a 40-minute single function is not possible. Step Functions gives managed orchestration with retries, and Fargate runs long tasks without servers; self-managed EC2 adds overhead and chained Lambdas are fragile.

objective.question: Consumers of an Amazon SQS standard queue take about 2 minutes to process each message. The team sees the same message processed multiple times. The queue uses default settings. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the queue's visibility timeout to longer than the processing time
Reduce the delivery delay to 0 seconds
Switch to long polling
Increase the message retention period to 14 days
objective.explanation: The default visibility timeout is 30 seconds, so the message becomes visible again before processing finishes and another consumer picks it up. Retention, long polling and delivery delay do not control re-delivery during processing.

objective.question: A lifecycle rule moves objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days. Many objects are deleted 10 days after the transition. What will the company see on its bill?
options: A charge for the remaining days up to the 30-day minimum storage duration for Standard-IA
A charge for 90 days of storage
A retrieval fee for every deleted object
No storage charge after deletion
objective.explanation: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum storage duration, so early deletion is billed for the remaining days. The 90-day minimum applies to Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval, and deletion itself is not a retrieval.

objective.question: An RDS for MySQL database is overloaded by reporting queries. The primary must also survive an AZ failure with automatic failover. Which combination meets both needs?
options: Enable Multi-AZ for high availability and add one or more read replicas for the reporting queries
Add read replicas only, since they replicate synchronously
Take hourly snapshots and restore them for reporting
Enable Multi-AZ and send reporting queries to the Multi-AZ standby
objective.explanation: Multi-AZ (standard deployment with one standby) uses synchronous replication for failover, and that standby does not serve reads. Read replicas use asynchronous replication and offload reads; snapshots do not give live reporting or HA.

objective.question: Which statement about Amazon Aurora's storage and replicas is correct?
options: Aurora keeps 3 copies across 3 Regions and supports unlimited replicas
Aurora replicas must be in the same AZ as the writer
Aurora keeps 6 copies of data across 3 AZs and supports up to 15 Aurora Replicas
Aurora keeps 2 copies of data in one AZ and supports up to 5 replicas
objective.explanation: Aurora's shared cluster volume stores 6 copies across 3 AZs, and a cluster can have up to 15 Aurora Replicas that also act as failover targets. The other options give wrong numbers or wrong placement.

objective.question: An application stores user profiles in DynamoDB. A new feature attaches documents up to 5 MB to each profile. What is the recommended design?
options: Store documents in Amazon S3 and save the S3 object key in the DynamoDB item
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to raise the item size limit
Split each document across many DynamoDB items
Store the documents as binary attributes in the DynamoDB item
objective.explanation: DynamoDB's maximum item size is 400 KB, so large objects go to S3 with a pointer in DynamoDB. Splitting items adds complexity, and DAX is a cache that does not change item limits.

objective.question: An e-commerce site behind an ALB stores session state on each EC2 instance. Users are logged out when Auto Scaling removes instances. The company wants stateless web servers with fast session access. What should the architect use?
options: Store sessions in Amazon ElastiCache
Store sessions on an EBS volume attached to each instance
Store sessions in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
Enable sticky sessions on the ALB
objective.explanation: ElastiCache gives an external, in-memory session store so any instance can serve any user. Sticky sessions still lose state when an instance terminates, EBS is per instance, and Glacier is not designed for session data.

objective.question: Linux EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three AZs need a shared POSIX file system that grows automatically. Which service fits?
options: Amazon EFS
Amazon S3 mounted as a block device
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon EBS gp3 with Multi-Attach
objective.explanation: EFS is a managed NFS file system that many Linux instances across AZs can mount, and it scales automatically. EBS Multi-Attach works only within one AZ for specific volume types, FSx for Windows is SMB for Windows workloads, and S3 is object storage.

objective.question: A company needs a load balancer that routes /api/* to one target group and /images/* to another, based on the HTTP path. Which option should be used?
options: Application Load Balancer with path-based listener rules
Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer with TCP listeners
objective.explanation: ALB works at Layer 7 and supports path- and host-based routing rules. NLB is Layer 4 and cannot inspect paths, and Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting third-party virtual appliances.

objective.question: An Auto Scaling group should keep average CPU near 50% with the least manual tuning. Which scaling policy is best?
options: Target tracking scaling with a CPU target of 50%
Manually changing desired capacity
Scheduled scaling every hour
Simple scaling with a CloudWatch alarm at 80%
objective.explanation: Target tracking automatically creates and manages the alarms to hold a metric at the target value. Simple and scheduled scaling need more tuning and do not track the metric continuously.

objective.question: A company needs DR in a second Region with an RTO of minutes and accepts some running cost. A scaled-down but fully working copy of the stack should always run there. Which strategy is this?
options: Warm standby
Multi-site active/active
Pilot light
Backup and restore
objective.explanation: Warm standby keeps a smaller, always-running full copy that can scale up quickly. Pilot light keeps only core pieces such as replicated data with app servers off, backup and restore has the longest RTO, and active/active serves full production traffic in both Regions.

objective.question: When an order is placed, three independent services (billing, shipping, analytics) must each receive and process the event at their own pace, and no message should be lost if a service is down. What design should be used?
options: An SNS topic with three SQS queues subscribed (fan-out)
Three Lambda functions invoked synchronously by the order service
An Amazon ElastiCache pub/sub channel
One SQS queue polled by all three services
objective.explanation: SNS-to-SQS fan-out gives each service its own durable queue, so each consumes at its own rate and messages wait if a service is down. A single queue delivers each message to only one consumer, synchronous calls couple the services, and cache pub/sub does not keep messages durably.

objective.question: A company attaches this bucket policy to an S3 bucket. EC2 instances in a private subnet reach S3 through a gateway VPC endpoint with the ID shown. What is the effect of the policy?
options: Only requests from vpce-0a1b2c3d are denied; all other access is allowed.
The policy has no effect because gateway endpoints do not send the aws:SourceVpce key.
The policy grants all principals full access to the bucket through the endpoint.
Requests that do not arrive through endpoint vpce-0a1b2c3d are denied, including console and internet access by administrators.
objective.explanation: An explicit Deny with StringNotEquals blocks every request whose source endpoint is not vpce-0a1b2c3d, so even admins using the console over the internet are locked out. The policy only denies and grants nothing, and gateway endpoints do populate aws:SourceVpce.

objective.question: EC2 instances in a private subnet have no public IP addresses. They cannot download OS patches from the internet. The subnet's route table is shown. The company wants the instances to stay private. What should a solutions architect do?

code.code:
Route table: rtb-private (associated with subnet-private-a)
Destination      Target
10.0.0.0/16      local
0.0.0.0/0        igw-0abc1234

options: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet and change the 0.0.0.0/0 route in rtb-private to point to the NAT gateway.
Attach an Elastic IP address to each instance.
Add an outbound allow rule for 0.0.0.0/0 to the private subnet's network ACL.
Add an outbound HTTPS rule to the instances' security groups.
objective.explanation: Instances without public IPs cannot use an internet gateway directly; outbound internet access for private instances needs a NAT gateway in a public subnet as the default route target. Elastic IPs would make the instances public, and security group or NACL changes do not fix the missing translation.

objective.question: A research team runs a short-lived HPC job on hundreds of Linux EC2 instances. The input data sits in S3. The job needs a high-throughput, parallel file system that can load data from S3 and write results back. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket
A single large Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach
Amazon EFS with the Max I/O performance mode
objective.explanation: FSx for Lustre is built for HPC throughput and can be linked to an S3 bucket to import and export data. FSx for Windows targets SMB workloads, EFS is general-purpose NFS without native S3 linking, and EBS Multi-Attach is limited to a few instances in one AZ and needs a cluster-aware file system.

objective.question: A global application uses Amazon Aurora MySQL in us-east-1. The company needs DR in eu-west-1 with an RPO of about 1 second and an RTO of under a minute. Readers in Europe also need low-latency reads. Which solution meets these needs?
options: Enable Multi-AZ on the Aurora cluster and add more Aurora Replicas in us-east-1.
Use AWS DMS to replicate changes to an RDS for MySQL instance in eu-west-1.
Create an Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in eu-west-1.
Take automated snapshots and copy them to eu-west-1 every hour.
objective.explanation: Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer with typical lag under a second, supports fast cross-Region failover, and allows reads in the secondary Region. Snapshot copies give an RPO of hours, Multi-AZ stays in one Region, and DMS adds lag and operational work.

objective.question: A gaming leaderboard on DynamoDB is read-heavy. Reads of the same items spike sharply and the team needs microsecond read latency. They want minimal application code changes. What should they use?
options: DynamoDB global tables in a second Region
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with a cache-aside pattern written in the app
objective.explanation: DAX is an API-compatible in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond reads with only a client change. ElastiCache works but needs custom caching logic, global tables address multi-Region needs, and on-demand mode handles capacity, not latency.

objective.question: A payments service sends messages to an SQS FIFO queue with the command below. Messages for each order must be processed in order, but different orders should be processed in parallel. What does the --message-group-id value achieve?

code.code:
aws sqs send-message \
  --queue-url https://sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/111122223333/payments.fifo \
  --message-body '{"orderId":"A-1001","step":"capture"}' \
  --message-group-id A-1001 \
  --message-deduplication-id A-1001-capture

options: It keeps messages with the same order ID in strict order while allowing messages from different groups to be consumed in parallel.
It routes the message to a separate queue named A-1001.
It sets the message's visibility timeout based on the group.
It makes all messages in the queue strictly ordered, so only one consumer can work at a time.
objective.explanation: In FIFO queues, ordering is guaranteed within a message group, and different groups can be processed concurrently. The deduplication ID separately prevents duplicates within the deduplication interval; the group ID does not create queues or set timeouts.

objective.question: A Lambda function behind API Gateway connects to an RDS for PostgreSQL database. During traffic spikes, the database reports too many connections and queries fail. What is the most suitable fix with the least code change?
options: Place Amazon RDS Proxy between Lambda and the database.
Add a read replica and point all Lambda functions to it.
Convert the RDS instance to Multi-AZ.
Increase the Lambda function's memory size.
objective.explanation: RDS Proxy pools and reuses database connections, so many concurrent Lambda invocations share a small set of connections. More memory does not reduce connections, Multi-AZ is for availability, and a read replica cannot accept writes and still has connection limits.

objective.question: An Auto Scaling group terminates instances during scale-in. Before an instance is terminated, a script must copy its application logs to S3. Which feature should the architect use?
options: An Auto Scaling lifecycle hook on the terminating transition
Instance scale-in protection on all instances
ELB connection draining (deregistration delay)
A scheduled scaling action that runs before scale-in
objective.explanation: A lifecycle hook puts the instance in a Terminating:Wait state so a script or Lambda can copy logs, then completes the action. Scale-in protection blocks termination entirely, scheduled actions do not run per-instance tasks, and deregistration delay only lets in-flight requests finish.

objective.question: An SNS topic publishes order events. The fraud-check SQS queue subscribes with the filter policy below. A message is published with attributes event_type = order_placed and amount = 75. What happens?
options: The fraud-check queue does not receive the message because all conditions must match and amount is below 100.
SNS rejects the publish request because the message fails the filter.
The message goes to the topic's dead-letter queue.
The fraud-check queue receives the message because event_type matches.
objective.explanation: Keys in an SNS filter policy are combined with AND, so both event_type and amount must match for delivery to that subscription. The publish still succeeds and other subscriptions may receive it; filtered-out messages are simply not delivered, not sent to a DLQ.

objective.question: A team creates an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon SQS in its private subnets and enables private DNS on the endpoint. SDK calls from the instances still time out, and nslookup shows the SQS hostname resolving to public IP addresses. What is the most likely cause?
options: Amazon SQS supports only gateway endpoints, not interface endpoints
The private subnet route table needs a prefix-list route that points to the endpoint
The SQS queue policy must list the endpoint ID before DNS can resolve
The VPC attributes enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames are not both set to true
objective.explanation: Private DNS for an interface endpoint works only when the VPC has both DNS support and DNS hostnames enabled. Without them, the default hostname keeps resolving to public IPs. SQS does use interface endpoints, prefix-list routes are only for gateway endpoints, and queue policies do not affect DNS.

objective.question: An architect creates a NAT gateway in a private subnet. The private subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to that NAT gateway. Instances still cannot reach the internet. What is wrong?
options: The instances need Elastic IP addresses to use a NAT gateway
The NAT gateway must be in a public subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway
The NAT gateway must be in a different VPC from the instances
NAT gateways need a security group that allows outbound traffic
objective.explanation: A public NAT gateway forwards traffic to the internet gateway, so it must sit in a subnet whose route table points to the IGW. NAT gateways have no security groups, and private instances do not need public or Elastic IPs.

objective.question: You are tearing down the three-tier lab: ALB, an Auto Scaling group of EC2, RDS Multi-AZ, a NAT gateway with an Elastic IP, and a custom VPC. Which order avoids errors and stray charges?
options: Terminate the EC2 instances, delete the ALB, delete RDS, delete the ASG, then delete the VPC
Release the Elastic IP, delete the NAT gateway, delete the VPC, then delete the ASG and RDS
Delete the ASG, delete the ALB and target group, delete RDS and any retained snapshots, delete the NAT gateway, release the Elastic IP, then delete the VPC
Delete the VPC, then terminate the EC2 instances, then delete RDS, then delete the ASG
objective.explanation: Deleting the ASG first stops it relaunching instances. An Elastic IP cannot be released while the NAT gateway still uses it, and a VPC cannot be deleted while ENIs from the ALB, RDS or NAT gateway remain. Terminating instances before deleting the ASG only triggers replacements.

objective.question: A multiplayer game uses a custom UDP protocol on EC2 behind Network Load Balancers in two Regions. Players need two static IP addresses that never change, traffic should enter the AWS network near each player, and failover between Regions must be automatic. Which service fits best?
options: AWS Global Accelerator with an endpoint group in each Region
An Application Load Balancer in each Region with Elastic IPs
Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to the NLBs
Amazon CloudFront with the NLBs as origins
objective.explanation: Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs, supports TCP and UDP, carries traffic over the AWS backbone from the nearest edge, and fails over based on endpoint health. CloudFront does not proxy custom UDP, Route 53 does not provide static IPs, and ALBs do not support UDP or Elastic IPs.

objective.question: Linux EC2 instances run the mount command below. It hangs and then times out. The file system, its mount targets and the instances are in the same VPC. What is the most likely cause?

code.code:
sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890:/ /mnt/efs
# hangs, then: mount.nfs4: Connection timed out

options: EFS cannot be mounted with TLS from EC2 instances
The instances need a gateway VPC endpoint for EFS
The EFS file system is using the Bursting throughput mode
The security group on the EFS mount targets does not allow inbound TCP 2049 from the instances
objective.explanation: EFS uses NFS on TCP port 2049. A timeout usually means the mount target security group, or a NACL, blocks that port. TLS mounting is supported through the EFS mount helper, EFS has no gateway endpoint, and the throughput mode affects speed, not connectivity.

objective.question: An engineer applies the lifecycle configuration below to a bucket in which objects are uploaded to S3 Standard. What happens?

code.code: {"Rules":[{"ID":"logs-to-ia","Filter":{"Prefix":"logs/"},"Status":"Enabled","Transitions":[{"Days":15,"StorageClass":"STANDARD_IA"}],"Expiration":{"Days":365}}]}

options: The rule is accepted, but S3 silently waits until day 30 to transition
The rule applies only to objects uploaded after the rule was created
S3 rejects the configuration because transitions to Standard-IA must be at least 30 days after object creation
Objects move to Standard-IA after 15 days and are deleted after 365 days
objective.explanation: S3 does not allow a lifecycle transition to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA within 30 days of object creation, so the request fails with an invalid-argument error. Lifecycle rules also apply to existing objects, not only new ones.

objective.question: A new internal app needs a MySQL-compatible relational database. Traffic is unpredictable: near zero at night and sharp bursts during the day. The team wants high availability, automatic capacity changes and the least operational overhead. Which option is best?
options: Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity
MySQL on EC2 in an Auto Scaling group
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 with a reader in a second AZ
RDS for MySQL Single-AZ with a large instance class
objective.explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 is MySQL compatible and scales capacity automatically in fine steps. A reader in another AZ gives automatic failover. A Single-AZ instance is not highly available and wastes money at night, DynamoDB is not MySQL compatible, and self-managed MySQL on EC2 adds heavy operational overhead.

objective.question: An Auto Scaling group uses ELB health checks. New instances launch, then are marked unhealthy and terminated a few minutes later, again and again. The application takes about 6 minutes to bootstrap, and it works once it is running. What should the architect change first?
options: Increase the health check grace period so it covers the bootstrap time
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the ALB
Lower the target group's healthy threshold to 1
Switch the health check type from ELB to EC2 permanently
objective.explanation: The grace period stops Auto Scaling from acting on failed health checks until the instance has had time to start. A grace period shorter than the bootstrap time causes this replace loop. Switching to EC2 checks hides real application failures, and the other options do not stop the early terminations.

objective.question: An RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ instance fails over during an AZ outage. RDS reports the failover finished in about two minutes, but a Java application keeps failing to connect for much longer. Other clients reconnect quickly. What is the most likely cause?
options: The application caches the resolved IP address of the DB endpoint for too long
The standby was serving read traffic and had to be drained first
Failover always needs a manual reboot of the new primary
Multi-AZ failover changes the endpoint hostname, so the app must be redeployed
objective.explanation: During failover RDS points the same DNS name to the standby's IP. A JVM or connection pool that caches DNS for a long time keeps trying the old IP, so set a low DNS TTL and enable reconnect logic. The endpoint name does not change, the standby serves no reads, and failover is automatic.

objective.question: A log-processing cluster reads large files sequentially and needs high throughput at the lowest cost per GB. The data is read often. The volume will not be a boot volume. Which EBS volume type fits best?
options: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
General Purpose SSD (gp3)
Cold HDD (sc1)
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)
objective.explanation: st1 is built for frequently accessed, throughput-heavy sequential workloads at a low price per GB, and it cannot be a boot volume. sc1 is cheaper but meant for infrequently accessed data with lower throughput, and the SSD types cost more per GB and are tuned for IOPS.

objective.question: A security engineer adds the inbound network ACL rules below to block a malicious IP address. Traffic from 203.0.113.5 still reaches the web servers. Why?

code.code:
Rule # | Type        | Source           | Allow/Deny
100    | All traffic | 0.0.0.0/0        | ALLOW
200    | All traffic | 203.0.113.5/32   | DENY
*      | All traffic | 0.0.0.0/0        | DENY

options: NACL rules are evaluated in order from the lowest number, and rule 100 matches first
A /32 CIDR is not valid in a network ACL
The deny rule must be added to the outbound rules as well
NACLs cannot deny traffic, only security groups can
objective.explanation: NACLs evaluate rules from the lowest number up and stop at the first match, so rule 100 allows the traffic before rule 200 is checked. The deny rule needs a lower number, such as 90. Security groups cannot deny at all, which is why the NACL is the right tool here.

objective.question: A company wants to react to events from a SaaS partner and from its own services. Rules must match on fields inside the event body, route to different targets, and the team must be able to archive events and replay them after a bug fix. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon SQS FIFO queues with message groups
Amazon EventBridge event buses with rules, archives and replay
AWS Step Functions Standard workflows
Amazon SNS standard topics with subscription filter policies
objective.explanation: EventBridge supports SaaS partner event sources, content-based rules on the event body, many targets, and built-in archive and replay. SNS can filter but has no archive and replay, SQS is a queue rather than a router, and Step Functions orchestrates steps rather than routing events.

objective.question: A company needs DR in a second Region. The RPO is a few minutes and the RTO is under one hour. The database must be continuously replicated, but the company wants to pay as little as possible for application servers until a disaster. Which strategy is the best fit?
options: Warm standby
Multi-site active-active
Pilot light
Backup and restore
objective.explanation: Pilot light keeps the core data layer live and replicated while application servers are off or only defined as AMIs and templates, then launched during recovery. Backup and restore cannot give an RPO of minutes from continuous replication, while warm standby and multi-site keep compute running and cost more.

objective.question: A static website is served from a private S3 bucket through Amazon CloudFront. Security finds that some users download files directly from the S3 URL and bypass CloudFront and AWS WAF. What is the recommended fix?
options: Add a NACL to block S3 traffic from the internet
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Use CloudFront origin access control (OAC), keep Block Public Access on, and allow only the distribution in the bucket policy
Enable S3 static website hosting and make the bucket public
objective.explanation: With OAC, CloudFront signs requests to S3, and a bucket policy that allows only the cloudfront.amazonaws.com principal for that distribution's ARN blocks direct access. Making the bucket public worsens the problem, NACLs do not apply to S3 public endpoints, and Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads only.

objective.question: A Lambda function is attached to a VPC so it can reach an RDS database. It is configured with public subnets that route 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. The function can query RDS, but calls to a public third-party API time out. What fixes this?
options: Enable the 'auto-assign public IPv4' setting on the public subnets
Attach the function to private subnets that route 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway
Increase the function's timeout and memory
Assign an Elastic IP to the Lambda function
objective.explanation: The network interfaces that Lambda creates in a VPC never get public IPs, so an internet gateway route alone does not work. Private subnets with a NAT gateway route give outbound internet access. Lambda does not support Elastic IPs, and more timeout or memory does not fix routing.

objective.question: An unencrypted RDS for PostgreSQL instance must be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. Which order of steps is correct?
options: Take a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption using the KMS key, restore a new instance from the encrypted copy, then point the application to the new endpoint
Enable encryption on the DB subnet group, then fail over the Multi-AZ instance
Create an encrypted read replica from the unencrypted instance, then promote it
Modify the instance and tick 'Enable encryption', then reboot
objective.explanation: Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing RDS instance, but you can encrypt a snapshot copy and restore from it. You cannot create an encrypted read replica from an unencrypted instance, and subnet groups have no encryption setting.

subjective.question: What makes a subnet public or private in a VPC, and where would you place each tier of a three-tier app?
subjective.answer: A subnet is public when its route table has a route, usually 0.0.0.0/0, to an internet gateway attached to the VPC. Instances there also need a public IP or Elastic IP to be reached. A private subnet has no route to the internet gateway. If it needs outbound internet, it routes 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway in a public subnet. In a three-tier app I put the Application Load Balancer in public subnets across at least two AZs. The web or app EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group go in private subnets, and the RDS database goes in separate private database subnets with no internet route at all. Security groups then chain the tiers: the ALB accepts 443 from the internet, the app tier accepts traffic only from the ALB's security group, and the database accepts its port only from the app tier's security group.
keyPoints: Public means a route table entry to an internet gateway
Private subnets use a NAT gateway for outbound-only access
ALB in public subnets, app and DB in private subnets across AZs
Security groups reference each other to chain tiers

subjective.question: Compare security groups and network ACLs. When would you use a NACL instead of only security groups?
subjective.answer: Security groups attach to network interfaces such as EC2 instances. They are stateful, so if inbound traffic is allowed, the response is allowed automatically. They support allow rules only, and all rules are evaluated together. They can reference other security groups, which makes tier-to-tier rules clean. NACLs attach to subnets. They are stateless, so return traffic needs its own rule, usually for the ephemeral port range. They support both allow and deny, and rules are evaluated in order from the lowest rule number, stopping at the first match. I use security groups as the main control. I add a NACL when I need an explicit deny, for example blocking a known bad IP range for a whole subnet, or as a coarse second layer of defence. On the exam, 'block a specific IP address' almost always points to a NACL, because security groups cannot deny.
keyPoints: SG: instance level, stateful, allow only, can reference SGs
NACL: subnet level, stateless, allow and deny
NACL rules evaluated lowest number first, first match wins
Use NACL for explicit deny of IP ranges

subjective.question: Explain gateway VPC endpoints and interface VPC endpoints. How do you choose between them?
subjective.answer: Both let resources in a VPC reach AWS services privately without an internet gateway or NAT. A gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB. It works by adding a prefix-list route to chosen route tables, and it has no hourly charge. It is reachable only from within that VPC, not from on-premises over VPN or Direct Connect, or from peered VPCs. An interface endpoint uses AWS PrivateLink. It creates elastic network interfaces with private IPs in your subnets, protected by security groups, and private DNS can make the normal service name resolve to them. It costs per hour per AZ plus per GB processed, but it works for most AWS services and can be reached from on-premises. My rule: for S3 or DynamoDB access from inside the VPC, use the gateway endpoint for cost. Use an interface endpoint for other services, or when on-premises clients need private access.
keyPoints: Gateway endpoints: S3 and DynamoDB only, route-table based, no hourly charge
Interface endpoints: PrivateLink ENIs, security groups, private DNS
Interface endpoints are billed hourly and per GB
On-premises access needs interface endpoints

subjective.question: How would you design NAT for high availability and cost, and what are its limits?
subjective.answer: A NAT gateway is a managed, zonal service placed in a public subnet with an Elastic IP. It gives private instances outbound-only internet access. Because it lives in one AZ, a single NAT gateway is a single point of failure for the other AZs and also adds cross-AZ data charges. For HA I create one NAT gateway per AZ and give each AZ's private subnets their own route table pointing to the local NAT gateway. For cost, I send S3 and DynamoDB traffic through gateway endpoints so it does not pass through NAT, because NAT charges per GB processed. Limits to remember: a NAT gateway does not allow inbound connections from the internet, and resources in a peered VPC or on-premises cannot use it through peering. For a non-production environment, a single NAT gateway may be an acceptable cost trade-off if downtime is tolerable.
keyPoints: NAT gateway is zonal and sits in a public subnet
One per AZ with per-AZ route tables for HA
Use gateway endpoints to cut NAT data charges
No inbound connections and no use via VPC peering

subjective.question: Compare Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer and Gateway Load Balancer with a use case for each.
subjective.answer: The Application Load Balancer works at Layer 7. It understands HTTP and HTTPS, so it can route by path, host header, query string or headers, and it can target EC2, IP addresses, containers and Lambda. It is the default for web apps and microservices. The Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4 for TCP, UDP and TLS. It handles very high throughput with low latency and gives a static IP per AZ, and you can attach Elastic IPs. I use it for gaming, IoT, non-HTTP protocols, or when clients need to allow-list fixed IPs. It can also front a PrivateLink endpoint service. The Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls or intrusion detection systems transparently into the traffic path, using GENEVE encapsulation. On the exam, 'path-based routing' means ALB, 'static IP or extreme performance' means NLB, and 'third-party firewall appliances' means GWLB.
keyPoints: ALB: Layer 7, path/host routing, Lambda targets
NLB: Layer 4, static IPs, very high performance, PrivateLink
GWLB: third-party appliances, GENEVE
Map exam keywords to each type

subjective.question: Describe how EC2 Auto Scaling works with an ELB, including scaling policies and health checks.
subjective.answer: An Auto Scaling group uses a launch template and keeps capacity between a minimum and maximum, aiming at a desired count. I spread it across subnets in multiple AZs and register it with an ALB target group. For health, I enable ELB health checks on the group, so an instance that fails the load balancer's check is replaced, not just one that fails EC2 status checks. For scaling, target tracking is my default, for example average CPU at 50% or ALB requests per target. Step scaling gives finer control based on alarm size. Scheduled scaling suits known patterns like business hours, and predictive scaling forecasts cyclical load. A health check grace period stops new instances from being killed before the app starts. Lifecycle hooks let me run setup or drain tasks during launch or termination. The group also rebalances across AZs, which supports high availability.
keyPoints: Launch template, min/max/desired across multiple AZs
Enable ELB health checks for app-level replacement
Target tracking, step, scheduled and predictive policies
Grace period and lifecycle hooks

subjective.question: A company keeps logs that are read often for 30 days, rarely for a year, and must be kept for 7 years for audit. Design an S3 storage and lifecycle plan.
subjective.answer: I would land logs in S3 Standard because they are read often in the first month. A lifecycle rule then transitions them to S3 Standard-IA at day 30, since access drops but quick retrieval is still needed. Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum storage duration and a per-GB retrieval fee, which is fine for rare reads. After one year I would move them to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which is the lowest-cost class, with retrieval in hours and a 180-day minimum. If auditors might need data in milliseconds, Glacier Instant Retrieval is the alternative, with a 90-day minimum. An expiration action deletes objects after 7 years. For compliance, I would turn on S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period, plus versioning. I would also avoid moving very small objects to IA classes, because they are billed at a minimum object size. If access patterns were unknown, S3 Intelligent-Tiering would be the simpler choice.
keyPoints: Standard → Standard-IA at 30 days → Deep Archive after 1 year
Respect minimum durations: IA 30, Glacier IR/Flexible 90, Deep Archive 180 days
Expiration at 7 years; Object Lock for compliance
Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns

subjective.question: Compare Amazon EBS, EFS and FSx. Give a scenario for each.
subjective.answer: EBS is block storage attached to an EC2 instance in a single AZ. It suits boot volumes and databases on EC2. gp3 is general purpose with performance set independently of size, and io2 gives high, consistent IOPS. Multi-Attach is limited to certain io1/io2 volumes within one AZ. Snapshots go to S3 and can be copied across Regions for DR. EFS is a managed NFS file system for Linux. Many instances across AZs can mount it at once and it grows automatically, so it fits shared web content or home directories for an Auto Scaling group. Lifecycle management can move cold files to cheaper storage classes. FSx gives managed third-party file systems: FSx for Windows File Server for SMB and Active Directory workloads, FSx for Lustre for high-performance computing and ML that can link to S3, and FSx for NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS for multi-protocol or migration needs. I choose by protocol, sharing needs and operating system.
keyPoints: EBS: single-AZ block storage, gp3/io2, snapshots
EFS: shared NFS for Linux across AZs, elastic
FSx for Windows (SMB/AD), Lustre (HPC/ML), ONTAP, OpenZFS
Choose by protocol, OS and sharing

subjective.question: Explain RDS Multi-AZ, read replicas and Aurora. How would you pick one for a given requirement?
subjective.answer: RDS Multi-AZ, in its standard form, keeps a standby in another AZ using synchronous replication. If the primary fails, RDS fails over automatically by updating the DNS endpoint. The standby does not serve reads, so its purpose is high availability. Read replicas use asynchronous replication. They serve read traffic, can be in another Region for DR, and can be promoted to a standalone database, but they may lag. Aurora is AWS's MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine. It stores 6 copies across 3 AZs on a shared cluster volume and supports up to 15 Aurora Replicas that serve reads and act as failover targets, usually with faster failover than standard RDS. Aurora Global Database adds low-lag cross-Region replication, and Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity automatically. My mapping: survive AZ failure means Multi-AZ; scale reads means read replicas; cross-Region DR means a cross-Region replica or Aurora Global Database; highest availability with less overhead usually means Aurora.
keyPoints: Multi-AZ: synchronous, automatic failover, standby not readable
Read replicas: asynchronous, read scaling, cross-Region, promotable
Aurora: 6 copies in 3 AZs, up to 15 replicas
Global Database and Serverless v2 options

subjective.question: When would you choose DynamoDB over RDS, and what design rules matter most?
subjective.answer: I choose DynamoDB when access patterns are known, the workload needs single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, and I want no servers to manage. Examples are user sessions, shopping carts, game state and IoT data. RDS is better when I need complex joins, ad hoc SQL queries or strong relational constraints. Key design rules: pick a partition key with high cardinality so traffic spreads evenly and avoids hot partitions. Use a sort key and global or local secondary indexes to support query patterns, and avoid table scans. Keep items under the 400 KB limit; large files go to S3 with a pointer in the item. Choose on-demand capacity for unpredictable traffic and provisioned with auto scaling for steady traffic. Other features I mention: TTL to expire old items, Streams to trigger Lambda on changes, global tables for multi-Region active-active, point-in-time recovery for backups, and DAX for microsecond read caching.
keyPoints: DynamoDB for known access patterns, scale, serverless
High-cardinality partition key, indexes, avoid scans
400 KB item limit; large objects in S3
On-demand vs provisioned; TTL, Streams, global tables, DAX

subjective.question: How does ElastiCache help an architecture, and what caching strategies and engine choices would you discuss?
subjective.answer: ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache. It reduces read load on databases and cuts latency, and it also stores session state so web servers can stay stateless behind a load balancer. Two common strategies: lazy loading (cache-aside), where the app reads the cache, and on a miss reads the database and writes the result to the cache. It caches only what is used, but data can be stale and the first read is slower. Write-through updates the cache whenever the database is written, so data stays fresh, but it can fill the cache with unused items. I add a TTL in both cases to limit staleness. For engines, Redis OSS or Valkey gives replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, persistence options, and rich data types like sorted sets for leaderboards. Memcached is simple, multi-threaded and has no replication, suited to a basic cache. Note the app code must change to use the cache, unlike DAX, which is API-compatible with DynamoDB.
keyPoints: Reduces DB load and latency; external session store
Lazy loading vs write-through, with TTL
Redis OSS/Valkey: replication, failover, data types
Memcached: simple, no replication; app changes needed

subjective.question: Compare SQS, SNS and EventBridge for decoupling. When would you use each?
subjective.answer: SQS is a pull-based queue. A producer sends messages and consumers poll and delete them, so it buffers load and protects downstream systems. Standard queues give very high throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. FIFO queues give ordering and exactly-once processing. Key settings: visibility timeout defaults to 30 seconds and can go to 12 hours; retention defaults to 4 days, maximum 14 days; a dead-letter queue catches poison messages after a set number of receives. SNS is push-based pub/sub. One message goes to many subscribers such as SQS, Lambda, HTTP endpoints, email or SMS, and SNS plus SQS gives durable fan-out. EventBridge is an event bus with content-based rules that route events from AWS services, your own apps and SaaS partners to many targets. It adds schema registry, archive and replay, and scheduling. I use SQS for buffering work, SNS for simple fan-out, and EventBridge for event-driven routing across many sources and filtering rules.
keyPoints: SQS: pull queue, buffering, Standard vs FIFO
Visibility timeout 30 s default (12 h max); retention 4 days default (14 max); DLQ
SNS: push pub/sub, fan-out with SQS
EventBridge: rule-based routing, SaaS sources, replay

subjective.question: A team has a Lambda function that sometimes times out because it now does several steps taking up to 30 minutes in total. How would you redesign it?
subjective.answer: Lambda has a hard maximum timeout of 15 minutes, so raising the timeout cannot fix this. I would split the work into smaller steps and orchestrate them with AWS Step Functions. Each short step can stay a Lambda function. Any step that runs long, like a big file transform, can run as an ECS task on Fargate, which Step Functions can start and wait for, or as an AWS Batch job for heavy batch compute. Step Functions gives built-in retries with backoff, catch blocks for errors, parallel and map states for fan-out, and a visual history of each run, which makes debugging easier. Standard workflows suit long-running, auditable jobs; Express workflows suit high-volume, short runs. If the trigger is bursty, I would put an SQS queue in front to buffer requests. This keeps the solution serverless with low operational overhead, which is what the exam usually rewards.
keyPoints: Lambda maximum timeout is 15 minutes
Step Functions for multi-step orchestration with retries and error handling
ECS on Fargate or Batch for long steps
Standard vs Express workflows; SQS for buffering

subjective.question: Explain the four disaster recovery strategies on AWS and how RTO, RPO and cost change across them.
subjective.answer: RTO is how long recovery may take; RPO is how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable. Backup and restore is the cheapest: data is backed up to another Region using AWS Backup, snapshots or S3 replication, and infrastructure is rebuilt from code when needed. RTO and RPO are hours. Pilot light keeps core data live in the DR Region, for example a cross-Region read replica or Aurora Global Database, while app servers are off or not created; you start them in a disaster, giving RTO in tens of minutes. Warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully working copy that can take traffic and scale up quickly, giving RTO in minutes at higher cost. Multi-site active/active serves production traffic from two or more Regions, using Route 53 routing and services like DynamoDB global tables, giving near-zero RTO and RPO at the highest cost. I pick the cheapest option that meets the stated RTO and RPO.
keyPoints: Define RTO and RPO
Backup and restore: cheapest, hours
Pilot light: data live, compute off; warm standby: scaled-down running
Active/active: near-zero RTO/RPO, highest cost

subjective.question: Walk through how you built and tore down the three-tier lab (ALB → Auto Scaling EC2 → RDS Multi-AZ), and what you learned.
subjective.answer: I created a VPC with public subnets in two AZs for the ALB and NAT gateways, private app subnets, and private database subnets. I made three security groups: the ALB allowing HTTP/HTTPS from the internet, the app tier allowing traffic only from the ALB's group, and the database allowing its port only from the app group. I wrote a launch template with user data to install the app, created an Auto Scaling group across both AZs with ELB health checks and a target tracking policy, and attached it to an ALB target group. I launched RDS in a DB subnet group with Multi-AZ enabled and stored credentials in Secrets Manager. I tested by terminating an instance and rebooting RDS with failover. For teardown I deleted in reverse: Auto Scaling group, ALB and target group, RDS with a final snapshot decision, NAT gateways, Elastic IPs, then the VPC. Lesson: NAT gateways, idle load balancers and RDS are the usual surprise costs, so check billing afterwards.
keyPoints: Subnet layout across two AZs with SG chaining
Launch template, ASG with ELB health checks, target tracking
RDS Multi-AZ in DB subnet group; test failover
Reverse-order teardown; watch NAT, EIP and RDS costs

subjective.question: How do you approach SAA-C03 scenario questions and manage the exam, including 'least operational overhead' wording?
subjective.answer: The exam has 65 questions, of which 50 are scored and 15 unscored, in 130 minutes, with a pass mark of 720 out of 1000. That is about two minutes per question, so I do a first pass, answer what I know, flag the doubtful ones and return later. There is no penalty for guessing, so I never leave a blank. For each scenario I read the last line first to find the real requirement: cost, performance, availability, security or operational overhead. Then I underline constraints such as 'without internet', 'in minutes' or 'existing SQL'. I remove options that break a hard limit, such as a Lambda running over 15 minutes or a DynamoDB item over 400 KB. When the question says 'least operational overhead', I prefer managed or serverless choices like Fargate, Lambda, Aurora Serverless or DynamoDB over self-managed EC2. When it says 'most cost-effective', I look for things like gateway endpoints, Spot, or lifecycle rules. Before booking, I aim for two full practice exams above 80% with time left over.
keyPoints: 65 questions (50 scored), 130 minutes, pass 720/1000
Read the requirement line first; note constraints
Eliminate options that break service limits
'Least operational overhead' favours managed/serverless; target 80%+ in practice

subjective.question: The security group rules below are for a three-tier app. Explain what they do and why referencing security groups is better than using CIDR ranges.

code.code:
sg-alb  inbound:  TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0
sg-web  inbound:  TCP 8080 from sg-alb
sg-db   inbound:  TCP 3306 from sg-web
(all outbound: default allow all)

subjective.answer: The ALB security group accepts HTTPS from anywhere, so users on the internet can reach the load balancer. The web tier only accepts port 8080 from resources that carry sg-alb, which means only the ALB can talk to the instances. The database only accepts MySQL on 3306 from members of sg-web, so only web servers can query it. This is called security group chaining. Referencing groups is better than CIDRs because Auto Scaling keeps launching instances with new private IPs; the rule follows group membership, not addresses, so nothing needs updating. It also enforces least privilege: even a host in the same subnet cannot reach the database unless it carries sg-web. Because security groups are stateful, return traffic is allowed automatically, so no inbound rules for ephemeral ports are needed.
keyPoints: ALB open on 443, web only from ALB, DB only from web
Group references survive changing IPs from Auto Scaling
Least privilege between tiers, even within one subnet
Security groups are stateful, so return traffic is automatic

subjective.question: A company must copy every new object in an S3 bucket in ap-south-1 to a bucket in ap-southeast-1 for compliance. Explain how S3 Cross-Region Replication works, what it needs, and what it does not do by default.
subjective.answer: Cross-Region Replication copies new objects asynchronously from a source bucket to a destination bucket in another Region. Both buckets must have versioning enabled, and S3 needs an IAM role that allows it to read from the source and write to the destination. You can replicate the whole bucket or filter by prefix or tag, and you can change the storage class or owner in the destination. By default, objects that existed before the rule was created are not replicated; you use S3 Batch Replication for those. Delete markers are not replicated unless you turn that option on, and deletes of specific versions are never replicated, which protects against malicious deletes. Objects encrypted with SSE-KMS need extra configuration for the KMS keys. If the company needs a predictable replication time with metrics, S3 Replication Time Control adds an SLA-backed option at extra cost.
keyPoints: Versioning on both buckets and an IAM role are required
Existing objects need S3 Batch Replication
Delete marker replication is optional; version deletes are not replicated
SSE-KMS objects need key configuration; RTC gives predictable timing

subjective.question: A team wants to move a containerised web API to AWS. Compare Amazon ECS on Fargate, ECS on EC2, Amazon EKS and AWS Lambda, and say how you would choose.
subjective.answer: ECS on Fargate runs containers without managing servers. You define task CPU and memory, and AWS handles the hosts, so it is the usual answer for least operational overhead. ECS on EC2 gives more control over instance types, GPUs and placement, and can be cheaper at steady high utilisation, but you patch and scale the cluster yourself. EKS is managed Kubernetes; choose it when the team already uses Kubernetes tooling, needs portability, or runs Helm-based workloads. It is more complex to operate, though it can also use Fargate. Lambda suits short, event-driven work with spiky traffic, and it has a maximum run time per invocation, so it fits APIs only if requests are short and the code can be packaged for Lambda. For a typical stateless API with no Kubernetes requirement, I would pick ECS on Fargate behind an ALB with service auto scaling.
keyPoints: Fargate removes host management, best for low overhead
ECS on EC2 for control, GPUs or cost at high utilisation
EKS when Kubernetes skills or portability are required
Lambda for short event-driven work within its time limit

subjective.question: A company wants an active-active application in two Regions, with users routed to the nearest healthy Region and writes allowed in both. Design the data and routing layers.
subjective.answer: For data, I would use DynamoDB global tables. Each Region has a full replica that accepts reads and writes, and changes replicate asynchronously between Regions.
