With the default multi-Region eventual consistency, conflicting writes are resolved with last-writer-wins, so the app should avoid writing the same item in both Regions at once, for example by routing a user to a home Region. For routing, I would use Route 53 latency-based records pointing to an ALB in each Region, with health checks on each endpoint. If one Region fails its health check, Route 53 stops returning it and users go to the other Region. Each Region runs its own Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs. Stateless web tiers and sessions stored in DynamoDB mean any Region can serve any user. S3 Cross-Region Replication covers static assets.
keyPoints: DynamoDB global tables for multi-Region read and write
Understand last-writer-wins conflict handling
Route 53 latency routing with health checks
Stateless, Multi-AZ compute in each Region

subjective.question: After a deployment, users get HTTP 503 errors from an Application Load Balancer and the target group shows all targets unhealthy. How would you troubleshoot this?
subjective.answer: A 503 from the ALB usually means no healthy targets are registered. First I check the target group health status reason codes in the console. Then I confirm the health check settings: the path must return a success code, the port must match what the app listens on, and the timeout and threshold values must be sensible. A common cause is a new release that changed the health path or returns 302 or 404. Next I check networking. The instance security group must allow the health check port from the ALB security group, and the subnet NACLs must allow the traffic and the ephemeral return ports. I then log in or use Session Manager to confirm the app is running and listening on the right interface, not only localhost. Finally, if Auto Scaling uses ELB health checks, I set a suitable grace period so new instances are not replaced before they finish booting.
keyPoints: 503 means no healthy targets; read health reason codes
Verify health check path, port and success codes
Security group must allow traffic from the ALB group; check NACLs
Confirm the app listens correctly; tune health check grace period

subjective.question: A three-tier app runs 24/7 at a steady baseline, has daytime peaks, and has a nightly batch job that can be interrupted. How would you combine EC2 purchase options to cut cost?
subjective.answer: I would cover the steady baseline with Savings Plans or Reserved Instances. Compute Savings Plans give flexibility across instance families, Regions and even Fargate and Lambda, while EC2 Instance Savings Plans or Standard RIs give deeper discounts if the family is fixed. The database tier can use RDS Reserved Instances since it runs all the time. For daytime peaks, the Auto Scaling group adds On-Demand instances, or I use a mixed instances policy that puts part of the peak capacity on Spot across several instance types. The nightly batch job is a good fit for Spot because it is fault tolerant; I would use multiple instance types and AZs, and checkpoint progress so an interruption only loses a little work. I would also right-size instances with Compute Optimizer and consider Graviton instances for better price-performance.
keyPoints: Savings Plans or RIs for steady baseline
On-Demand or a mixed instances policy for peaks
Spot for interruptible batch, diversified across types and AZs
Right-size and consider Graviton

subjective.question: Explain what this SQS redrive policy does and how you would operate a dead-letter queue in production.
subjective.answer: This sets orders-dlq as the dead-letter queue for the source queue. Each time a consumer receives a message, its receive count goes up. If a message is received five times without being deleted, SQS moves it to the DLQ. The visibility timeout of 120 seconds hides a received message for two minutes so another consumer does not pick it up while it is being processed. Together this stops a poison message, such as bad data, from looping forever and blocking work. In production, I set a CloudWatch alarm on the DLQ's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric, investigate failed messages, fix the bug, and then use DLQ redrive to send them back to the source queue. The DLQ must be the same type as the source, standard or FIFO, and its retention period should be longer than the source so messages do not expire before review.
keyPoints: After 5 failed receives the message moves to the DLQ
Visibility timeout must exceed processing time
Alarm on DLQ depth and redrive after fixing
DLQ type matches source; longer retention

subjective.question: A mobile app must let users upload photos directly to a private S3 bucket without sending files through the web servers. The data must be encrypted and the company wants control over key access. Design this.
subjective.answer: The app calls a backend API, for example API Gateway with Lambda, after the user authenticates, perhaps with Amazon Cognito. The backend checks the user and generates an S3 presigned URL for a PUT to a specific key, with a short expiry. The app uploads the file straight to S3 using that URL, so web servers carry no file traffic and scale less. The bucket keeps Block Public Access on. For encryption, I would set default bucket encryption to SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. That gives control through the key policy, CloudTrail logs of key use, and the option to rotate keys. S3 Bucket Keys reduce KMS request cost. A bucket policy can deny uploads that do not use the expected encryption. An S3 event notification can then trigger Lambda to create thumbnails.
keyPoints: Backend issues short-lived presigned PUT URLs after auth
Direct upload removes load from web servers
Block Public Access stays on
SSE-KMS with customer managed key for control and audit; Bucket Keys cut cost

subjective.question: A company runs EC2 with EBS volumes and RDS. It needs a central backup policy with cross-Region copies and point-in-time restore for the database. How would you design backup and recovery?
subjective.answer: I would use AWS Backup as the central service. A backup plan defines schedules, retention and lifecycle, and resources are assigned by tags, so new servers tagged backup=daily are covered automatically. The plan includes a copy rule to a vault in another Region, and optionally another account, for DR and ransomware protection. AWS Backup Vault Lock can make backups immutable for compliance. For EC2, backups are EBS snapshots, which are incremental and stored durably by AWS; AMIs capture the whole instance. For RDS, automated backups with transaction logs allow point-in-time restore within the retention window, and the restore creates a new DB instance, so the app endpoint must be updated. I would also test restores regularly, because a backup is only proven when you have restored it and measured RTO and RPO.
keyPoints: AWS Backup plans with tag-based resource selection
Cross-Region and cross-account copies; Vault Lock for immutability
EBS snapshots are incremental; AMIs for full instances
RDS PITR restores to a new instance; test restores regularly

subjective.question: An Indian fintech runs its app in ap-south-1 (Mumbai). Regulators require data to stay in India. The business sets an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 15 minutes, and wants the lowest cost. The stack is ALB, EC2 Auto Scaling, RDS for PostgreSQL and S3. Design the DR approach.
subjective.answer: I would use ap-south-2 (Hyderabad) as the DR Region, so data stays in India. An RTO of 4 hours does not need warm standby, so I start from backup and restore, but the 15-minute RPO rules out hourly snapshot copies alone. For RDS I would enable cross-Region automated backup replication to Hyderabad, which copies snapshots and transaction logs so I can do point-in-time restore there. If testing shows the lag is too close to 15 minutes, I would add a small cross-Region read replica instead, which is pilot light for the data tier. For S3 I would use Cross-Region Replication with Replication Time Control if needed. AMIs, secrets and multi-Region KMS keys are copied ahead of time, and the whole stack is in CloudFormation or Terraform so it can be rebuilt in Hyderabad within hours. Route 53 failover records switch traffic. I would pre-raise service quotas in Hyderabad and run a game day to prove the RTO.
keyPoints: Use the Hyderabad Region to meet Indian data residency
RTO of hours means backup and restore or pilot light, not warm standby
Cross-Region automated backups or a read replica to meet 15-minute RPO
S3 CRR, copied AMIs, multi-Region keys and IaC for rebuild
Test with a game day and pre-raise quotas

subjective.question: EC2 instances in a private subnet cannot reach the internet, even though a NAT gateway exists in the VPC. Give a step-by-step troubleshooting checklist.
subjective.answer: I would work along the packet path. First, check that the NAT gateway is in the Available state, is a public NAT gateway with an Elastic IP, and sits in a public subnet. Second, check that the public subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway that is attached to the VPC. Third, check the private subnet's route table. A common mistake is that the subnet is still associated with the main route table, not the custom one that sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway. Fourth, check the instance security group allows the outbound traffic. Fifth, check NACLs on both subnets. They are stateless, so they must allow outbound traffic and the inbound ephemeral return ports 1024-65535. Finally, I would test with curl, check DNS resolution, and use VPC Reachability Analyzer or VPC Flow Logs to see where packets stop.
keyPoints: NAT gateway must be available, public, with an Elastic IP, in a public subnet
Public subnet routes to an attached internet gateway
Private subnet must be associated with the route table that points to NAT
Check security group outbound rules and stateless NACL ephemeral ports
Use Reachability Analyzer and VPC Flow Logs

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this Auto Scaling group definition for the web tier of a production three-tier app, and explain how you would fix each one.

code.code:
WebASG:
  Type: AWS::AutoScaling::AutoScalingGroup
  Properties:
    LaunchTemplate:
      LaunchTemplateId: !Ref WebLT
      Version: !GetAtt WebLT.LatestVersionNumber
    MinSize: "1"
    MaxSize: "1"
    DesiredCapacity: "1"
    VPCZoneIdentifier:
      - !Ref PublicSubnetA
    HealthCheckType: EC2
    TargetGroupARNs:
      - !Ref WebTG

subjective.answer: There are four problems. First, VPCZoneIdentifier lists one subnet, so the group lives in one AZ. An AZ failure takes the whole tier down. I would list private subnets in at least two, ideally three, AZs. Second, the instances are in a public subnet. Web servers behind an ALB should be in private subnets, with only the ALB in public subnets and outbound access through NAT or VPC endpoints. Third, MinSize, MaxSize and DesiredCapacity are all 1, so the group can never scale and there is no redundancy. I would set a minimum of 2 across AZs, a sensible maximum, and add a target tracking policy. Fourth, HealthCheckType is EC2, so if the application crashes but the instance is running, it is never replaced. I would use ELB health checks with a grace period that covers bootstrap time.
keyPoints: Single subnet means a single AZ and no AZ resilience
Web instances should be in private subnets behind the ALB
Min = max = 1 gives no scaling and no redundancy
EC2 health checks miss application failures; use ELB checks with a grace period

subjective.question: You must upgrade a production RDS for MySQL database to a new major version with minimal downtime. Put the steps in order using RDS Blue/Green Deployments and explain each.
subjective.answer: Step one: check prerequisites, such as binary logging being on, and take a manual snapshot as a fallback. Step two: create a blue/green deployment. RDS builds a green copy of the production blue environment and keeps it in sync with replication. Step three: upgrade the green environment to the new major version and apply any new parameter group. Step four: test green. It is read-only by default, so I point test readers at it and run checks on queries and performance. Step five: confirm replica lag is near zero, then plan the switchover in a low-traffic window. Step six: switch over. RDS runs guardrail checks, stops writes briefly, and renames the instances so green takes the production endpoint names. The app needs no connection string change. Step seven: monitor errors and latency. Step eight: after a safe period, delete the old blue environment to stop paying for it.
keyPoints: Snapshot and prerequisites first
Create blue/green, then upgrade and test green
Check replica lag before switchover
Switchover renames endpoints so the app needs no change
Delete old blue afterwards to stop costs

subjective.question: An order system will use Amazon SQS. The business says 'each order must be processed once, and events for the same order must stay in order'. Which is better here, a standard queue or a FIFO queue, and why?
subjective.answer: A FIFO queue fits better. It keeps strict order within a message group, so I would use the order ID as the message group ID. Events for one order stay in sequence, while different orders are processed in parallel. FIFO also removes duplicates sent within a five-minute deduplication window, using a deduplication ID or content-based deduplication. A standard queue gives at-least-once delivery and only best-effort ordering, so I would need extra sequencing logic. The trade-off is throughput: standard queues scale almost without limit, while FIFO has lower per-queue limits, though batching and high-throughput mode raise them. I would also tell the business that 'exactly once' really means 'processed once by the app'. Consumers should still be idempotent, for example with a conditional write on the order ID, because a consumer can fail after doing work but before deleting the message.
keyPoints: FIFO gives ordering per message group; use order ID as group ID
FIFO deduplicates within a five-minute window
Standard is at-least-once with best-effort ordering but higher throughput
Consumers should still be idempotent

subjective.question: A DynamoDB table with on-demand capacity shows throttled writes, yet total consumed capacity is far below what the account allows. The partition key is 'event_date'. What is the cause and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: This is a hot partition. With event_date as the partition key, every write for today lands on the same key, and so on the same partition. Each partition has a throughput limit, roughly 1,000 write units and 3,000 read units per second. On-demand capacity and adaptive capacity cannot spread load for a single key, so the table throttles even though total usage is low. The fix is a high-cardinality partition key that spreads writes evenly, such as device ID or user ID, with the date in the sort key. If I must group by date, I would use write sharding: add a random or calculated suffix like 2026-03-01#7 across N shards, and query all shards when reading. For hot reads, DAX or ElastiCache can help, but it does not fix hot writes. I would confirm the cause with CloudWatch Contributor Insights, which shows the most accessed keys.
keyPoints: Low-cardinality key concentrates traffic on one partition
Per-partition limits apply even in on-demand mode
Use a high-cardinality partition key or write sharding
Contributor Insights finds hot keys; caching helps reads only

subjective.question: A versioned S3 bucket has the lifecycle rule below. The team deletes old data, but the storage bill keeps growing. What is the mistake and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: In a versioned bucket, Expiration acts only on current versions. After 90 days S3 adds a delete marker, and the old data becomes a noncurrent version. Noncurrent versions are still stored and still billed, so the bucket keeps growing. Manual deletes behave the same way. The fix is to add NoncurrentVersionExpiration, for example NoncurrentDays of 30, optionally keeping a few newer noncurrent versions for safety. I would also add a rule to remove expired object delete markers once no versions remain, and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload, because unfinished multipart uploads are billed too and are invisible in normal listings. To check, I would use S3 Storage Lens or an S3 Inventory report to see how much storage is noncurrent versions and incomplete uploads.
keyPoints: Expiration in a versioned bucket only creates delete markers
Noncurrent versions keep being billed
Add NoncurrentVersionExpiration and delete marker cleanup
Abort incomplete multipart uploads; verify with Storage Lens or Inventory

subjective.question: A team will expose a set of Lambda functions as an HTTP API. Compare putting an Application Load Balancer in front of them with using Amazon API Gateway. Which is better for a public partner API with API keys and per-partner rate limits?
subjective.answer: For a public partner API, API Gateway is better. It has features built for APIs: usage plans with API keys, throttling per client and per method, request validation, Cognito, IAM or Lambda authorizers, response caching on REST APIs, stages and custom domains. Per-partner rate limits come straight from usage plans. An ALB can also invoke Lambda as a target. It suits internal or high, steady traffic, because pricing is per hour plus capacity units rather than per request, and it can mix Lambda and EC2 targets behind path rules. But it has no API keys or usage plans, so per-partner throttling would need custom code or AWS WAF rate-based rules, which are coarser. Both work with AWS WAF. So I would choose API Gateway for partner APIs and consider an ALB when cost at very high volume matters more than API management features.
keyPoints: API Gateway offers usage plans, API keys, throttling and authorizers
ALB can target Lambda and is cheaper at high steady volume
ALB lacks per-client API management
Choose by features needed versus cost at scale

subjective.question: A concert ticket site expects 20 times normal traffic when sales open at 10:00. Last time the RDS database was overwhelmed and seats were oversold. Design the architecture to handle the spike and prevent overselling.
subjective.answer: First, cut load before it reaches the app. CloudFront serves static pages and event details, and AWS WAF rate-based rules block bots. A virtual waiting room can control how fast users enter. Second, prepare compute. A scheduled scaling action raises the Auto Scaling group's capacity before 10:00, and a warm pool cuts launch time. Target tracking handles the rest. Third, protect the database. Seat inventory needs atomic updates, so I would either use a DynamoDB table with conditional writes, where a seat is reserved only if its status is 'available', or use database transactions with row locks. Orders go into an SQS queue so payment and confirmation workers process them at a steady rate, not all at once. RDS Proxy pools connections, and ElastiCache caches read-heavy data such as seat maps. Finally, I would load-test at the expected peak and pre-raise any service quotas.
keyPoints: Edge caching, WAF rate limits and a waiting room reduce load
Scheduled scaling and warm pools before the known peak
Atomic seat reservation with conditional writes or transactions
SQS buffers order processing; RDS Proxy and ElastiCache protect the database
Load-test and raise quotas in advance

subjective.question: An Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy on CPU does not add instances, even though CPU has been above target for 20 minutes. How would you find the cause?
subjective.answer: I start with the group's activity history, because it shows failed launches and their reasons. Common causes are: the group is already at MaxSize, so nothing more can launch; launches are failing because of a bad AMI, a deleted key pair, a missing IAM instance profile, or a security group from another VPC in the launch template; the account has hit its EC2 vCPU quota; the AZ has insufficient capacity for that instance type; or the subnets have run out of free IP addresses. I would then check the CloudWatch alarm that target tracking created, to confirm it is in ALARM state and uses the right metric for this group. I would also check whether someone suspended the Launch or AlarmNotification scaling processes, and whether instance warmup settings are delaying new decisions. Fixes include raising MaxSize, correcting the launch template, requesting a quota increase, adding instance types and AZs, or using larger subnets.
keyPoints: Read the Auto Scaling activity history first
Check MaxSize, launch template errors and suspended processes
Check vCPU quotas, AZ capacity and free subnet IPs
Confirm the target tracking alarm and metric are correct

subjective.question: A junior engineer proposes the design below for a production three-tier app. List the mistakes and give a corrected design.

code.code:
- VPC 10.0.0.0/16, public subnets in AZ-a and AZ-b, private subnets in AZ-a and AZ-b
- Internet-facing ALB in the public subnets
- Web/app EC2 Auto Scaling group in the public subnets, public IPs enabled
- RDS MySQL Single-AZ in a public subnet, Publicly accessible = Yes
- DB security group: inbound TCP 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0
- One NAT gateway in AZ-a for all private subnets
- DB master password hard-coded in EC2 user data

subjective.answer: Several mistakes stand out. The app instances sit in public subnets with public IPs, so they are exposed. They should be in private subnets and receive traffic only from the ALB. The database is Single-AZ, publicly accessible and in a public subnet, and its security group allows 3306 from anywhere. That is a serious security and availability risk. RDS should be Multi-AZ, not publicly accessible, use a DB subnet group of private subnets, and its security group should allow 3306 only from the app tier's security group. One NAT gateway in AZ-a is a single point of failure and adds cross-AZ data charges, so I would add one NAT gateway per AZ, each with its own route table. The password in user data can be read by anyone with instance metadata or console access. It should live in AWS Secrets Manager, read by the instance role, with rotation turned on.
keyPoints: App tier belongs in private subnets, reachable only from the ALB
RDS should be Multi-AZ, private, with SG referencing the app SG
One NAT gateway per AZ removes a single point of failure
Store credentials in Secrets Manager, not user data

subjective.question: A developer accidentally dropped an important table in a production RDS for MySQL database at 14:32. Automated backups are enabled. Put the recovery steps in order and explain the cut-over choices.
subjective.answer: First, find the exact time of the mistake from the application logs or MySQL logs, and choose a restore time just before it, such as 14:31. Second, run a point-in-time restore. This always creates a new DB instance with a new endpoint. It never overwrites the existing one. Third, restore it with the same DB subnet group, security groups, parameter group and option group, so it behaves like production. Fourth, validate the restored data. Then choose how to cut over. If only one table was lost and production has taken new writes since, I would export that table from the restored instance with mysqldump and import it into production, which keeps the new data. If the whole database is suspect, I would point the application to the new instance, or rename instances so the new one takes the old endpoint name. Finally, keep the old instance briefly for investigation, then delete it to stop charges.
keyPoints: Identify the exact time and restore to just before it
PITR creates a new instance with a new endpoint
Match subnet group, security groups and parameter group
Either copy the lost table back or cut over the endpoint
Clean up the extra instance afterwards

subjective.question: An SNS topic fans out to an SQS queue, but the queue receives nothing. The subscription shows as confirmed and the queue uses SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key aws/sqs. What is wrong, and what else would you check?
subjective.answer: The main problem is encryption. SNS must be able to use the queue's KMS key to send encrypted messages. The AWS managed key aws/sqs has a key policy you cannot change, so SNS cannot be granted access. The fix is to use a customer managed KMS key whose key policy allows the sns.amazonaws.com service principal to call kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt, or to use SQS managed encryption (SSE-SQS). Next, I would check the SQS queue policy. It must allow sns.amazonaws.com to call sqs:SendMessage, with an aws:SourceArn condition set to the topic ARN. Then I would check for a subscription filter policy that drops the messages. Finally, I would turn on SNS delivery status logging for SQS and watch the CloudWatch metric NumberOfNotificationsFailed, which confirms whether delivery is failing.
keyPoints: SNS cannot use the AWS managed aws/sqs key
Use a customer managed key that allows SNS, or SSE-SQS
Queue policy must allow SNS SendMessage with SourceArn
Check filter policies, delivery logs and failure metrics

subjective.question: A company has 15 VPCs across accounts and a Site-to-Site VPN to its data centre. All VPCs need to reach the data centre, and some need to reach each other. Which is better here, VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway, and why?
subjective.answer: Transit Gateway is better here. VPC peering is one-to-one and not transitive. Full connectivity between 15 VPCs needs 105 peering connections, each with route table entries, and a VPC cannot reach the data centre through another VPC's VPN. That becomes hard to manage quickly. Transit Gateway is a regional hub. Each VPC and the VPN attach once, routing is transitive, and it can be shared across accounts with AWS RAM. Transit Gateway route tables let me segment traffic, for example so production and development VPCs both reach the data centre but not each other. The trade-off is cost and a small extra hop: Transit Gateway charges per attachment-hour and per GB processed, while peering has no hourly charge and no processing fee. So I might still use direct peering for one or two very high-volume VPC pairs. Both options need CIDR ranges that do not overlap.
keyPoints: Peering is non-transitive and needs a full mesh
Transit Gateway is a hub with transitive routing and VPN attachment
TGW route tables provide segmentation; share via AWS RAM
TGW costs per attachment and per GB; peering can suit high-volume pairs
Avoid overlapping CIDRs

subjective.question: A database on EC2 uses a 200 GiB gp2 EBS volume. It runs fine for an hour each morning, then disk latency rises sharply and stays high until the next day. What is the likely cause and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: This is gp2 burst credit exhaustion. A gp2 volume gets baseline IOPS of 3 per GiB, so 200 GiB gives about 600 IOPS. Volumes under 1 TiB can burst to 3,000 IOPS using a credit bucket. The morning load drains the bucket, and then the volume drops to its baseline, which causes the latency. I would confirm it with the CloudWatch BurstBalance metric falling to zero, alongside VolumeReadOps and VolumeWriteOps. The best fix is to change the volume to gp3 using Elastic Volumes. This is done online without detaching. gp3 gives a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size, with no burst credits, and you can provision more IOPS and throughput separately. It is usually cheaper per GiB than gp2. If the workload needs very high, steady IOPS and higher durability, io2 is the next option. I would also check that the instance type's EBS bandwidth is not the limit.
keyPoints: gp2 baseline is 3 IOPS per GiB with burst credits
BurstBalance falling to zero confirms the cause
Modify online to gp3 with Elastic Volumes
Check instance EBS bandwidth; io2 for very high sustained IOPS

subjective.question: In a DR game day, a warm standby failover to the second Region took two hours instead of the planned 15 minutes. What are the likely causes, and how would you bring the RTO down?
subjective.answer: Slow failovers usually come from manual steps and things that were never prepared. Typical causes: engineers worked from an out-of-date runbook and ran commands by hand; the standby Auto Scaling group was too small and took a long time to scale up; the latest AMIs, secrets or configuration were not in the DR Region; service quotas in that Region were too low; the read replica promotion and the application config change were done manually; and DNS records had a long TTL, so clients kept using the old Region. To fix this, I would automate failover with a tested script or Step Functions workflow, keep the full stack in infrastructure as code, and replicate AMIs, parameters and secrets on every release. I would set a higher minimum capacity in standby, pre-raise quotas, use Route 53 health checks with failover routing and a low TTL, and run game days regularly to measure the RTO.
keyPoints: Manual runbook steps and missing artifacts slow recovery
Standby capacity and DR Region quotas must be ready
Long DNS TTLs delay client cut-over
Automate promotion and failover; replicate AMIs and secrets
Test regularly and measure the real RTO

steps.overview: This step covers choosing one Associate specialisation after Solutions Architect – Associate. You can pick Developer (DVA-C02), Machine Learning Engineer (MLA-C01) or Data Engineer (DEA-C01). Each exam has 65 questions in 130 minutes, costs USD 150 and needs 720/1000 to pass. Over Weeks 16–22 you study one path deeply and ship a matching project. That project becomes your exam revision tool and your interview portfolio piece.
objectives: Choose the Associate exam that fits your role, then map its official domains to a 7-week study plan.
Build and deploy one project with infrastructure as code: a serverless API, a SageMaker endpoint or a data pipeline.
Apply the service limits and decision rules each exam tests, for example Lambda timeouts, DynamoDB capacity, SageMaker endpoint types and Kinesis shard throughput.
Instrument your project with CloudWatch, plus X-Ray or SageMaker Model Monitor, so you can troubleshoot it the way exam scenarios expect.
Publish the project in a public repository with a README, an architecture diagram and teardown steps.

concepts.explanation: Lambda can be invoked synchronously (API Gateway), asynchronously (S3, SNS, EventBridge) or through an event source mapping (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams). Async invocations retry and can send failures to a destination or dead-letter queue. With event source mappings, Lambda polls the source and processes records in batches. Cold starts can be reduced with provisioned concurrency or SnapStart for supported runtimes.

concepts.term: API Gateway REST vs HTTP APIs (DVA)
concepts.explanation: REST APIs support API keys and usage plans, request validation, caching and edge-optimized endpoints. HTTP APIs are cheaper and faster, with native JWT authorizers, but have fewer features. Use Lambda authorizers or Cognito user pools for authentication. Use stages and stage variables to separate dev and prod.

Design the partition key for high cardinality so traffic spreads evenly; use a sort key for range queries. Choose GSIs for alternate access patterns and LSIs (created only at table creation) for an alternate sort key. On-demand mode suits spiky or unknown traffic; provisioned mode with auto scaling suits steady traffic. Query is efficient; Scan reads the whole table and is usually the wrong answer.

CodePipeline orchestrates the source, build (CodeBuild with buildspec.yml) and deploy stages. CodeDeploy runs canary or linear traffic shifting for Lambda using aliases, and can roll back automatically on CloudWatch alarms. SAM and CloudFormation define the infrastructure. X-Ray traces requests across services; use annotations (indexed, searchable) for filtering and metadata (not indexed) for extra detail.

Data Wrangler and Processing jobs clean and transform data; Feature Store holds features in online and offline stores. Training jobs read data from S3 and write model artefacts back to S3. You can use built-in algorithms like XGBoost, bring your own script, or bring your own container. Automatic Model Tuning searches hyperparameters, and Clarify detects bias and explains predictions.

Real-time endpoints serve low-latency, steady traffic. Serverless Inference suits intermittent traffic and tolerates cold starts. Asynchronous Inference handles large payloads and long processing times, and can scale to zero. Batch Transform scores whole datasets offline with no persistent endpoint. Model Registry versions approved models, and SageMaker Pipelines automates the ML workflow.

Model Monitor compares live traffic against a baseline to detect data quality drift, model quality drift, bias drift and feature attribution drift. It needs data capture enabled on the endpoint. Results go to S3, and metrics go to CloudWatch for alarms and retraining triggers.

Glue crawlers infer schemas into the Glue Data Catalog, and Glue ETL jobs (Spark or Python shell) transform the data. Job bookmarks prevent reprocessing old data. Athena queries S3 with SQL and is billed per data scanned, so use columnar formats (Parquet/ORC), compression and partitioning. Lake Formation adds fine-grained permissions on top of the Catalog, at database, table, column, row and cell level, including tag-based access control.

Kinesis Data Streams gives ordered, replayable streaming with on-demand or provisioned shards. Amazon Data Firehose loads streams into S3, Redshift or OpenSearch with buffering and no code. Redshift is the data warehouse: choose distribution style (AUTO, KEY, EVEN, ALL) and sort keys for performance, and load data with COPY from S3. Redshift Spectrum queries S3 data directly without loading it.

keyFacts:
Exam domain weights:
- DVA-C02: Development 32%, Security 26%, Deployment 24%, Troubleshooting and Optimization 18%.
- MLA-C01: Data Preparation 28%, Model Development 26%, Deployment and Orchestration 22%, Monitoring, Maintenance and Security 24%.
- DEA-C01: Ingestion and Transformation 34%, Store Management 26%, Operations and Support 22%, Security and Governance 18%.
Lambda limits: maximum timeout 15 minutes; memory 128 MB to 10,240 MB (CPU scales with memory); ephemeral /tmp storage up to 10 GB; synchronous request and response payload 6 MB each.
API Gateway has a default integration timeout of 29 seconds. Long-running work should go asynchronous, for example through SQS, Step Functions or SageMaker Async Inference.

DynamoDB: maximum item size 400 KB. 1 RCU = 1 strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB, or 2 eventually consistent reads. 1 WCU = 1 write per second of up to 1 KB. Transactional operations cost double.
Kinesis Data Streams provisioned shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s for writes, and 2 MB/s for reads. Enhanced fan-out gives each consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard.

SageMaker endpoint choice:
- Real-time for steady, low-latency traffic.
- Serverless for spiky traffic with idle gaps.
- Asynchronous for payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to 1 hour.
- Batch Transform for offline scoring of whole datasets.
To reduce Athena cost and scan time: convert to Parquet or ORC, compress, partition (for example by date), and use partition projection when there are many partitions.
Secrets go in Secrets Manager (supports rotation) or SSM Parameter Store SecureString, never in code or plain environment variables. KMS envelope encryption is used for data over 4 KB.

example.caption: Developer path: a minimal AWS SAM template for a serverless notes API (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB) with X-Ray tracing. Deploy with `sam build && sam deploy --guided`.
example.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Description: Notes API for DVA-C02 portfolio
Globals:
  Function:
    Runtime: python3.12
    Timeout: 10
    MemorySize: 256
    Tracing: Active
Resources:
  NotesTable:
    Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
    Properties:
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
      AttributeDefinitions:
        - {AttributeName: noteId, AttributeType: S}
      KeySchema:
        - {AttributeName: noteId, KeyType: HASH}
  NotesFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      CodeUri: src/
      Handler: app.handler
      Environment:
        Variables: {TABLE_NAME: !Ref NotesTable}
      Policies:
        - DynamoDBCrudPolicy: {TableName: !Ref NotesTable}
      Events:
        GetNote: {Type: Api, Properties: {Path: /notes/{id}, Method: get}}
        PutNote: {Type: Api, Properties: {Path: /notes, Method: post}}
Outputs:
  ApiUrl:
    Value: !Sub https://${ServerlessRestApi}.execute-api.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com/Prod/notes

pitfalls: Picking an exam by hype, not by your job. Choose Developer if you write application code, ML Engineer if you train or deploy models, and Data Engineer if you build pipelines or warehouses. Interviewers will probe your project deeply.
Answering 'Scan' or 'increase Lambda timeout' by reflex. The exam usually prefers Query with a GSI, or an asynchronous pattern, because the API Gateway integration timeout is 29 seconds by default.

Confusing similar services:
- Kinesis Data Streams (custom consumers, replay) vs Amazon Data Firehose (managed delivery, near real-time).
- SageMaker Serverless Inference vs Asynchronous Inference.
- X-Ray annotations (indexed) vs metadata (not indexed).
Ignoring security questions, which carry 18–26% weight on every exam. Expect least-privilege IAM roles, KMS encryption, VPC endpoints, Lake Formation permissions and Secrets Manager rotation.
Leaving resources running after the project. SageMaker real-time endpoints, Redshift clusters, NAT gateways and provisioned Kinesis shards bill by the hour. Add budgets, alerts and a teardown script.
Publishing a repo with hard-coded access keys or account IDs. Use IAM roles and OIDC for CI, add a .gitignore, and run a secrets scanner before making the repo public.

workflow.title: From exam choice to public portfolio project

steps.label: Pick exam and read guide
steps.detail: Download the official exam guide for DVA-C02, MLA-C01 or DEA-C01 and list every in-scope service against its domain weight.

steps.label: Design a matching architecture
steps.detail: Pick one project: an API Gateway–Lambda–DynamoDB API, an S3–SageMaker training-to-endpoint flow, or a Kinesis/S3–Glue–Athena/Redshift pipeline.

steps.label: Define everything as code
steps.detail: Write SAM, CloudFormation or CDK templates with least-privilege IAM roles and KMS encryption so the stack deploys and deletes in one command.

steps.label: Automate deployment with CI/CD
steps.detail: Use CodePipeline or GitHub Actions with OIDC to test, build and deploy on every push, using canary deployment for Lambda or Model Registry approval for ML.

steps.label: Add monitoring and tracing
steps.detail: Enable CloudWatch alarms plus X-Ray, Model Monitor or Glue job metrics, then deliberately break something and practise troubleshooting it.

steps.label: Document and publish
steps.detail: Push to a public repository with a README, an architecture diagram, cost notes and teardown steps, then destroy the stack.

steps.label: Practise and book exam
steps.detail: Take official practice question sets, review every wrong answer against your project, and book once you score consistently above 80%.

project.title: orders-api
project.summary: A serverless orders API for the Developer – Associate (DVA-C02) path: API Gateway HTTP API → Lambda (Python) → DynamoDB single table, deployed with AWS SAM, traced with X-Ray and shipped through a CodePipeline/CodeBuild buildspec with a canary Lambda deployment. template.yaml is the infrastructure, src/app.py shows the Lambda execution model and DynamoDB access patterns, tests/test_app.py and buildspec.yml show CI, and README.md holds the architecture diagram for the checkpoint.
project.run:
python3 -m pip install pytest boto3
python3 -m pytest tests -q
sam build
sam deploy --guided
curl -X POST "$API_URL/orders" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"customerId":"c1","amount":499.50}'
curl "$API_URL/customers/c1/orders"

files.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31   # SAM transform expands Serverless::* resources
Description: orders-api - HTTP API + Lambda + DynamoDB (DVA-C02 sample)

Globals:
  Function:
    Runtime: python3.12
    Architectures: [arm64]      # Graviton: lower cost per GB-second
    MemorySize: 256             # CPU scales with memory
    Timeout: 10                 # seconds; keep below the API integration timeout
    Tracing: Active             # X-Ray active tracing for Lambda

Resources:
  OrdersTable:
    Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
    Properties:
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST   # on-demand capacity, no RCU/WCU planning
      AttributeDefinitions:
        - { AttributeName: PK, AttributeType: S }
        - { AttributeName: SK, AttributeType: S }
      KeySchema:
        - { AttributeName: PK, KeyType: HASH }    # partition key: CUSTOMER#<id>
        - { AttributeName: SK, KeyType: RANGE }   # sort key: ORDER#<timestamp>#<id>

  OrdersApi:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::HttpApi   # HTTP API: cheaper, lower latency than REST API

  OrdersFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      CodeUri: src/
      Handler: app.handler           # file app.py, function handler
      Environment:
        Variables:
          TABLE_NAME: !Ref OrdersTable
      Policies:
        - DynamoDBCrudPolicy:        # least-privilege policy template scoped to one table
            TableName: !Ref OrdersTable
      AutoPublishAlias: live         # publishes a version and points alias 'live' at it
      DeploymentPreference:
        Type: Canary10Percent5Minutes   # CodeDeploy shifts 10% traffic, then 100% after 5 min
      Events:
        CreateOrder:
          Type: HttpApi
          Properties:
            ApiId: !Ref OrdersApi
            Path: /orders
            Method: POST
        ListOrders:
          Type: HttpApi
          Properties:
            ApiId: !Ref OrdersApi
            Path: /customers/{customerId}/orders
            Method: GET

Outputs:
  ApiUrl:
    Description: Base URL of the HTTP API ($default stage)
    Value: !Sub https://${OrdersApi}.execute-api.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com
  TableName:
    Value: !Ref OrdersTable

import json
import os
import sys

# Set env vars before import: app.py reads TABLE_NAME at init time
os.environ.setdefault("TABLE_NAME", "test-orders")
os.environ.setdefault("AWS_DEFAULT_REGION", "ap-south-1")
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "src"))

import app  # noqa: E402


class FakeTable:
    """Stands in for the DynamoDB Table so tests need no AWS account."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []

    def put_item(self, Item, ConditionExpression):
        self.items.append(Item)


def test_create_order_ok(monkeypatch):
    fake = FakeTable()
    monkeypatch.setattr(app, "TABLE", fake)
    event = {"routeKey": "POST /orders", "body": json.dumps({"customerId": "c1", "amount": 499.5})}
    resp = app.handler(event, None)
    assert resp["statusCode"] == 201
    assert fake.items[0]["PK"] == "CUSTOMER#c1"
    assert fake.items[0]["SK"].startswith("ORDER#")


def test_create_order_rejects_bad_amount():
    event = {"routeKey": "POST /orders", "body": json.dumps({"customerId": "c1", "amount": -1})}
    assert app.handler(event, None)["statusCode"] == 400


def test_unknown_route():
    assert app.handler({"routeKey": "DELETE /orders"}, None)["statusCode"] == 404

# CodeBuild spec used by the Build stage of CodePipeline (Source -> Build -> Deploy)
version: 0.2

env:
  variables:
    ARTIFACT_BUCKET: "replace-with-your-artifact-bucket"   # S3 bucket for packaged code

phases:
  install:
    runtime-versions:
      python: 3.12
    commands:
      - pip install pytest boto3
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - python -m pytest tests -q          # fail the pipeline if unit tests fail
  build:
    commands:
      - sam build                          # SAM CLI is preinstalled on standard CodeBuild images
      - sam package --s3-bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" --output-template-file packaged.yaml

artifacts:
  files:
    - packaged.yaml   # Deploy stage: CloudFormation action creates/executes a change set from this

# orders-api (DVA-C02 hands-on)

Serverless orders API: API Gateway HTTP API -> Lambda (Python 3.12) -> DynamoDB.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Client] -->|HTTPS| A[API Gateway HTTP API]
  A -->|payload v2.0| L[Lambda OrdersFunction alias live]
  L -->|PutItem / Query| D[(DynamoDB OrdersTable PK/SK)]
  L -.->|traces| X[AWS X-Ray]
  L -.->|logs| W[CloudWatch Logs]
  G[GitHub repo] --> P[CodePipeline] --> B[CodeBuild buildspec.yml] --> CF[CloudFormation deploy]
  CF -.->|canary 10% / 5 min| L
```

## Endpoints
- `POST /orders` body `{"customerId":"c1","amount":499.50}` -> 201
- `GET /customers/{customerId}/orders` -> newest 25 orders

## Deploy
1. `python3 -m pytest tests -q`
2. `sam build && sam deploy --guided` (pick a region such as ap-south-1)
3. Copy the `ApiUrl` output into `API_URL` and run the curl commands.
4. Clean up: `sam delete`

## Exam points shown here
- Init code outside the handler is reused on warm starts (Lambda execution model).
- HTTP API is cheaper and faster; REST API adds usage plans, API keys, request validation, caching and X-Ray tracing at the API stage.
- Single-table design: access patterns drive PK/SK; use Query, avoid Scan.
- On-demand capacity vs provisioned RCU/WCU; ConditionExpression for safe writes.
- `AutoPublishAlias` + `DeploymentPreference` = CodeDeploy canary for Lambda.
- `Tracing: Active` sends Lambda traces to X-Ray; view them in the CloudWatch console.

## Checkpoint
Push this folder to a public GitHub repo; the Mermaid diagram above renders on GitHub.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to DVA-C02 Development, Security and Troubleshooting; MLA-C01 Deployment and Orchestration and Monitoring; and DEA-C01 Ingestion and Transformation and Store Management. All three exams use long scenario questions with several technically valid options. The winning answer is the one that meets the stated constraint, such as least operational overhead, lowest cost, replay or strict latency, without over-engineering. Security choices like IAM, KMS, Secrets Manager and Lake Formation appear inside almost every scenario, not only in the security domain.

compare.difference: Data Streams keeps records for a retention period, so multiple custom consumers can read and replay them. Firehose is a fully managed delivery service that buffers data and writes it to destinations such as S3, Redshift or OpenSearch, with no replay.
compare.chooseA: Pick Data Streams when the question mentions replay, ordering per partition key, multiple independent consumers or sub-second custom processing.
compare.chooseB: Pick Firehose when the goal is to land streaming data in S3 or Redshift with the least operational overhead, optionally converting it to Parquet or transforming it with Lambda.

compare.difference: Serverless gives a synchronous response for small, quick requests and scales to zero during idle gaps, but cold starts can occur. Async queues requests, handles very large payloads and long processing, and writes results to S3.
compare.chooseA: Pick Serverless for intermittent or spiky traffic with small payloads where the caller waits for the answer and some cold-start latency is acceptable.
compare.chooseB: Pick Async when payloads are large or inference takes minutes, the caller can poll or receive an SNS notification, and you want to scale to zero between bursts.

compare.difference: A GSI can use a different partition key, can be added at any time, has its own capacity, and supports only eventually consistent reads. An LSI shares the table's partition key, must be created with the table, and supports strongly consistent reads.
compare.chooseA: Pick a GSI when you need to query by a different attribute on an existing table. This is the usual exam fix for a slow Scan.
compare.chooseB: Pick an LSI only when the table is being created, the partition key stays the same, you need an alternate sort key, and strongly consistent reads are required.

compare.difference: REST APIs have more features: usage plans and API keys, request validation, response caching, AWS WAF integration and private endpoints. HTTP APIs are cheaper and lower-latency, with native JWT/OIDC authorizers.
compare.chooseA: Pick REST when the question needs throttling per customer with API keys, caching, WAF, request validation or a private API.
compare.chooseB: Pick HTTP API for a simple, low-cost Lambda or HTTP proxy, especially with Cognito or another OIDC provider issuing JWTs.

compare.difference: Secrets Manager has built-in automatic rotation, for example for RDS credentials, and charges per secret. Parameter Store stores KMS-encrypted values with a free standard tier but no native rotation.
compare.chooseA: Pick Secrets Manager whenever the question says rotate automatically or mentions database credentials with rotation.
compare.chooseB: Pick Parameter Store SecureString for configuration values or secrets that do not need rotation when cost matters.

cues.cue: Filter or search traces by user ID or order ID
cues.pick: X-Ray annotations
cues.why: Annotations are indexed and usable in filter expressions; metadata is not indexed.

cues.cue: Latency-sensitive Lambda suffers cold starts
cues.pick: Provisioned concurrency on an alias or version
cues.why: It keeps execution environments initialised, so the first requests avoid init time.

cues.cue: Shift traffic gradually to a new Lambda version and roll back on alarms
cues.pick: CodeDeploy with Lambda aliases (canary or linear) plus CloudWatch alarms
cues.why: CodeDeploy shifts alias weights and rolls back automatically when an alarm fires.

cues.cue: Athena queries are slow and expensive on raw CSV logs
cues.pick: Convert to compressed Parquet and partition by date (Glue ETL or Firehose format conversion)
cues.why: Columnar format plus partition pruning cuts the bytes scanned, which is what Athena bills on.

cues.cue: Grant column-level or row-level access to data lake tables across teams
cues.pick: AWS Lake Formation permissions (LF-Tags or data filters)
cues.why: Lake Formation centralises fine-grained access on the Glue Data Catalog instead of complex S3 bucket policies.

cues.cue: Glue job reprocesses old files on every run
cues.pick: Glue job bookmarks
cues.why: Bookmarks track already processed data so each run handles only new input.

cues.cue: Production model accuracy drops as input data changes over time
cues.pick: SageMaker Model Monitor (data quality and model quality), with Clarify for bias and feature attribution drift
cues.why: It compares live captured data against a baseline and raises CloudWatch alerts on drift.

cues.cue: ProvisionedThroughputExceeded on a Kinesis stream or DynamoDB table with one hot key
cues.pick: A higher-cardinality partition key (then add shards or capacity if still needed)
cues.why: Throttling from uneven key distribution is not fixed by capacity alone; spread the writes first.

scenario.situation: A company exposes a report-generation feature through Amazon API Gateway (REST API) backed by AWS Lambda. Generating a report takes 2 to 4 minutes. Users get 504 errors even though the Lambda timeout is set to 10 minutes. The team wants a reliable fix with minimal operational overhead. What should a developer do?
reasoning: Find the real bottleneck: the 504 comes from the API Gateway integration timeout, not the Lambda timeout, so raising the Lambda timeout or memory does not fix the client error.
Reject 'increase the API Gateway timeout'. Even where a quota increase is possible, holding a synchronous HTTP connection open for minutes is fragile, and it is not the pattern the exam rewards.
Reject running the job on EC2 or ECS behind the API. That adds servers and operational overhead without solving the synchronous wait.

Choose an asynchronous pattern. API Gateway or a front Lambda puts a job on SQS or starts a Step Functions execution and returns 202 with a job ID. A worker Lambda builds the report and stores it in S3. The client polls a status endpoint or is notified.
scenario.answer: Make the workflow asynchronous: accept the request and return a job ID immediately, process the report through SQS or Step Functions with Lambda, and serve the result from S3. This removes the 29-second synchronous limit using fully managed services.

memoryAids: Streams = Store and replay; Firehose = Fire and forget into a destination.
SageMaker endpoints, RSAB: Real-time for Regular traffic, Serverless for Sporadic traffic, Async for big and slow requests, Batch for bulk offline scoring.
DynamoDB math: 'Read 4, Write 1': divide the item size by 4 KB for reads and 1 KB for writes, always round up. Eventually consistent = half, transactional = double.
cheatSheet: RCU example: a 10 KB strongly consistent read uses ceil(10/4) = 3 RCU; eventually consistent uses 1.5; transactional uses 6.
WCU example: a 2.5 KB item write uses 3 WCU; a transactional write uses 6.
Query with a partition key (plus a GSI if needed) beats Scan; Scan is the wrong answer unless you truly need the whole table.
Lambda gets more CPU only by adding memory; CPU-bound and slow often means raise memory, not timeout.
SQS triggering Lambda: set the queue visibility timeout well above the function timeout, and use a DLQ or on-failure destination for poison messages.
Lambda permissions: an execution role for what the function calls, and a resource-based policy for who can invoke it.
Redshift: bulk load with COPY from S3, not row-by-row INSERTs; query S3 data in place with Redshift Spectrum.
Glue crawler builds the Data Catalog schema; Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR all read that catalog.
Kinesis: many consumers competing for read throughput means enhanced fan-out; write throttling means a better partition key or more shards (or on-demand mode).
SageMaker: training data comes from S3; use Pipe or FastFile mode for large datasets; use Spot training with checkpoints to cut cost.
Encryption cue: S3 or EBS data with audit of key usage means SSE-KMS with a customer managed key; cross-account access needs both a key policy and an IAM grant.
Private access to S3 or DynamoDB from a VPC without a NAT gateway means a gateway VPC endpoint; most other services use interface endpoints (PrivateLink).
selfCheck: I can calculate RCU and WCU for any item size and consistency mode without a calculator.
I can explain why a 504 from API Gateway needs an asynchronous design, and draw that design with SQS or Step Functions.
I can choose between real-time, serverless, async and batch SageMaker inference from a traffic and payload description.
I can choose between Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose, and between a GSI and an LSI, and justify each in one sentence.
I can list three ways to cut Athena cost, and say where Lake Formation fits in data lake security.
I can walk an interviewer through my public project repo: the architecture diagram, IAM roles, how secrets are stored, and how to tear it down.

objective.question: A developer has a Lambda function that processes uploaded video files. Some files take about 25 minutes to process, and the function fails on those files. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Increase the function memory to 10,240 MB so it always finishes within the timeout
Move the long-running processing to AWS Fargate or split it into steps orchestrated by AWS Step Functions
Enable provisioned concurrency so the function does not time out
Increase the Lambda timeout to 30 minutes in the function configuration
objective.explanation: The maximum Lambda timeout is 15 minutes, so 25-minute jobs need a different compute option or must be broken into smaller steps. More memory may speed up the code but does not guarantee the job finishes in time. Provisioned concurrency only reduces cold starts; it does not change the timeout.

objective.question: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway invokes a Lambda function synchronously to generate a report. Report generation takes about 2 minutes, and clients receive HTTP 504 errors. Which design solves this with the least client-side waiting?
options: Switch from a REST API to an HTTP API, which has no integration timeout
Enable API Gateway caching so repeated requests return faster
Have the API send the request to an SQS queue, return HTTP 202 with a job ID, and let a worker process the queue and store the result for the client to fetch later
Increase the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes
objective.explanation: API Gateway has a default integration timeout of 29 seconds, so long work should be made asynchronous, for example with SQS and a job-status endpoint. Raising the Lambda timeout does not change the API Gateway limit, and HTTP APIs also have an integration timeout. Caching does not help the first request.

objective.question: An application performs 80 strongly consistent reads per second on a DynamoDB table. Each item is 6 KB. How many read capacity units (RCUs) are needed in provisioned mode?
objective.explanation: One RCU covers one strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB, so a 6 KB item rounds up to 8 KB and needs 2 RCUs. 80 reads × 2 RCUs = 160 RCUs. With eventually consistent reads the answer would be 80.

objective.question: A payment service uses DynamoDB TransactWriteItems to write 50 items per second. Each item is 1.5 KB. How many write capacity units (WCUs) are needed?
objective.explanation: One WCU covers one 1 KB write per second, so a 1.5 KB item rounds up to 2 WCUs. Transactional writes cost double, so each write needs 4 WCUs, and 50 × 4 = 200 WCUs.

objective.question: A team deploys a Lambda-based API with AWS SAM. They want new versions to receive 10% of traffic for 5 minutes and to roll back automatically if errors rise. What should they use?
options: AWS CodeBuild with a buildspec that deletes the old function version
An API Gateway stage variable switched manually after testing
Lambda reserved concurrency set to 10% of the account limit
AWS CodeDeploy with a canary deployment preference on a Lambda alias, linked to CloudWatch alarms
objective.explanation: SAM's DeploymentPreference uses CodeDeploy to shift traffic on a Lambda alias, for example with a canary 10% for 5 minutes setting, and rolls back when the linked CloudWatch alarms fire. CodeBuild only builds and tests. Stage variables and reserved concurrency do not give automatic traffic shifting or rollback.

objective.question: A company needs a public API that gives partners API keys with per-partner throttling and quotas. It must also validate request bodies before invoking Lambda. Which API Gateway option should they choose?
options: REST API with usage plans, API keys and request validation
HTTP API with a Lambda authorizer and stage variables
WebSocket API with a Lambda authorizer
HTTP API with a JWT authorizer
objective.explanation: API keys, usage plans and built-in request validation are REST API features. HTTP APIs are cheaper and simpler and support JWT authorizers, but they do not offer usage plans or request validation. WebSocket APIs are for two-way persistent connections.

objective.question: A developer uses AWS X-Ray to trace a Lambda function. The support team needs to search traces by customer ID in the X-Ray console using filter expressions. How should the developer record the customer ID?
options: Add it as an annotation on the segment or subsegment
Put it in the Lambda function's environment variables
Write it to CloudWatch Logs with console.log
Add it as metadata on the segment
objective.explanation: Annotations are indexed key-value pairs, so you can use them in X-Ray filter expressions. Metadata is stored with the trace but is not indexed for search. Logs and environment variables are not part of trace filtering.

objective.question: A Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database. Security requires that the password is not stored in code and is rotated automatically every 30 days. What is the best solution?
options: Store the password in an S3 object encrypted with SSE-S3
Hard-code the password and encrypt the deployment package with KMS
Store the password as a plain Lambda environment variable and update it monthly
Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager with rotation enabled and retrieve it at runtime
objective.explanation: Secrets Manager stores secrets securely and supports built-in automatic rotation, including for RDS. Plain environment variables and code are not acceptable for secrets. S3 is not a secrets store and gives no rotation.

objective.question: A retail company has a SageMaker model that gets traffic in bursts during sales hours and almost no requests overnight. They want to pay nothing for idle compute and can accept occasional cold-start latency. The model does not need a GPU. Which inference option fits best?
options: Serverless Inference
Batch Transform
Real-time inference on a GPU instance with auto scaling
Real-time inference endpoint with a fixed instance count
objective.explanation: Serverless Inference suits spiky traffic with idle gaps, scales automatically and charges only for compute used, at the cost of possible cold starts. Real-time endpoints keep instances running and billing all the time. Batch Transform is for offline scoring of whole datasets, not live requests.

objective.question: A medical imaging team sends 600 MB image files to a SageMaker model. Each inference takes about 20 minutes. Clients can wait for a notification when results are ready. Which option should they use?
options: Asynchronous Inference
A Lambda function that loads the model from S3
Serverless Inference
Real-time inference
objective.explanation: Asynchronous Inference supports payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to 1 hour, queues requests, writes results to S3 and can send SNS notifications. Real-time and Serverless Inference are for small payloads and short responses. Lambda has a 15-minute timeout and a 6 MB synchronous payload limit.

objective.question: An ML team computes customer features for training. They also need the same features with millisecond latency at inference time, and want to avoid training-serving skew. Which SageMaker capability should they use?
options: SageMaker Model Monitor
SageMaker Clarify
SageMaker Batch Transform
SageMaker Feature Store with both online and offline stores
objective.explanation: Feature Store keeps an online store for low-latency lookups at inference and an offline store in S3 for training. Both come from the same feature definitions, which reduces training-serving skew. Model Monitor and Clarify watch models and explain them; Batch Transform scores offline.

objective.question: A loan-approval model is deployed on a SageMaker real-time endpoint. Regulators require the company to detect if the model starts treating an age group unfairly over time. What should the ML engineer set up?
options: Endpoint auto scaling based on InvocationsPerInstance
A data quality monitor that checks only for missing values
A SageMaker Model Monitor bias drift monitoring schedule using SageMaker Clarify, with a baseline from training data
A CloudWatch alarm on the endpoint's Invocation5XXErrors metric
objective.explanation: Model Monitor's bias drift monitoring uses Clarify to compare live predictions against a bias baseline and flags changes in fairness metrics. Error and scaling metrics show health, not fairness. A data quality check finds schema and statistics drift, not bias.

objective.question: Analysts run daily Amazon Athena queries on 5 TB of CSV logs in S3. Most queries filter on a single day. Costs are high because each query scans the whole dataset. Which change reduces cost the most?
options: Convert the data to compressed Parquet and partition it by date in S3
Create more Glue crawlers to scan the data more often
Move the CSV files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Run the queries in a larger Athena workgroup
objective.explanation: Athena charges by data scanned. Columnar, compressed Parquet reads only the needed columns, and date partitions let Athena skip days that are not queried. Workgroups and extra crawlers do not reduce scanned data, and Athena cannot query objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval directly.

objective.question: A data lake on S3 is catalogued in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. The finance team must see all columns of the sales table. The marketing team must not see the customer_email column, and should see only rows for their region. What is the simplest way to enforce this for Athena users?
options: Use AWS Lake Formation permissions with data filters for column-level and row-level access
Encrypt the customer_email column with a separate KMS key
Use S3 bucket policies with conditions on column names
Create separate S3 buckets with copies of the data for each team
objective.explanation: Lake Formation provides fine-grained access, including column, row and cell-level security through data filters, and Athena enforces it. S3 bucket policies work at object level, not column level. Copying data adds cost and drift, and KMS keys do not filter rows.

objective.question: An IoT application writes 5 MB/s of data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams in provisioned mode, at 3,000 records per second. What is the minimum number of shards required to handle the writes?
objective.explanation: Each provisioned shard accepts up to 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s for writes. 5 MB/s needs 5 shards and 3,000 records/s needs 3 shards, so the larger value, 5 shards, is the minimum.

objective.question: A Lambda function processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue with a batch size of 10. The event source mapping has ReportBatchItemFailures enabled. One message in a batch fails. What happens?
options: Only the failed message becomes visible again for retry; the other 9 are deleted from the queue
The failed message is sent straight to the dead-letter queue without any retry
Lambda ignores the return value and deletes all 10 messages because the function did not raise an error
The whole batch of 10 messages becomes visible again and is retried
objective.explanation: With ReportBatchItemFailures enabled, Lambda deletes the successful messages and returns only the listed message IDs to the queue. Without this setting, a failed batch would be retried in full. Messages reach the DLQ only after the queue's maxReceiveCount is exceeded.

objective.question: Two users edit the same DynamoDB item at the same time, and one update silently overwrites the other. The developer changes the update call as shown. What does this change achieve?
options: It implements optimistic locking; the write fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException if another writer has already changed the version
It locks the item for 5 seconds so other writers must wait
It makes the read strongly consistent before the write
It enables DynamoDB transactions across multiple tables
objective.explanation: A condition on a version attribute is optimistic locking. The update succeeds only if the item still has the expected version, and otherwise DynamoDB throws ConditionalCheckFailedException so the client can re-read and retry. DynamoDB does not hold time-based locks, and this call has nothing to do with read consistency or multi-table transactions.

objective.question: An API Gateway REST API uses Lambda proxy integration. The function runs without error, but clients receive HTTP 502 Bad Gateway. What is the most likely cause?
options: The API stage has not been deployed
The Lambda function has exceeded its reserved concurrency
The client did not send an API key
The function returns a plain object instead of the proxy format with statusCode and a string body
objective.explanation: Proxy integration expects a response such as {'statusCode': 200, 'headers': {...}, 'body': json.dumps(result)}. Any other shape gives a 502 malformed proxy response. A missing API key gives 403, and throttling gives 429.

objective.question: A Lambda function must read from an Amazon RDS instance in private subnets. It must also call a third-party payment API on the public internet. After the function is attached to the VPC, the external calls time out. What should the developer do?
options: Run the function in private subnets whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway in a public subnet
Move the function to a public subnet with a route to the internet gateway
Create a VPC interface endpoint for the third-party API
Attach an Elastic IP address to the Lambda function
objective.explanation: Lambda ENIs in a VPC never get public IPs, so a public subnet with an internet gateway does not give them internet access. A NAT gateway does. You cannot attach an Elastic IP to a function. VPC endpoints only reach AWS services or PrivateLink services, not an arbitrary internet API.

objective.question: A SageMaker training job reads a 2 TB dataset of many files from S3. It uses File input mode, and each job spends a long time before training starts. The algorithm reads files sequentially. Which change reduces start-up time with the least code change?
options: Increase the EBS volume size of the training instance
Use a larger instance type with more GPUs
Enable managed spot training
Switch the input mode to FastFile so data is streamed from S3 on demand through a file-system interface
objective.explanation: File mode copies the whole dataset to the instance before training begins. FastFile mode streams objects from S3 as they are read, and the training code still sees ordinary file paths. Bigger volumes, more GPUs or spot capacity do not remove the initial download time.

objective.question: An ML engineer wants to test a new model version on a live SageMaker real-time endpoint. 90% of traffic should go to the current model and 10% to the new model, with metrics for each version in CloudWatch. What is the best approach?
options: Deploy a batch transform job for the new model and compare outputs
Add the new model as a second production variant in the endpoint configuration with weights of 0.9 and 0.1
Use SageMaker Model Monitor to split the traffic
Create a second endpoint and use Route 53 weighted records
objective.explanation: A SageMaker endpoint can host several production variants with traffic weights. SageMaker reports per-variant CloudWatch metrics, and you can shift the weights without redeploying. Route 53 would need two endpoints and more work, batch transform is offline, and Model Monitor does not route traffic.

objective.question: An AWS Glue ETL job runs every hour on an S3 prefix where new files arrive all the time. Each run reprocesses all historical files, which creates duplicates and higher cost. What should the data engineer enable?
options: S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the source bucket
Glue Flex execution class
Glue job bookmarks
Glue crawler schema change policy
objective.explanation: Job bookmarks store state from earlier runs, so the job processes only new data. Crawler policies control schema updates, Intelligent-Tiering changes storage cost, and Flex lowers the cost of non-urgent jobs. None of these stop reprocessing.

objective.question: A nightly Redshift load runs the command below on a provisioned cluster with many slices. The source is a single 40 GB gzip file, and the load is slow. What change will speed it up most?

code.code:
COPY sales
FROM 's3://lake/exports/sales_full.csv.gz'
IAM_ROLE 'arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/RedshiftLoad'
FORMAT AS CSV
GZIP;

options: Run VACUUM before the COPY
Split the data into multiple compressed files, ideally a multiple of the number of slices, and COPY from the prefix or a manifest
Remove GZIP so the file is uncompressed
Replace COPY with many INSERT statements run in parallel
objective.explanation: COPY loads in parallel across slices, but a single gzip file can be read by only one slice. Splitting into evenly sized files lets every slice work at once. Row-by-row INSERTs are much slower, and VACUUM does not affect load parallelism.

objective.question: A Kinesis Data Streams producer gets ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors. CloudWatch shows that total stream throughput is well below the combined capacity of all shards. The producer uses the device type (only 3 values) as the partition key. What is the best fix?
options: Switch consumers to enhanced fan-out
Use a high-cardinality partition key, such as the device ID, so records spread across all shards
Increase the stream data retention period
Double the number of shards
objective.explanation: With only 3 partition key values, records hash to at most 3 shards, and those hot shards exceed their per-shard write limits. A high-cardinality key spreads the load evenly. Adding shards does not help when keys map to few shards, and enhanced fan-out and retention affect reads, not writes.

objective.question: A Lambda function consumes messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue. The function timeout is 5 minutes and the queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds. Many messages are processed two or three times. What is the most likely cause?
options: The visibility timeout is shorter than the function's run time, so messages become visible again and are picked up while still being processed.
Reserved concurrency is set too low, so Lambda retries each message on another instance.
The batch size is too large, so Lambda splits batches and resends them.
Standard queues deliver every message at least twice by design.
objective.explanation: If a message becomes visible again before the function finishes, another poller receives it again. AWS recommends a visibility timeout of at least six times the function timeout. Standard queues can deliver duplicates occasionally, but not routinely, and batch size or concurrency does not cause this pattern.

objective.question: A Lambda function processes a DynamoDB stream. One malformed record makes the function throw an exception. Processing of that shard stops for hours, and the IteratorAge metric keeps rising. Which configuration fixes this with the least data loss?
options: Enable BisectBatchOnFunctionError, set a limited MaximumRetryAttempts, and configure an on-failure destination such as an SQS queue.
Replace the DynamoDB stream with an SQS FIFO queue.
Increase the function timeout to 15 minutes.
Increase the batch size so the bad record is processed with more good records.
objective.explanation: For stream sources, a failing record blocks its shard until it expires or succeeds. Bisecting isolates the bad record, limited retries stop endless blocking, and the on-failure destination keeps a record of the failed batch for later fixing. A larger batch or a longer timeout does not remove the bad record, and replacing the stream is a redesign, not a fix.

objective.question: A Lambda function reads objects from an S3 bucket. The bucket uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. The function's role has the policy below, and GetObject returns AccessDenied. What should the developer add?
options: kms:Encrypt on the KMS key ARN
s3:GetObjectVersion on the object ARN
kms:Decrypt on the KMS key ARN, with the key policy also allowing the role
s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN
objective.explanation: Reading an SSE-KMS object needs s3:GetObject and also kms:Decrypt on the key, which the key policy must permit. s3:ListBucket only changes how missing objects are reported, and kms:Encrypt is needed for writes, not reads.

objective.question: A React app on https://app.example.com calls an API Gateway REST API that uses Lambda proxy integration. The developer used 'Enable CORS' in the console, so OPTIONS preflight requests succeed. The browser still blocks the GET responses. What is the cause?
options: The API needs a Cognito authorizer before CORS headers are added.
The API stage must be redeployed as an edge-optimised endpoint.
REST APIs do not support CORS; only HTTP APIs do.
With proxy integration, the Lambda function must return the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header in its own response.
objective.explanation: In proxy integration, API Gateway passes the Lambda response through unchanged, so the function must include the CORS headers on every actual response. REST APIs do support CORS, and the authorizer and endpoint type are unrelated to this browser error.

objective.question: You are deploying a trained model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint with the low-level API. In which order must you call the operations?
options: CreateModel → CreateEndpointConfig → CreateEndpoint
CreateModel → CreateEndpoint → CreateEndpointConfig
CreateEndpointConfig → CreateModel → CreateEndpoint
CreateEndpoint → CreateModel → CreateEndpointConfig
objective.explanation: The model (container image plus model artifacts) comes first. The endpoint configuration then refers to the model and sets the instance type and count. The endpoint is created last from that configuration.

objective.question: A DynamoDB table in provisioned mode has 1,000 WCUs. Writes are throttled, but CloudWatch shows the table consuming only about 400 WCUs. The table has one GSI with 100 WCUs that projects ALL attributes. What is the cause?
options: The GSI does not have enough write capacity, and GSI throttling creates back-pressure that throttles writes to the base table.
Provisioned tables can only use 40% of their WCUs until auto scaling is enabled.
Strongly consistent reads on the GSI are using the table's write capacity.
The partition key of the base table has too many distinct values.
objective.explanation: Every base-table write that changes an indexed attribute also writes to the GSI. If the GSI runs out of WCUs, DynamoDB throttles the base-table writes too. Many distinct partition keys is good, not bad, and GSIs do not support strongly consistent reads at all.

objective.question: A teammate commits the CodeBuild buildspec below so the build can deploy with SAM. What is the best fix?

code.code:
version: 0.2
env:
  variables:
    AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: AKIAEXAMPLE123
    AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: wJalrEXAMPLEKEY
phases:
  build:
    commands:
      - sam build
      - sam deploy --no-confirm-changeset

options: Move the keys to plaintext environment variables in the CodeBuild project settings.
Add buildspec.yml to .gitignore.
Remove the keys, give the needed permissions to the CodeBuild service role, and deactivate and rotate the leaked keys.
Base64-encode the keys so they are not readable in the file.
objective.explanation: CodeBuild runs with its service role, so no long-term keys are needed in the build. Keys that were committed must be treated as leaked and deactivated. Base64 is not encryption, plaintext project variables still expose the keys, and ignoring the buildspec breaks the build.

objective.question: A team lets GitHub Actions deploy to AWS with OIDC using the role trust policy below. What is the security mistake?
options: The aud value must be the repository URL.
OIDC roles must also include an access key in the trust policy.
The action should be sts:AssumeRole, not sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.
There is no condition on the token's sub claim, so a workflow in any GitHub repository could assume the role.
objective.explanation: Without a sub condition such as repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main, any GitHub workflow that gets a token for this audience can assume the role. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is the correct action, the aud value sts.amazonaws.com is correct, and OIDC needs no access keys.
