objective.question: A SageMaker real-time endpoint must add instances when request volume grows and remove them when it falls. Which configuration is the standard approach?
options: Switching the endpoint to Batch Transform during peak hours
Application Auto Scaling with a target-tracking policy on the SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance metric
Enabling data capture so SageMaker scales on captured requests
A CloudWatch alarm that calls UpdateEndpoint with a new endpoint configuration every hour
objective.explanation: SageMaker endpoint variants scale through Application Auto Scaling, and target tracking on invocations per instance is the common policy. Swapping endpoint configurations manually is slow and brittle, Batch Transform is not a live endpoint, and data capture is for monitoring, not scaling.

objective.question: An ML engineer schedules a SageMaker Model Monitor data quality job for a real-time endpoint. A baseline was created from the training data. Every scheduled run fails because it finds no data to analyse. What is the most likely cause?
options: Model Monitor only works with Batch Transform jobs.
The endpoint needs at least three instances for monitoring to work.
Data capture is not enabled in the endpoint configuration, so no request and response data is saved to S3.
The baseline must be recreated before every run.
objective.explanation: Model Monitor analyses the data that the endpoint captures to S3, which needs DataCaptureConfig in the endpoint configuration. One baseline can be reused for many runs, real-time endpoints are supported, and instance count does not matter.

objective.question: A SageMaker training job runs for about 12 hours on GPU instances. The team wants to cut training cost a lot and can accept that a job sometimes takes longer. What should they do?
options: Enable managed spot training, set a maximum wait time, and save checkpoints to S3 so interrupted jobs resume.
Use Batch Transform to run the training script.
Use the smallest CPU instance and train for longer.
Move training to a SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint.
objective.explanation: Managed spot training uses spare EC2 capacity at a large discount. Checkpoints in S3 let the job resume after an interruption instead of starting again. Inference options cannot run training jobs, and a small CPU instance may be far slower or unable to fit the model.

objective.question: An Athena table is partitioned by dt. An external process writes new data to s3://logs/events/dt=2026-01-15/. Queries with WHERE dt = '2026-01-15' return zero rows, but older dates work. What is the cause and fix?
options: The new partition is not registered in the Glue Data Catalog; run MSCK REPAIR TABLE or ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION, or use partition projection.
The dt column must be an integer, not a string.
The S3 bucket needs versioning before Athena can read new prefixes.
Athena caches results for 24 hours; wait for the cache to expire.
objective.explanation: Athena only reads partitions that exist in the catalog, unless partition projection is configured. Adding the partition, or using projection so partitions are computed from the query, fixes this. Athena result reuse is optional and off by default, and versioning and data type are unrelated.

objective.question: A company streams JSON events and wants them stored in S3 as Parquet for Athena. A delay of a few minutes is acceptable. They want the least custom code. Which solution fits best?
options: A Lambda function that writes every event to S3 as its own Parquet file
An hourly AWS Glue crawler on the raw JSON bucket
Amazon Data Firehose with record format conversion to Parquet, using a Glue Data Catalog table for the schema
Kinesis Data Streams with a custom consumer on EC2 that writes Parquet files
objective.explanation: Firehose buffers records, converts JSON to Parquet using a Glue table schema, and delivers to S3 with no servers to manage. A custom EC2 consumer is more code, one file per event creates a small-files problem, and a crawler only catalogues data without converting it.

objective.question: In Redshift, a billion-row fact table is often joined to a 50,000-row dimension table. EXPLAIN shows DS_BCAST_INNER or DS_DIST_BOTH on every join, and the queries are slow. What is the best change?
options: Set the fact table to DISTSTYLE ALL.
Add a sort key to the dimension table only.
Run VACUUM on the fact table before each query.
Set the dimension table to DISTSTYLE ALL so each node has a full copy.
objective.explanation: A small, rarely changed dimension table with DISTSTYLE ALL is copied to every node, so joins need no data movement at query time. Copying the huge fact table everywhere wastes storage and slows loads, while sort keys and VACUUM do not remove redistribution.

objective.question: A data engineer grants a user Lake Formation SELECT on a Glue table. The user queries it in Athena and gets an S3 Access Denied error. The user's IAM policy has no S3 permissions, by design. What is missing?
options: The Glue crawler must be run again after the grant.
The table's S3 location has not been registered with Lake Formation, so Lake Formation is not providing temporary credentials for the data.
Athena must use a different workgroup for Lake Formation tables.
The user needs the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy.
objective.explanation: Lake Formation provides temporary credentials for S3 data only when the data location is registered. Without registration, access falls back to the user's own IAM and S3 permissions, which this user does not have. Admin rights break least privilege, and running the crawler or changing workgroups does not provide credentials.

objective.question: A Lambda function has X-Ray active tracing turned on. The service map shows the Lambda nodes but no DynamoDB node, although the function calls DynamoDB on every request. What should the developer do?
options: Increase the X-Ray sampling rate to 100%.
Add X-Ray metadata with the table name.
Instrument the AWS SDK client with the X-Ray SDK, for example with Powertools for AWS Lambda Tracer, so downstream calls are recorded as subsegments.
Turn on X-Ray tracing on the DynamoDB table.
objective.explanation: Active tracing records the Lambda segments only. Calls made through the SDK show up as subsegments only when the SDK client is instrumented. DynamoDB has no tracing setting, sampling controls how many requests are traced, not what is captured, and metadata does not create nodes on the service map.

subjective.question: Explain the AWS Lambda execution model. What is a cold start, and how would you reduce its impact?
subjective.answer: When Lambda receives a request and no warm execution environment is free, it creates one. It downloads the code, starts the runtime and runs the initialisation code outside the handler. This is a cold start. Later requests can reuse the same environment, so anything created during init, such as SDK clients or database connections, is reused. Each environment handles one request at a time, so concurrency equals the number of environments. To reduce cold starts, I keep the deployment package small, initialise clients outside the handler, and avoid heavy frameworks. For latency-sensitive APIs I use provisioned concurrency, which keeps environments initialised. For supported runtimes such as Java, SnapStart restores a snapshot of an initialised environment. Memory also matters: CPU scales with memory from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, so more memory can shorten init and run time, sometimes at the same or lower cost.
keyPoints: Cold start = new environment plus init code; warm environments are reused
Initialise SDK clients and connections outside the handler
One request per environment; concurrency equals environments
Provisioned concurrency and SnapStart reduce cold starts
CPU scales with memory, so tune memory for speed and cost

subjective.question: Describe synchronous, asynchronous and event source mapping invocations in Lambda. How are errors and retries handled in each?
subjective.answer: In synchronous invocation, for example from API Gateway, the caller waits for the response. Lambda does not retry; the client must handle errors. The request and response payloads are limited to 6 MB each, so large files should go through S3 with presigned URLs. In asynchronous invocation, for example from S3 or SNS, Lambda queues the event and returns immediately. On failure it retries twice by default, and you can send failed events to a dead-letter queue or, better, to an on-failure destination that includes more context. With event source mappings, Lambda polls sources such as SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams and invokes the function with batches. For SQS, failed messages return to the queue after the visibility timeout and can move to a DLQ via a redrive policy. For streams, a failed batch blocks the shard until it succeeds or expires, so I use bisect-on-error, maximum retry attempts and partial batch responses to avoid poison records.
keyPoints: Synchronous: caller handles errors; 6 MB payload limit each way
Asynchronous: two retries by default, DLQ or on-failure destinations
Event source mappings poll SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams in batches
Streams can block on bad records; use bisect, retry limits, partial batch response

subjective.question: Compare API Gateway REST APIs and HTTP APIs. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: HTTP APIs are the newer, simpler option. They cost less and have lower latency. They support Lambda and HTTP proxy integrations, private integrations through VPC links, native JWT authorizers for Cognito or any OIDC provider, Lambda authorizers, IAM authorisation and simple CORS setup. REST APIs have more features. These include API keys and usage plans for per-client throttling and quotas, request validation, request and response mapping templates, response caching, AWS WAF integration, edge-optimised and private endpoint types, and a wider set of direct AWS service integrations. I choose an HTTP API for a straightforward serverless backend with JWT authentication where cost matters. I choose a REST API when I must monetise or meter partners with API keys, need WAF, caching or validation, or must expose a private API only inside a VPC. Both have a default integration timeout of 29 seconds, so long work should be made asynchronous.
keyPoints: HTTP API: cheaper, lower latency, native JWT authorizers
REST API: API keys, usage plans, validation, caching, WAF, private endpoints
Choose by required features first, then cost
Both have a default 29-second integration timeout

subjective.question: How do you design a DynamoDB data model? Explain partition keys, sort keys, GSIs and how to avoid hot partitions.
subjective.answer: I start from access patterns, not entities. I list every query the application needs, then design keys to serve them with Query operations rather than Scans. The partition key decides which partition stores an item, so it needs high cardinality and even traffic, such as userId rather than status. The sort key groups related items and supports range queries, for example ORDER#2026-01-15, which lets me fetch a user's orders by date. In single-table design, I store several entity types under shared keys so one query returns related data. Global secondary indexes give alternative keys for other patterns, with their own capacity, and are eventually consistent. Local secondary indexes share the partition key and must be created with the table. To avoid hot partitions, I avoid low-cardinality keys and can add write sharding with a random or calculated suffix. Items are limited to 400 KB, so large blobs go to S3 with a pointer in the item.
keyPoints: Design from access patterns; prefer Query over Scan
High-cardinality partition key for even distribution
Sort key for grouping and range queries; single-table design
GSIs for other patterns, eventually consistent; LSIs at table creation
Write sharding for hot keys; 400 KB item limit, large data in S3

subjective.question: Explain DynamoDB provisioned and on-demand capacity. Walk through a capacity calculation.
subjective.answer: On-demand mode charges per request and scales automatically. It suits new or unpredictable workloads. Provisioned mode lets you set RCUs and WCUs, usually with auto scaling. It is cheaper for steady, predictable traffic. One RCU gives one strongly consistent read per second for an item up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent reads. One WCU gives one write per second for up to 1 KB. Sizes always round up. For example, 100 eventually consistent reads per second of 10 KB items: 10 KB rounds to 12 KB, which is 3 RCUs for a strongly consistent read, halved for eventually consistent, so 1.5 RCUs each, giving 150 RCUs. For 40 writes per second of 2.5 KB, each write is 3 WCUs, so 120 WCUs. If those writes use transactions, the cost doubles to 240 WCUs. If throughput exceeds capacity, you get ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, and the SDK retries with exponential backoff.
keyPoints: On-demand for unpredictable load; provisioned plus auto scaling for steady load
RCU = 4 KB strongly consistent read/s, or two eventually consistent
WCU = 1 KB write/s; always round up item size
Transactions cost double
Throttling errors handled by SDK retries with exponential backoff

subjective.question: Design a CI/CD pipeline for a serverless API using AWS developer tools. How do you make deployments safe?
subjective.answer: I keep the application and infrastructure as code with AWS SAM or CDK in a Git repository. CodePipeline triggers on a push to the main branch. In the build stage, CodeBuild runs unit tests, linting and a security scan, then runs sam build and sam package to upload artefacts to S3. The pipeline deploys to a test stage through CloudFormation, runs integration tests, and then waits for a manual approval before production. For safe releases, I publish a new Lambda version and use a SAM DeploymentPreference. This uses CodeDeploy to shift traffic on an alias using a canary or linear pattern. I add pre-traffic and post-traffic hook functions for smoke tests and link CloudWatch alarms on errors and latency, so CodeDeploy rolls back automatically. Secrets stay in Secrets Manager, and each stage uses a least-privilege IAM role.
keyPoints: Infrastructure as code with SAM or CDK in Git
CodePipeline with CodeBuild tests and packaging
Test stage, integration tests, manual approval for production
CodeDeploy canary or linear traffic shifting on Lambda aliases
Hooks and CloudWatch alarms for automatic rollback

subjective.question: How do you use AWS X-Ray and CloudWatch to troubleshoot a slow serverless API?
subjective.answer: First I enable active tracing on the Lambda functions and tracing on the API Gateway stage. I instrument the code with the X-Ray SDK or AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry so calls to DynamoDB, S3 and HTTP services appear as subsegments. The X-Ray trace map then shows each service, its latency and its error rate, so I can see whether time goes into a cold start, the function code or a downstream call. I add annotations such as customerId or orderType, because annotations are indexed and can be used in filter expressions. Metadata is for extra detail that I do not need to search. In CloudWatch I check Lambda Duration, Throttles, Errors and ConcurrentExecutions, plus API Gateway Latency and IntegrationLatency. I use structured JSON logs and CloudWatch Logs Insights to find slow requests. Once I find the cause, I fix it, for example by raising memory, adding a GSI or reusing connections.
keyPoints: Enable active tracing on Lambda and API Gateway
Instrument SDK calls to get subsegments for downstream services
Annotations are indexed for filtering; metadata is not
Use CloudWatch metrics and Logs Insights alongside traces
Compare Latency with IntegrationLatency to locate delay

subjective.question: How should a developer handle secrets and encryption in an AWS application? Explain envelope encryption.
subjective.answer: Secrets never go in code, Git or plain environment variables. I store database passwords and API tokens in AWS Secrets Manager, which supports automatic rotation. For simpler configuration values or secrets that do not need rotation, I use SSM Parameter Store SecureString, which is encrypted with KMS. The function's IAM role gets permission to read only the specific secrets it needs, and I cache values in memory to reduce calls and latency. For data encryption I use AWS KMS. KMS Encrypt directly handles only small data, up to 4 KB. For larger data I use envelope encryption. I call GenerateDataKey to get a plaintext data key and an encrypted copy. I encrypt the data locally with the plaintext key, then discard it, and store the encrypted data key with the ciphertext. To decrypt, I call KMS Decrypt on the data key, then decrypt the data locally. The AWS Encryption SDK does this for me.
keyPoints: Secrets Manager for secrets with rotation; Parameter Store SecureString as alternative
Least-privilege IAM access and in-memory caching
KMS direct encryption only for data up to 4 KB
Envelope encryption with GenerateDataKey for larger data
Store encrypted data key with the ciphertext

subjective.question: Describe how you would prepare data and train a model in Amazon SageMaker for the MLA-C01 exam scope.
subjective.answer: Data usually starts in S3. I explore and clean it with SageMaker Data Wrangler or a notebook, then run repeatable transformations as SageMaker Processing jobs, or with Glue for large ETL. I handle missing values, encode categories, scale numbers, check class imbalance and split into train, validation and test sets. Clarify can check pre-training bias. Shared features go into Feature Store. For training, I pick a built-in algorithm such as XGBoost, a framework container like PyTorch, or my own container. The training job reads data from S3 using File, Pipe or FastFile mode and writes model artefacts back to S3. To cut cost, I use managed Spot training with checkpoints so interrupted jobs can resume. I use automatic model tuning to search hyperparameters against a target metric, and Experiments to track runs. Finally, I register the best model in Model Registry with its metrics for approval.
keyPoints: Data Wrangler and Processing jobs for repeatable data prep
Handle missing values, encoding, imbalance, splits; Clarify for bias
Built-in algorithms, framework containers or custom containers
Managed Spot training with checkpoints; automatic model tuning
Register approved models in Model Registry

subjective.question: Compare SageMaker real-time, serverless, asynchronous and batch inference. How do you choose?
subjective.answer: Real-time endpoints run on dedicated instances, give low and steady latency and support GPUs and auto scaling. They fit steady traffic such as a fraud check on every payment, but you pay while instances run. Serverless Inference scales automatically and charges for compute used, so it fits spiky traffic with idle gaps. It has cold starts and no GPU support. Asynchronous Inference queues requests, supports payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to 1 hour, writes results to S3, can notify through SNS and can scale to zero. It fits large documents, images or video. Batch Transform has no endpoint at all. It scores a whole dataset in S3 and shuts down, which suits nightly scoring. I choose by traffic pattern, latency need, payload size and processing time. For cost, I also consider multi-model endpoints when many small models share traffic.
keyPoints: Real-time: steady, low-latency traffic, always-on cost
Serverless: spiky traffic with idle gaps, cold starts, no GPU
Async: up to 1 GB payload and 1 hour processing, results in S3
Batch Transform: offline scoring of full datasets
Decide on latency, traffic pattern, payload size and duration

subjective.question: How do you monitor a deployed ML model and keep it accurate over time?
subjective.answer: I enable data capture on the endpoint so SageMaker stores a sample of requests and responses in S3. Then I set up SageMaker Model Monitor with baselines created from the training data. Model Monitor has four types: data quality monitoring for schema and statistical drift, model quality monitoring that compares predictions with ground-truth labels, bias drift monitoring and feature attribution drift monitoring, the last two using SageMaker Clarify. Each runs on a schedule and publishes violations and metrics to CloudWatch. I create CloudWatch alarms on these metrics plus operational ones such as latency, errors and CPU or GPU use. When drift crosses a threshold, an EventBridge rule can trigger a SageMaker Pipeline that retrains, evaluates and registers a new model. Deployment then goes through Model Registry approval and a safe rollout, such as blue/green with traffic shifting. Security includes VPC endpoints, KMS encryption and least-privilege roles.
keyPoints: Enable data capture on the endpoint
Baselines from training data
Four monitor types: data quality, model quality, bias drift, feature attribution drift
CloudWatch alarms and EventBridge-triggered retraining pipeline
Model Registry approval and safe deployment

subjective.question: Explain how AWS Glue and AWS Lake Formation work together to build a governed data lake.
subjective.answer: S3 stores the raw, cleaned and curated layers of the data lake. Glue crawlers scan the data, infer schemas and create tables and partitions in the Glue Data Catalog, which Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR all use. Glue ETL jobs, written in PySpark or with Glue Studio, transform data, for example from CSV to partitioned Parquet. DynamicFrames handle messy schemas. Job bookmarks track processed data so incremental runs do not reprocess old files. Glue Data Quality can check rules, and workflows or Step Functions orchestrate the jobs. Lake Formation adds governance on top of the catalog. Instead of managing many S3 bucket policies, I grant database, table, column, row and cell-level permissions in Lake Formation, often using LF-Tags to scale. Data filters hide sensitive columns such as email and restrict rows by region. Integrated services such as Athena enforce these permissions, and access can be audited through CloudTrail.
keyPoints: Glue crawlers populate the Data Catalog
Glue ETL jobs transform to optimised formats; job bookmarks for incremental loads
Data Catalog shared by Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR
Lake Formation for fine-grained column, row and cell permissions
LF-Tags and data filters simplify governance at scale

subjective.question: A team says Athena is slow and expensive. What steps would you take to optimise it?
subjective.answer: Athena charges by data scanned, so the goal is to scan less. First, I convert raw CSV or JSON to a columnar format such as Parquet or ORC, usually with a Glue job or an Athena CTAS query. Columnar formats let Athena read only the needed columns and skip blocks using statistics. Second, I compress with Snappy or ZSTD. Third, I partition by columns used in filters, often date, and make sure queries filter on partition columns. When there are very many partitions, I use partition projection, so Athena calculates partitions from table properties instead of looking them up in the catalog. It also removes the need for MSCK REPAIR or crawlers to add partitions. I also fix the small-files problem by compacting into larger files, and select only needed columns instead of SELECT *. Workgroups can set data-scanned limits per query for cost control.
keyPoints: Athena pricing is per data scanned
Convert to Parquet or ORC and compress
Partition by commonly filtered columns such as date
Partition projection for many partitions
Compact small files, avoid SELECT *, use workgroup limits

subjective.question: Compare Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose. Explain shard limits and enhanced fan-out.
subjective.answer: Kinesis Data Streams is a real-time stream that you read with your own consumers, such as Lambda, Managed Service for Apache Flink or KCL applications. Data is retained for replay, and ordering is kept per shard using the partition key. In provisioned mode each shard accepts 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s for writes and gives 2 MB/s for reads. On-demand mode scales capacity automatically. With standard consumers, all consumers share the 2 MB/s read limit per shard. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard using push delivery, with lower latency. It is good when several applications read the same stream. Amazon Data Firehose is fully managed delivery. It buffers data and loads it into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch and other destinations, with optional Lambda transformation and format conversion to Parquet. It needs no shard management, but it is near real time, not for custom replay. I use Data Streams for custom real-time processing and Firehose for simple loading.
keyPoints: Data Streams: custom consumers, replay, per-shard ordering
Shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s write, 2 MB/s read
Enhanced fan-out: 2 MB/s per shard per consumer
Firehose: managed buffered delivery to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch
Firehose can transform and convert formats with no shards to manage

subjective.question: How do you design Amazon Redshift tables and loads for good performance? Walk through the project you shipped for this step.
subjective.answer: For Redshift, I load data with the COPY command from S3, which loads in parallel. Splitting input into multiple compressed files helps. I avoid single-row inserts. I choose a distribution style: KEY on the join column for large fact tables, ALL for small dimension tables, EVEN when there is no clear join, or AUTO to let Redshift decide. Sort keys on commonly filtered columns, such as date, let Redshift skip blocks. I use materialised views for repeated aggregations, Redshift Spectrum to query cold data in S3, and Redshift Serverless when workloads are irregular. For my project, I built a pipeline: Firehose ingests clickstream data to S3, a Glue job converts it to date-partitioned Parquet, Lake Formation controls access, Athena serves ad-hoc queries and Redshift serves dashboards. The public repository contains infrastructure as code, a README and an architecture diagram showing data flow, IAM boundaries and monitoring.
keyPoints: COPY from S3 in parallel with multiple compressed files
Distribution styles: KEY, ALL, EVEN, AUTO
Sort keys for block skipping; materialised views
Spectrum for S3 data; Serverless for irregular workloads
Project in public repo with IaC, README and architecture diagram

subjective.question: Explain Lambda concurrency. What is the difference between reserved concurrency and provisioned concurrency, and when would you use each?
subjective.answer: Concurrency is the number of requests a function handles at the same time. Each concurrent request needs its own execution environment. All functions in an account and Region share a concurrency quota. Reserved concurrency sets aside part of that pool for one function and also caps it there. I use it to guarantee capacity for a critical function, or to protect a downstream system like an RDS database from too many connections. Setting it to zero stops the function. Requests above the cap are throttled. Synchronous callers get a 429 error, and asynchronous events are retried. Provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of environments initialised and ready, which removes cold starts for that traffic. It costs money even when idle. It must be set on a version or alias, and Application Auto Scaling can adjust it on a schedule. I use it for latency-sensitive APIs with predictable peaks.
keyPoints: Concurrency means simultaneous executions, drawn from a shared account and Region quota
Reserved concurrency both guarantees capacity and caps the function; excess requests are throttled
Provisioned concurrency pre-initialises environments to remove cold starts, and is billed while configured
Provisioned concurrency applies to versions or aliases and can be auto scaled
Throttle behaviour differs: 429 for synchronous calls, retries for asynchronous events

subjective.question: Why must Lambda functions that consume events be idempotent, and how would you implement idempotency?
subjective.answer: Lambda gives at-least-once delivery for asynchronous invocations and event source mappings. SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams and EventBridge retries can all deliver the same event more than once. A client may also retry an API call after a timeout. If the function charges a card or sends an email, a duplicate causes real harm. So I make processing idempotent: running it twice gives the same result as running it once. I pick an idempotency key, such as the message ID or a client-supplied request ID. Before doing the work, I write that key to a DynamoDB table with a conditional put (attribute_not_exists). If the put fails, the event was already handled and I return the stored result. I add a TTL so old keys expire. Powertools for AWS Lambda has an idempotency utility that does this for you. Where possible, I also make the downstream operations naturally idempotent, such as upserts instead of inserts.
keyPoints: Lambda event delivery is at-least-once, so duplicates will happen
Choose a unique idempotency key, such as a message ID or request ID
Use a DynamoDB conditional write (attribute_not_exists) to record processed keys
Add a TTL to the idempotency records; Powertools for AWS Lambda provides this utility
Prefer naturally idempotent operations such as upserts

subjective.question: Explain what this AWS SAM template creates and how deployments of it behave.

code.code:
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Resources:
  OrdersFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: app.handler
      CodeUri: src/
      AutoPublishAlias: live
      DeploymentPreference:
        Type: Linear10PercentEvery1Minute
      Policies:
        - DynamoDBCrudPolicy:
            TableName: !Ref OrdersTable
      Events:
        GetOrder:
          Type: HttpApi
          Properties:
            Path: /orders/{id}
            Method: get
  OrdersTable:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::SimpleTable

subjective.answer: The Transform line tells CloudFormation to expand the SAM resources into standard resources. OrdersFunction becomes a Python 3.12 Lambda function with an execution role. The DynamoDBCrudPolicy template grants that role create, read, update and delete access to OrdersTable only, which follows least privilege. The HttpApi event creates an API Gateway HTTP API with a GET /orders/{id} route integrated with the function. SimpleTable creates a DynamoDB table with a single primary key. AutoPublishAlias publishes a new version whenever the code changes and points the alias 'live' at it. Because DeploymentPreference is set, SAM creates a CodeDeploy application and deployment group. On each change, traffic shifts to the new version by 10% every minute until it reaches 100%. If I added CloudWatch alarms and pre-traffic or post-traffic hooks, CodeDeploy would roll back automatically when an alarm fires.
keyPoints: The SAM transform expands into Lambda, IAM, API Gateway HTTP API and DynamoDB resources
DynamoDBCrudPolicy is a scoped policy template for least privilege
AutoPublishAlias creates a new version on each change and moves the alias
DeploymentPreference uses CodeDeploy for linear traffic shifting
Alarms and hooks enable automatic rollback

subjective.question: A developer says this query 'only returns 5 items, so it is cheap'. Explain what the query really consumes, and how you would improve it.

code.code:
resp = table.query(
    KeyConditionExpression=Key('customerId').eq('C42'),
    FilterExpression=Attr('status').eq('OPEN')
)
items = resp['Items']   # 5 items returned
# customer C42 has 4,000 orders

subjective.answer: DynamoDB applies a FilterExpression after it reads the items, so you pay for everything the key condition matched. Here that is all 4,000 orders for C42, not the 5 that are returned. A single Query also returns at most 1 MB of data before the filter is applied. So the code must check LastEvaluatedKey and paginate, or it may miss OPEN orders entirely. To fix the cost, I would bring the status into a key. One option is a sort key like 'OPEN#2026-01-15' and a query with begins_with('OPEN#'). Another is a GSI with customerId as the partition key and status as the sort key. A sparse GSI also works well: only open orders carry the GSI key attribute, so the index holds only open orders and stays small. I would also use ProjectionExpression to return only the attributes I need. Note that projection reduces network payload, not RCUs.
keyPoints: Filter expressions are applied after the read, so RCUs are charged for all items the key condition matched
Query pages are limited to 1 MB; you must handle LastEvaluatedKey
Model access patterns into keys, such as a composite sort key or a GSI
A sparse GSI is efficient for querying a small subset like open orders
ProjectionExpression does not reduce consumed capacity

subjective.question: Describe an MLOps workflow on AWS using SageMaker Pipelines and SageMaker Model Registry. How does a model move from training to production safely?
subjective.answer: I define a SageMaker Pipeline with a few steps. A processing step cleans the data and creates features. A training step trains the model. An evaluation processing step writes metrics such as AUC to a property file. A condition step checks those metrics against a threshold. If the model passes, a RegisterModel step adds a new version to a model package group in Model Registry with the status PendingManualApproval. The registry stores the version's lineage, metrics and container image. A reviewer, or an automated check, changes the status to Approved. An EventBridge rule catches that status change and starts a deployment pipeline, for example CodePipeline with CloudFormation, which deploys to staging first. After tests pass and a manual approval, it deploys to production, using deployment guardrails such as canary traffic shifting with CloudWatch alarm rollback. Model Monitor then watches the production endpoint. Retraining can be triggered on a schedule or by drift alerts. Everything is version-controlled, so it is reproducible and auditable.
keyPoints: The pipeline steps are processing, training, evaluation, condition check and model registration
Model Registry handles versioning, lineage and approval status
An EventBridge event on approval starts CI/CD deployment through staging to production
Deployment guardrails use canary or linear shifting with auto rollback
Monitoring and drift alerts close the loop for retraining

subjective.question: A fraud-detection dataset has 0.5% positive cases. A model shows 99.5% accuracy. Explain why this is misleading, and how you would train and evaluate the model properly in SageMaker.
subjective.answer: A model that always predicts 'not fraud' scores 99.5% accuracy and catches no fraud, so accuracy is the wrong metric here. I would use precision, recall, F1 and the area under the precision-recall curve, and pick a decision threshold based on the business cost of missed fraud versus false alarms. To deal with the imbalance, I can weight the minority class. In SageMaker XGBoost, that means setting scale_pos_weight to roughly the ratio of negatives to positives. I can also oversample positives, for example with SMOTE in a processing step, or undersample negatives. Resampling must happen only on the training split, never on the validation or test data. I would use a stratified split so each set keeps the real class ratio. During automatic model tuning, the objective metric should be something like validation AUC or F1, not accuracy. Finally, I would check overfitting by comparing training and validation metrics, and use early stopping.
keyPoints: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data
Use precision, recall, F1 and PR-AUC, and tune the threshold to business cost
Use class weighting (scale_pos_weight) or resampling on the training split only
Use stratified splits and set the tuning objective to a suitable metric
Watch for overfitting with validation metrics and early stopping

subjective.question: How would you orchestrate a daily batch data pipeline that crawls new data, transforms it with Glue, loads Redshift and alerts on failure? Compare the orchestration options.
subjective.answer: AWS offers three main orchestration options. Glue workflows chain crawlers and Glue jobs with triggers. They are simple, but limited when you need to call non-Glue services. AWS Step Functions is serverless and integrates directly with Glue (with .sync to wait for the job to finish), Lambda, Athena, the Redshift Data API, SNS and many other services. It also has built-in Retry and Catch blocks. Amazon MWAA (Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow) suits teams that already use Airflow DAGs or need complex dependencies across many systems, but it has always-on environment cost. For this pipeline, I would use Step Functions. An EventBridge Scheduler rule starts it daily. The steps are: start the crawler, or skip the crawler and use partition projection; run the Glue job with bookmarks; run COPY or a stored procedure through the Redshift Data API; then check row counts. Each task gets retries with backoff. A Catch block sends failures to SNS. I would also add CloudWatch alarms on execution failures.
keyPoints: Glue workflows are simple but limited to Glue-centric pipelines
Step Functions offers serverless service integrations, .sync, and Retry/Catch
MWAA suits existing Airflow DAGs but has an always-on cost
Use EventBridge Scheduler for triggering and the Redshift Data API for loads
Alert on failures through SNS and CloudWatch alarms

subjective.question: How do you enforce data quality in an AWS data pipeline so that bad data does not reach analysts?
subjective.answer: I add quality checks at ingestion and after each transformation. AWS Glue Data Quality lets me write rules in DQDL (Data Quality Definition Language), such as IsComplete "order_id", IsUnique "order_id", ColumnValues "amount" > 0 and RowCount > 1000. I can run these rules against Data Catalog tables, or inside a Glue ETL job as an evaluation step. The job can then route failing records to a quarantine S3 prefix and write only clean data to the curated zone. Alternatively, the job can fail the run and stop the pipeline. Glue Data Quality can also recommend rules from data statistics. Results are published to CloudWatch and EventBridge, so I can alert through SNS or stop the Step Functions workflow. I also enforce the schema with the Data Catalog and reject unexpected columns. I use a raw, cleaned and curated zone layout so bad data never overwrites trusted tables. Lake Formation permissions then give analysts access only to the curated zone.
keyPoints: Glue Data Quality uses DQDL rules for completeness, uniqueness, ranges and row counts
Run the checks inside ETL jobs and quarantine failing records
Results go to CloudWatch and EventBridge for alerts or stopping the pipeline
Use a raw, cleaned and curated zone design
Give analysts access to curated data only, using Lake Formation

subjective.question: A newly deployed Lambda function fails with the error below. Walk through how you would troubleshoot and fix it.

code.code:
An error occurred (AccessDeniedException) when calling the GetItem operation:
User: arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/orders-fn-role/orders-fn
is not authorized to perform: dynamodb:GetItem on resource:
arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-south-1:111122223333:table/Orders
because no identity-based policy allows the dynamodb:GetItem action

subjective.answer: The message tells me most of what I need. The caller is the function's execution role, orders-fn-role, and the action is dynamodb:GetItem on the Orders table in ap-south-1. The phrase 'no identity-based policy allows' means the role has no Allow statement for this action. So it is not an explicit deny or an SCP problem, because those errors are worded differently. First, I check the role's policies in IAM. Common mistakes are a wrong table ARN, the wrong Region or account, a typo in the table name, or a policy that grants only Query or PutItem. I fix it by adding a least-privilege statement that allows dynamodb:GetItem on that table's ARN. If the code later uses a GSI, I also add the index ARN (table/Orders/index/*). I can use the IAM policy simulator to confirm the fix. If the table used a customer managed KMS key, I would also check kms:Decrypt. Finally, I manage the policy in SAM or CloudFormation so it does not drift.
keyPoints: Read the error: it names the principal (execution role), the action and the resource
'No identity-based policy allows' means a missing Allow, not an explicit deny or SCP
Check the ARN, Region and action names in the role's policy
Add a least-privilege Allow, including index ARNs if GSIs are used
Verify with the policy simulator and manage the policy as code

subjective.question: Case study: design a serverless order API. Requirements: mobile users sign in; reads of a customer's recent orders must be fast; partners get higher rate limits than the app; order confirmation emails must not slow the response; data is encrypted with a key the company controls; and you must be able to audit changes. Walk through your design.
subjective.answer: I would use a REST API in API Gateway, because I need usage plans and API keys to give partners their own throttling. Mobile users sign in with a Cognito user pool, and the API uses a Cognito authorizer. Each route calls a small Lambda function with its own least-privilege role. Orders go in DynamoDB with PK = CUSTOMER#id and SK = ORDER#timestamp, so 'recent orders' is one Query with ScanIndexForward=false and a Limit. I can add a GSI for lookups by order ID. The table uses SSE with a customer managed KMS key. To keep the response fast, the function only writes the order. DynamoDB Streams then triggers a separate Lambda that sends the email through SES, with retries and an on-failure destination. For auditing, CloudTrail records API and KMS calls, and the stream gives an item-level change history that I can archive to S3. X-Ray and structured logs cover troubleshooting.
keyPoints: REST API for usage plans and API keys; Cognito authorizer for users
DynamoDB key design so reads are a Query, not a Scan
Asynchronous email through Streams, EventBridge or SQS so the response stays fast
Customer managed KMS key, least-privilege roles per function
CloudTrail and the stream archive for auditing

subjective.question: During a flash sale, many Lambda functions return throttling errors (TooManyRequestsException). Even a low-traffic admin function fails. What is happening, and how do you fix it and prevent it?
subjective.answer: All functions in an account and Region share one concurrency pool. The regional quota is often 1,000 by default and can be raised. During the sale, the busy checkout function used almost all of it, so other functions, including the admin one, had nothing left and were throttled. To confirm, I check the ConcurrentExecutions and Throttles metrics per function and for the account. For the fix, I set reserved concurrency on critical functions so they always have capacity. I also set reserved concurrency on the noisy function as a cap, so it cannot starve the others. I request a quota increase through Service Quotas before known events. Where the work does not need a synchronous reply, I put an SQS queue in front so spikes are buffered instead of rejected. I set maximum concurrency on the event source mapping to protect downstream databases. Finally, I add CloudWatch alarms on throttles and load-test before the next sale.
keyPoints: Account-level concurrency pool shared by all functions in a Region
Check ConcurrentExecutions and Throttles metrics
Reserved concurrency to guarantee capacity and to cap noisy functions
Quota increase before planned peaks
SQS buffering and maximum concurrency to absorb spikes

subjective.question: This role is attached to a Lambda function that reads from the Orders table and writes receipts to the receipts bucket. Spot the mistakes and rewrite it the way you would for the exam and for production.
subjective.answer: The policy breaks least privilege. dynamodb:* on every resource lets the function delete any table in the account. s3:* on everything lets it read or delete any bucket, including other teams' data. If the function is compromised, the damage is account-wide. I would allow only the actions it uses: dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query on the Orders table ARN, and on arn:.../table/Orders/index/* if it queries a GSI. For S3 it needs only s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::receipts-bucket/*, or a narrower prefix. If the bucket uses SSE-KMS, I add kms:GenerateDataKey on that key. The logs actions can be scoped to the function's own log group. In SAM, policy templates such as DynamoDBReadPolicy and S3WritePolicy do this with less effort. IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from CloudTrail activity. On the exam, when 'least privilege' appears, pick specific actions on specific ARNs.
keyPoints: Wildcard actions and resources give account-wide damage if the function is compromised
Specific actions on specific table, index and bucket ARNs
KMS permissions when SSE-KMS is used
SAM policy templates and IAM Access Analyzer policy generation

subjective.question: Compare AWS Step Functions Standard and Express workflows. Which would you choose for (a) an order fulfilment flow that waits up to three days for a manager's approval, and (b) transforming 20,000 IoT events per second, each in under a second?
subjective.answer: Standard workflows run for up to one year. They use exactly-once execution of each step and keep a full, visual execution history. They are billed per state transition. That fits case (a). A fulfilment flow that waits days for approval can use the callback pattern with a task token: the workflow pauses, the manager approves through an API, and the workflow resumes. Each step, such as charging a card, must not run twice, so exactly-once behaviour matters. Express workflows run for up to five minutes. They support very high event rates and are billed by number of requests and duration, so they are much cheaper for short, high-volume work. They give at-least-once execution for asynchronous runs, so steps must be idempotent, and their history goes to CloudWatch Logs. That fits case (b). A common pattern is a Standard parent workflow that calls Express child workflows for the fast, high-volume parts.
keyPoints: Standard: up to one year, exactly-once, full history, billed per transition
Express: up to five minutes, high volume, billed per request and duration
Callback with task token for human approval
Express needs idempotent steps; mixing parent and child workflows

subjective.question: Put these steps in the right order before you make your Step 5 project repository public, and explain why the order matters: write the README and architecture diagram; run a secrets scanner on the full git history; rotate any exposed keys; move hard-coded credentials and account IDs into parameters; add a .gitignore; switch CI to OIDC; make the repo public and enable secret scanning.
subjective.answer: First, move hard-coded credentials and account IDs out of the code. Use IAM roles, Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and pseudo-parameters such as AWS::AccountId in templates. Second, add a .gitignore for .env files, .aws folders, Terraform state and local SAM config, so secrets are not committed again. Third, switch CI to OIDC with a tightly scoped role, so the pipeline needs no stored keys. Fourth, run a scanner such as gitleaks or trufflehog over the whole history, not just the latest commit. A key deleted in a later commit is still in history. Fifth, if anything is found, deactivate and rotate the key first, then rewrite history. Rewriting history does not undo a leak that may already have happened. Sixth, write the README, with a diagram, setup steps, cost notes and a teardown command. Last, make the repo public and turn on secret scanning with push protection. The order matters because once the repo is public, automated bots can find exposed keys very quickly.
keyPoints: Remove credentials and account IDs before anything else
Scan the full history, not only the current files
Rotate leaked keys before rewriting history
OIDC for CI and a .gitignore to prevent new leaks
Go public last, with push protection enabled

subjective.question: You finished your ML Engineer project two weeks ago, but your AWS bill is still growing every day. How do you find what is running, stop it safely, and make sure this does not happen on the next project?
subjective.answer: I start in Cost Explorer, grouped by service and then by usage type and Region. That shows where the money is going, for example SageMaker endpoint hours, NAT gateway hours or Kinesis shard hours. If I tagged resources with a project tag, I filter by that tag. Resource Explorer or Tag Editor helps me find leftovers in every Region. Then I clean up. I delete the SageMaker endpoint, then its endpoint configuration and model. I stop Studio apps and notebook instances. I delete NAT gateways and release unused Elastic IPs. I delete or scale down Kinesis streams, and I snapshot and then delete or pause Redshift clusters. If I built everything with SAM, CDK or CloudFormation, deleting the stack removes most of it. To prevent this next time, I set AWS Budgets with email alerts, turn on Cost Anomaly Detection, tag everything, and keep a tested teardown script in the repo. I run that script as the last step of every project.
keyPoints: Cost Explorer by service, usage type, Region and tag
Know the hourly billers: endpoints, NAT gateways, shards, Redshift
Delete in a safe order and snapshot data you need
Infrastructure as code makes teardown one command
Budgets, anomaly detection and a teardown script for the future

subjective.question: Compare Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS and Amazon EventBridge for decoupling services. Give a scenario where each one is the better choice.
subjective.answer: SQS is a queue. One consumer group pulls messages at its own pace, and messages wait until they are processed. It is best for buffering work and smoothing spikes. Example: orders queued for a Lambda function that writes to a database that can only handle limited load. SNS is pub/sub push. One message fans out quickly to many subscribers, such as SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email or SMS. Example: an 'order placed' message that must reach billing, shipping and analytics queues at the same time. That is the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern. EventBridge is an event bus with content-based routing rules. It accepts events from AWS services and SaaS partners, and it supports a schema registry, archive and replay, and scheduling. Example: routing events by fields such as region or amount to different targets, or reacting to AWS service events. In short, choose SQS for buffering, SNS for simple high-throughput fan-out, and EventBridge for rich routing and integrations.
keyPoints: SQS: pull-based queue that buffers work
SNS: push fan-out to many subscribers; SNS-to-SQS pattern
EventBridge: content-based rules, SaaS and AWS events, archive and replay
Match the service to the scenario

subjective.question: Users report that a SageMaker real-time endpoint has become slow. The p99 latency doubled after a traffic increase. How do you troubleshoot it?
subjective.answer: First I split the latency using CloudWatch endpoint metrics. ModelLatency is the time the model container takes to respond. OverheadLatency is the time SageMaker adds around it, such as handling the request and response. If ModelLatency went up, the container is the problem. I check CPUUtilization, MemoryUtilization and GPU metrics for the variant. If instances are saturated, I add instances or set up auto scaling on InvocationsPerInstance. I may also choose a larger or GPU instance, make the model smaller or compile it, or tune the number of serving workers. If OverheadLatency went up, I look at payload size and compress requests or send smaller ones. I also check whether clients are calling from far away. Then I check Invocations and the 4xx and 5xx error metrics to see if retries are adding load. Finally, I load-test, for example with Inference Recommender, to find the right instance type and count, and I set an alarm on p99 latency.
keyPoints: ModelLatency versus OverheadLatency to locate the problem
Instance utilisation metrics and auto scaling on invocations per instance
Model optimisation, compilation or a different instance type
Payload size and client-side retries
Inference Recommender or load tests, and latency alarms

subjective.question: Compare SageMaker built-in algorithms, script mode with a framework container, and bring-your-own-container (BYOC). When would you pick each?
subjective.answer: Built-in algorithms, such as XGBoost, Linear Learner or BlazingText, need the least code. You choose the algorithm, set hyperparameters and point it at data in S3. They are well optimised and good for standard problems, but you cannot change the algorithm's internals. Script mode uses AWS-managed framework containers for PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn or Hugging Face. You supply your own training script and a requirements file. This is the common middle ground: full control of the model code, while AWS manages the container, drivers and distributed training support. BYOC means you build your own Docker image, push it to Amazon ECR, and follow SageMaker's container rules for training and serving. Choose it for unusual languages, custom system libraries or strict, pinned dependencies. It gives the most control and the most maintenance work. For the exam, 'least operational overhead' usually points to built-in algorithms. 'Custom code in a popular framework' points to script mode, and 'custom runtime or dependencies' points to BYOC.
keyPoints: Built-in: least code, limited control
Script mode: your code in an AWS-managed framework container
BYOC: your own image in ECR for custom runtimes
Map the exam wording to the right option

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this training code for a fraud model. The data covers two years and is sorted by time. The reported score looks excellent, but the model performs poorly in production.

code.code:
df = pd.read_csv('transactions.csv')  # 2 years, sorted by time
scaler = StandardScaler()
X = scaler.fit_transform(df[features])
y = df['is_fraud']
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, shuffle=True)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)))

subjective.answer: There are three problems. First, the scaler is fitted on the whole dataset before the split. The test data's mean and variance leak into training, which is data leakage. The scaler should be fitted on the training set only, ideally inside a pipeline, and then applied to the test data. Second, the data is time-ordered, but the split is random. The model trains on future transactions and is tested on past ones, which cannot happen in production. I would split by time, for example train on the first 20 months, validate on the next 2 and test on the last 2. Third, accuracy is misleading because fraud is rare. I would report precision, recall, F1 and area under the precision-recall curve, and choose a decision threshold based on business cost. There is also no separate validation set for tuning. In SageMaker, I would do the time-based split and scaling in a Processing job, so the same code runs in training and in the pipeline.
keyPoints: Scaler fitted before the split causes leakage
Random shuffle on time-series data leaks the future
Accuracy is wrong for imbalanced data
Time-based train, validation and test sets; same processing code in the pipeline

subjective.question: How does SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning work? Compare its search strategies and explain how you would control tuning cost.
subjective.answer: Automatic Model Tuning runs many training jobs with different hyperparameter values and keeps the best one. You define the ranges, such as continuous, integer or categorical, and an objective metric, like validation:auc, to maximise or minimise. For custom scripts, the metric is read from training logs with a regular expression. The strategies are as follows. Grid search tries every combination of categorical values, which is exhaustive but only practical for small spaces. Random search samples values independently and runs well in parallel. Bayesian optimisation uses results so far to pick promising values, so it usually needs fewer jobs, but it gains less from high parallelism. Hyperband stops weak jobs early and gives more resources to strong ones, which suits long, iterative training. To control cost, I set maximum total jobs and maximum parallel jobs, and I enable early stopping. I use log scaling for ranges like learning rate, and I use warm start to reuse earlier tuning results. Managed spot training can also cut the cost of each job.
keyPoints: Ranges plus an objective metric, read from logs for custom scripts
Grid, random, Bayesian and Hyperband trade-offs
Parallelism versus Bayesian efficiency
Job limits, early stopping, warm start, spot training

subjective.question: Case study: a news website needs (1) a live dashboard of top articles that updates within seconds, (2) all raw clickstream stored for years and queryable with SQL at low cost, (3) the ability to replay the last few days after a bug fix, and (4) three teams consuming the same stream independently. Design the pipeline.
subjective.answer: Events go into Kinesis Data Streams. I choose on-demand mode if traffic is unpredictable, or provisioned mode if it is steady. Data Streams fits because it allows custom consumers and replay. I set the retention period to cover the replay window, for example 7 days, since the default is 24 hours and it can be extended to 365 days. Each of the three teams uses enhanced fan-out, so each gets dedicated read throughput per shard and they do not slow each other down. For the dashboard, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink reads the stream and computes top articles over short windows. It writes results to DynamoDB or OpenSearch for the dashboard to read. For long-term storage, Firehose reads from the stream, converts records to Parquet and writes them to S3 partitioned by date. A Glue Data Catalog table makes the data queryable with Athena. S3 lifecycle rules move old data to cheaper storage classes. I encrypt with KMS throughout and give each consumer a least-privilege role.
keyPoints: Data Streams for replay and custom consumers, with extended retention
Enhanced fan-out for independent consumers
Flink for real-time windowed aggregations
Firehose to Parquet on S3, Glue catalog and Athena for history
Lifecycle rules, KMS and least-privilege roles

subjective.question: An AWS Glue Spark job reads about two million small JSON files from S3. It runs for hours and sometimes fails with a driver out-of-memory error. What is the cause, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The main cause is the small-files problem. Spark has to list and track two million objects, which puts heavy load on the driver. Each file also becomes a tiny task, so scheduling overhead dominates the job. To fix it, I first enable file grouping with the groupFiles option set to inPartition and a sensible groupSize, so many small files are read as one larger input. I add a pushdown predicate or partition filter so the job reads only the partitions it needs. I enable job bookmarks so each run processes only new files. If memory is still tight, I move to a larger worker type such as G.2X. Long term, I fix the source. If Firehose writes the data, I increase its buffer size so it produces fewer, larger files. I also add a compaction step that rewrites the data into larger Parquet files. I confirm the improvement with Glue job metrics and the Spark UI.
keyPoints: Too many small files overload the driver and create tiny tasks
groupFiles and groupSize to combine inputs
Pushdown predicates and job bookmarks to read less
Larger worker types when needed
Fix the source: bigger buffers and compaction to Parquet

subjective.question: Compare three ways to query data for analytics: Amazon Athena on S3, Redshift Spectrum, and loading data into Redshift managed storage. Which is better for which workload?
subjective.answer: Athena is serverless and queries data in S3 directly, using the Glue Data Catalog. You pay per data scanned, and there is nothing to manage. It is best for ad hoc or infrequent queries, data exploration, and log analysis. Redshift Spectrum lets a Redshift cluster or Redshift Serverless query S3 tables in place and join them with tables stored inside Redshift. It is useful when you keep hot, frequently used data in Redshift but want to join it with large, cold history in S3 without loading it. Loading data into Redshift managed storage, with COPY or zero-ETL integrations, gives the best and most consistent performance for frequent, complex BI queries with many concurrent users. That is because you control distribution and sort keys and can use features such as materialised views. So choose Athena for ad hoc work, Spectrum for hot plus cold joins, and loaded tables for heavy, repeated dashboard queries. For both Athena and Spectrum, store data as partitioned Parquet to cut cost.
keyPoints: Athena: serverless, pay per scan, ad hoc queries
Spectrum: join Redshift tables with S3 data in place
Loaded Redshift tables: best performance for frequent BI queries
Partitioned columnar formats reduce scan cost

subjective.question: Spot the design mistakes in this Athena table definition for 3 TB of web events per day from about 10 million users. Analysts mostly query by date range.

code.code:
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE events (
  event_id string,
  page string,
  payload string
)
PARTITIONED BY (user_id string, event_time timestamp)
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.openx.data.jsonserde.JsonSerDe'
STORED AS TEXTFILE
LOCATION 's3://web-events/raw/';

subjective.answer: First, the partition keys are wrong. user_id has about 10 million values, and event_time is a full timestamp. Together they create a huge number of tiny partitions and files. Query planning becomes slow, catalog updates become heavy, and analysts do not filter by user anyway. I would partition by date, for example a dt string such as 2026-01-15, and maybe add a low-cardinality column like region. If user lookups are common, I would bucket by user_id instead of partitioning on it. Second, the data is stored as JSON text. Every query reads every column and every byte. I would convert it with CTAS, a Glue job or Firehose into compressed Parquet, for example with Snappy, so queries read only the columns they need. Third, with daily partitions, I would use partition projection, so new dates need no crawler or MSCK REPAIR TABLE. Together, these changes cut both data scanned and cost a lot.
keyPoints: High-cardinality partition keys create too many small partitions
Partition by date to match how analysts query
Bucketing for user_id lookups
Compressed Parquet instead of JSON text
Partition projection for new dates

subjective.question: A team wants daily analytics on an operational DynamoDB table without hurting the live application. A developer proposes a nightly Glue job that runs Scan on the table. Which approach is better, and why?
subjective.answer: A nightly Scan reads every item. It uses a lot of read capacity and can throttle the live application unless you limit its rate carefully, and it costs more as the table grows. A better option for daily batch work is DynamoDB export to S3. It needs point-in-time recovery enabled, it does not use the table's read capacity, and it supports full and incremental exports. The output lands in S3, where Glue can convert it to Parquet and Athena or Redshift can query it. If analysts need near real-time data, I would use DynamoDB Streams or Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB with Firehose to deliver changes into S3. If the target is Redshift, the DynamoDB zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift removes the need for a custom pipeline. In every case, the live table is protected, the analytics copy is in a format built for analytics, and IAM and Lake Formation control who can see the data.
keyPoints: Scan uses read capacity and can throttle production
Export to S3 uses point-in-time recovery and no table read capacity
Streams with Firehose for near real-time changes
Zero-ETL to Redshift as a managed option
Governed analytics copy in a columnar format

steps.overview: This step prepares you for the two Professional exams: SAP-C02 (Solutions Architect) and DOP-C02 (DevOps Engineer). Both have 75 questions in 180 minutes and a 750/1000 pass mark. They test design trade-offs across many accounts, hybrid networks, migrations, cost, infrastructure as code, safe deployments and incident response. Long, dense scenarios are the real challenge, so speed-reading and elimination matter as much as service knowledge.
objectives: Design a multi-account landing zone using AWS Organizations, Control Tower, OUs and SCPs
Choose the right hybrid connectivity (Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, Transit Gateway) for a given scenario
Select a migration strategy from the 7 Rs and the right migration tools
Build and explain a blue/green or canary pipeline using CloudFormation or CDK, CodePipeline and CodeDeploy
Answer 75 long scenario questions in 180 minutes and score above 75% on practice exams

concepts.explanation: Organizations groups accounts into OUs under one management account, with consolidated billing. Service control policies (SCPs) set the maximum permissions for member accounts. They never grant access, so IAM policies are still needed. SCPs do not apply to the management account, so keep workloads out of it.

Control Tower automates a landing zone on top of Organizations. It creates a Security OU with Log Archive and Audit accounts, sets up IAM Identity Center, and applies controls (guardrails). Controls are preventive (SCPs), detective (AWS Config rules) or proactive (CloudFormation hooks). Account Factory vends new, pre-configured accounts.

Site-to-Site VPN is quick, encrypted, runs over the internet, and gives about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel. Direct Connect is a private, consistent-latency link but takes weeks to provision and is not encrypted by default (use MACsec or a VPN over it). Transit Gateway is a hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks. A Direct Connect gateway links one DX connection to VPCs in many Regions.

The 7 Rs are Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform and Refactor. Rehost (lift and shift) usually uses AWS Application Migration Service. Databases use AWS DMS, plus the Schema Conversion Tool for engine changes. Use Migration Hub to track progress and Application Discovery Service to inventory servers. Use Snowball for large offline data transfers.

Right-size first with Compute Optimizer. Then commit with Savings Plans (Compute is most flexible; EC2 Instance is cheaper but tied to one family and Region) or Reserved Instances. Use Spot for fault-tolerant work. Reduce data transfer costs with VPC endpoints and CloudFront, and use S3 lifecycle rules or Intelligent-Tiering. Cost Explorer, Budgets and cost allocation tags give visibility.

StackSets deploy one template to many accounts and Regions, and can auto-deploy to new accounts in an OU. Change sets preview changes before you apply them. DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy (Retain or Snapshot) protect data. Drift detection finds manual changes. CreationPolicy with cfn-signal waits for instances to report that they are healthy.

CDK lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python and other languages. It synthesises (cdk synth) to CloudFormation templates. Each account and Region must be bootstrapped (cdk bootstrap) before deployment. CDK Pipelines provides a self-mutating CodePipeline for multi-account delivery.

Choose between in-place, rolling, immutable, blue/green and canary or linear. CodeDeploy supports blue/green for EC2, ECS and Lambda. ECS and Lambda can shift traffic in canary, linear or all-at-once steps. CloudWatch alarms can trigger automatic rollback.

CloudWatch provides metrics, Logs, alarms, composite alarms and Synthetics canaries. X-Ray provides tracing. EventBridge rules route events such as GuardDuty findings or Config non-compliance to Lambda, SSM Automation or Step Functions for auto-remediation. Systems Manager OpsCenter and Incident Manager help run the incident process.

keyFacts: SAP-C02 and DOP-C02: 75 questions (65 scored + 10 unscored), 180 minutes, USD 300, pass 750/1000. That is about 2.4 minutes per question.
SCPs restrict permissions but never grant them. They do not affect the management account.
Control Tower's core accounts are Management, Log Archive and Audit. The last two sit in the Security OU.
A Site-to-Site VPN tunnel gives about 1.25 Gbps. Use ECMP over Transit Gateway to aggregate bandwidth.
Direct Connect has no encryption by default. Add MACsec or an IPsec VPN over it if encryption is required.
For DX resilience, use two connections at two different DX locations for maximum resiliency, or a VPN as a low-cost backup.
A Compute Savings Plan covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda across Regions and families. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives the deepest discount but is locked to one family and Region.
CodeDeploy predefined configs include Canary10Percent5Minutes, Linear10PercentEvery1Minute and AllAtOnce, for Lambda and ECS.
Use StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment to cover accounts that join an OU later.
Decision rule: if the question says 'least operational overhead', prefer a managed service such as Control Tower, MGN or managed rotation over custom scripts.

example.caption: Landing zone SCP: deny actions outside approved Regions (ap-south-1, ap-south-2), but allow global services and a break-glass admin role

pitfalls: Picking an answer that puts workloads or SCP-based controls in the management account. SCPs do not apply there.
Assuming Direct Connect is encrypted, or choosing Direct Connect when the scenario needs connectivity within days. VPN is the fast option.
Choosing a custom Lambda or script solution when a managed feature (Control Tower controls, StackSets, Config remediation) meets the need with less effort.
Confusing blue/green (two full environments, instant switch, fast rollback) with rolling or in-place updates, which reduce capacity and roll back slowly.
Reading every option in full before reading the last sentence of the question. Read the actual ask first ('most cost-effective', 'least downtime').
Spending more than 4 minutes on one question. Flag it, move on and come back. Unanswered questions score zero, and there is no penalty for guessing.

workflow.title: Hands-on: design a multi-account landing zone end to end

steps.label: Set up Control Tower
steps.detail: Enable Control Tower in your home Region (for example ap-south-1) to create the Log Archive and Audit accounts and IAM Identity Center.

steps.label: Design the OU structure
steps.detail: Create Security, Infrastructure, Workloads/Prod, Workloads/NonProd and Sandbox OUs, each with different controls.

steps.label: Apply SCPs and controls
steps.detail: Attach Region-deny, root-user-deny and 'do not disable CloudTrail or GuardDuty' SCPs, then enable detective Config controls.

steps.label: Build shared networking
steps.detail: In a Network account, deploy Transit Gateway, shared via RAM, plus Direct Connect or VPN to on-premises and centralised egress.

steps.label: Centralise security and logs
steps.detail: Delegate GuardDuty, Security Hub and Config aggregation to the Audit account, and send organisation CloudTrail logs to Log Archive.

steps.label: Automate account baselines
steps.detail: Use Account Factory and CloudFormation StackSets with auto-deployment to push VPCs, roles and budgets into every new account.

steps.label: Add cost governance
steps.detail: Enable cost allocation tags, AWS Budgets alerts and Cost Explorer, and buy Savings Plans centrally in the management account.

project.title: bluegreen-orders-cdk
project.summary: A CDK (TypeScript) app that deploys an 'orders' Lambda behind API Gateway and releases every new version blue/green through CodeDeploy. Traffic shifts canary-style, a pre-traffic hook tests the new version, and a CloudWatch alarm triggers automatic rollback. bin/app.ts is the infrastructure as code (alias, deployment group, alarm, API). src/handler.js is the service being released. src/pretraffic.js is the CodeDeploy lifecycle hook. The JSON files are the CDK and TypeScript config.
project.run:
npm install
npx cdk bootstrap
npx cdk deploy -c appVersion=v1
curl $API_URL
npx cdk deploy -c appVersion=v2
npx cdk deploy -c appVersion=v3 -c failRate=0.5
npx cdk destroy

files.code:
# bluegreen-orders-cdk

Hands-on for Step 6 (DOP-C02): a blue/green release pipeline, end to end.
CodeDeploy treats all Lambda and ECS deployments as blue/green. Here the old
version is 'blue', the new version is 'green', and the `live` alias shifts traffic.

## Flow
1. `cdk deploy` publishes a new Lambda version (code or env changed).
2. CloudFormation hands the alias update to CodeDeploy.
3. The PreTraffic hook (`src/pretraffic.js`) invokes the new version directly.
   It reports Succeeded or Failed to CodeDeploy.
4. Canary10Percent5Minutes: 10% of traffic goes to green for 5 minutes, then 100%.
5. If the `AliasErrors` alarm fires, CodeDeploy rolls back to blue automatically.

## Try it
- Deploy v1 first. This is the first deployment, so there is no traffic shifting.
  CodeDeploy runs only on updates.
- Deploy v2 and call the API in a loop:
  `for i in $(seq 30); do curl -s $API_URL; echo; done`
  You will see a mix of v1 and v2 responses for about 5 minutes.
- Deploy v3 with `failRate=0.5`. The hook passes, because health checks skip
  the simulated failure. Live errors then trip the alarm, and CodeDeploy
  rolls back to v2. Check the CodeDeploy console to watch it happen.

## In a real pipeline
Run `npx cdk deploy --require-approval never` from CodePipeline or CodeBuild,
or use CDK Pipelines. The release logic stays the same.

## Exam notes
- Lambda configs: Canary, Linear, AllAtOnce.
- ECS blue/green: two target groups, a production listener and an optional test listener.
- EC2 in-place deployments are not blue/green.
- Rollback triggers: a failed deployment or an alarm. CodeDeploy redeploys the last good revision.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to SAP-C02 Domains 1–4: organisational complexity, design for new solutions, continuous improvement, and migration and modernisation. It also maps to DOP-C02 domains on SDLC automation, configuration management and IaC, resilient cloud solutions, monitoring and logging, incident and event response, and security and compliance. Both exams use long multi-account or hybrid scenarios with four plausible answers. The winner is decided by one qualifier in the last sentence, such as cost, speed, overhead or downtime, so you are tested on trade-offs, not definitions.

compare.difference: An SCP caps what principals in member accounts can do. An RCP caps what can be done to resources in member accounts, including access by principals outside your organisation. Neither grants access.
compare.chooseA: Pick an SCP when the ask is to stop users or roles in member accounts from taking an action, such as leaving the organisation, disabling CloudTrail or using an unapproved Region.
compare.chooseB: Pick an RCP when the ask is an organisation-wide data perimeter on resources, for example blocking external identities from reading S3 buckets or KMS keys in every account.

compare.difference: VPN runs over the internet, is encrypted with IPsec and can be live in hours. Direct Connect is a private dedicated link with consistent latency and higher bandwidth, but provisioning takes weeks.
compare.chooseA: Choose VPN for 'needed this week', 'encrypted', 'low cost' or 'backup path'.
compare.chooseB: Choose Direct Connect for 'consistent network performance', 'large steady data transfer', 'reduce data transfer out cost' or 'avoid the public internet'.

compare.difference: Transit Gateway is a transitive hub for many VPCs, VPNs and DX, with central route tables. Peering is one-to-one, non-transitive, needs non-overlapping CIDRs and has no per-attachment hourly charge.
compare.chooseA: Choose Transit Gateway when there are tens or hundreds of VPCs, shared on-premises connectivity, or a need for centralised inspection or egress.
compare.chooseB: Choose VPC peering when only a few VPCs must talk, you need the lowest cost and latency, and no transitive routing is required.

compare.difference: Rehost moves servers as they are, for the fastest migration with no code change. Replatform makes small changes to gain a managed benefit, such as moving a self-managed database to RDS, without rewriting the application.
compare.chooseA: Pick Rehost when the scenario stresses a deadline, a data-centre exit or 'no changes to the application'.
compare.chooseB: Pick Replatform when the scenario wants less management of the database or OS, but still forbids a code rewrite.

compare.difference: Blue/green runs a full second environment and shifts all traffic at once, with rollback by switching back. Canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first and watches alarms before shifting the rest.
compare.chooseA: Choose blue/green when the ask is the fastest full rollback or zero downtime with a complete parallel stack.
compare.chooseB: Choose canary when the ask is to limit blast radius, test with real users and roll back automatically on a CloudWatch alarm.

cues.cue: New accounts must automatically receive the baseline
cues.pick: Control Tower Account Factory with controls, or StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment on the OU
cues.why: Both apply the baseline at account creation or OU move with no custom code.

cues.cue: On-premises servers must resolve names in a Route 53 private hosted zone
cues.pick: Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint (outbound endpoint for the reverse direction)
cues.why: Resolver endpoints are the managed way to forward DNS between a VPC and on-premises DNS.

cues.cue: Share subnets, Transit Gateway or other resources with other accounts
cues.pick: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)
cues.why: RAM shares resources within the organisation without duplicating them or setting up peering.

cues.cue: Hundreds of TB to move with limited or no bandwidth, deadline in weeks
cues.pick: AWS Snowball Edge
cues.why: Physical transfer beats a slow WAN link. Use DataSync instead when the network can carry the data in time.

cues.cue: Single pane of glass for security findings across all accounts
cues.pick: Security Hub with a delegated administrator account (often the Audit account)
cues.why: Delegated admin aggregates findings centrally and keeps the management account free of workloads.

cues.cue: Automatically roll back the deployment if errors rise
cues.pick: CodeDeploy deployment group with CloudWatch alarms and automatic rollback enabled
cues.why: This is a native feature, so no Lambda watcher is needed.

cues.cue: Detect and auto-fix non-compliant resources
cues.pick: AWS Config rules with remediation through Systems Manager Automation documents
cues.why: It is a managed detect-and-remediate loop, and it can be deployed organisation-wide with conformance packs.
