cues.cue: Find over-provisioned or idle instances to cut cost
cues.pick: AWS Compute Optimizer, plus Cost Explorer rightsizing recommendations
cues.why: They give data-driven rightsizing before you commit to Savings Plans.

scenario.situation: A company has 60 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations, created over time without standards. Security wants every existing and future account to have CloudTrail enabled, to be unable to disable it, and to use only two approved Regions. A read-only security audit role must also exist in every account. The team is small and wants the solution with the least operational overhead. Which approach meets these requirements?
reasoning: Read the last sentence first. The deciding qualifier is 'least operational overhead', and the solution must also cover future accounts.
Eliminate any option that uses a scheduled Lambda to scan accounts and re-enable CloudTrail. It is custom code that fixes things after the fact instead of preventing them.
Eliminate any option that puts the audit role or the controls only in the management account. SCPs do not apply there, and workloads do not belong there.
Eliminate options that create the role by hand in each account. They do not scale and will miss new accounts.

The remaining choice is Control Tower: enrol the existing accounts and use its organisation trail, preventive controls (the Region deny and the CloudTrail protection) and Account Factory. Add the audit role through a StackSet with service-managed permissions and auto-deployment, or through Control Tower customisations.
scenario.answer: Set up AWS Control Tower and enrol the existing accounts. Enable the Region deny and CloudTrail protection controls, and deploy the audit role with a service-managed StackSet set to automatic deployment. It is preventive, covers new accounts automatically and needs no custom code.

memoryAids: 7 Rs by rising effort, 'Retire, Retain, Relocate, Rehost, Replatform, Repurchase, Refactor': the further right, the more change, the more time and the more cloud benefit.
SCP is a fence, not a key. It only shrinks what IAM already allows, and the management account sits outside the fence.
Deployments by rollback speed, 'Blue flips, Canary peeks, Linear creeps, Rolling and in-place weep': blue/green rolls back instantly, while rolling and in-place roll back slowly.
cheatSheet: Effective permission is the overlap of SCP, permission boundary, identity policy, resource policy and any session policy. An explicit Deny anywhere wins.
SCPs do not restrict service-linked roles. If an option relies on an SCP to block one, it is wrong.
Direct Connect LAGs add bandwidth at one location. Resilience needs connections at separate DX locations.
A Direct Connect gateway reaches VPCs in many Regions and accounts. Use a transit VIF to attach it to a Transit Gateway.
Use AWS Application Discovery Service and Migration Hub to plan, MGN to rehost servers, and DMS plus SCT for heterogeneous database moves.
Cost levers, in order: rightsize first, then commit (Savings Plans or RIs), use Spot for interruptible work, consider Graviton, and use S3 Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access patterns.
CloudFormation safety: use change sets to preview, stack policies to protect resources, DeletionPolicy Retain or Snapshot for data, and drift detection for manual changes.
Use CreationPolicy with cfn-signal so the stack waits for the instance to confirm it is healthy. Use custom resources (Lambda-backed) only when no native resource type exists.
CDK synthesises to CloudFormation. Run cdk bootstrap once per account and Region. CDK Pipelines gives a self-mutating pipeline.
Elastic Beanstalk: 'immutable' and 'rolling with additional batch' keep full capacity, while plain 'rolling' and 'all at once' reduce it.
Incident automation pattern: EventBridge rule, then an SSM Automation runbook or Lambda, then SNS or Systems Manager Incident Manager for paging.
Time plan: about 60 questions done by minute 150, then review flagged questions. Never leave a blank.
selfCheck: I can explain why a control placed in the management account fails, and say where to put it instead.
I can pick between VPN, Direct Connect with a VPN backup, and two DX locations from a scenario's time, cost, encryption and resilience needs.
I can map any migration scenario to one of the 7 Rs and name the AWS service that executes it.
I can choose blue/green, canary, linear, rolling or in-place from the downtime, capacity and rollback wording.
I can design a landing zone or blue/green pipeline end to end and justify each managed service I used over custom code.
I can finish a 75-question practice exam in 180 minutes with a score above 75%, using the read-the-last-sentence-first method.

objective.question: A company uses AWS Organizations. A security engineer attaches an SCP that denies all EC2 actions to the root of the organization. Which accounts can still launch EC2 instances, provided their IAM policies allow it?
options: Only the management account
Only accounts that have a delegated administrator
Only accounts in the Security OU
No account in the organization
objective.explanation: SCPs never affect users or roles in the management account, so it can still launch EC2 if IAM allows it. Every member account is restricted, including Security OU and delegated administrator accounts.

objective.question: An OU has an SCP that allows only Amazon S3 and Amazon EC2 actions. The default FullAWSAccess SCP has been removed from that OU. An IAM user in a member account in this OU has the AdministratorAccess policy. What happens when the user tries to create a DynamoDB table?
options: The action is denied because the SCP does not allow DynamoDB
The action succeeds only if a permissions boundary also allows it
The action succeeds because SCPs only apply to roles, not users
The action succeeds because AdministratorAccess grants all actions
objective.explanation: Effective permissions are the intersection of what SCPs allow and what IAM policies grant. SCPs never grant permissions, so AdministratorAccess cannot go beyond the SCP allow list, and DynamoDB is blocked. SCPs apply to both users and roles in member accounts.

objective.question: A company sets up a new landing zone with AWS Control Tower. Where are the Log Archive and Audit accounts placed by default?
options: In the Sandbox OU
In the Infrastructure OU
In the Security OU
In the Root, next to the management account
objective.explanation: Control Tower creates the Log Archive and Audit accounts inside the Security OU. The management account stays at the root. The Sandbox OU is for workload accounts.

objective.question: A platform team uses AWS Control Tower. They want to stop non-compliant resources, such as unencrypted S3 buckets, before CloudFormation provisions them, instead of finding them after creation. Which type of control should they enable?
options: Detective controls implemented as AWS Config rules
Detective controls implemented as Amazon GuardDuty findings
Proactive controls implemented as CloudFormation hooks
Preventive controls implemented as SCPs
objective.explanation: Proactive controls use CloudFormation hooks to check resources before provisioning. Detective controls only report after a resource exists. Preventive SCPs block API actions but cannot inspect resource properties in a template.

objective.question: A company needs about 4 Gbps of encrypted bandwidth between its data centre and many VPCs. Direct Connect will take months to arrive. What should a solutions architect do now?
options: Create multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections to a Transit Gateway and enable ECMP
Create a Client VPN endpoint for the data centre router
Use VPC peering from the data centre to each VPC
Create one Site-to-Site VPN to a virtual private gateway and increase the tunnel size
objective.explanation: Each VPN tunnel gives about 1.25 Gbps and its size cannot be increased. ECMP on a Transit Gateway spreads traffic across multiple VPN tunnels to aggregate bandwidth. A virtual private gateway does not support ECMP across connections, VPC peering cannot connect on-premises networks, and Client VPN is for individual users.

objective.question: A bank uses a dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection. A new compliance rule says all traffic between on premises and AWS must be encrypted in transit. What should the architect do?
options: Enable MACsec on a supported dedicated connection, or run an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect
Switch the private VIF to a public VIF
Enable encryption on the Direct Connect gateway
Nothing, because Direct Connect encrypts traffic by default
objective.explanation: Direct Connect is private, but traffic is not encrypted by default. MACsec, on supported dedicated connections, or an IPsec VPN over DX adds encryption. A public VIF and the Direct Connect gateway do not provide encryption.

objective.question: A company has one Direct Connect connection for a production workload. It wants a backup path at the lowest cost and accepts lower bandwidth during a failure. What should it do?
options: Add a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path
Add a second private VIF on the same connection
Add connections at two different DX locations
Add a second Direct Connect connection at the same DX location
objective.explanation: A Site-to-Site VPN is the low-cost backup for Direct Connect when lower bandwidth is acceptable. Connections at two DX locations give the highest resiliency but cost much more. A second VIF on the same connection, or a second connection at the same location, does not remove the single point of failure.

objective.question: A company wants to move 300 VMware vSphere VMs to AWS quickly. It wants no changes to the VMs and wants to keep its existing VMware tools and skills. Which migration strategy fits best?
options: Relocate using VMware Cloud on AWS
Replatform to Amazon ECS
Repurchase to a SaaS product
Rehost using AWS Application Migration Service
objective.explanation: Relocate moves VMs as they are to VMware Cloud on AWS, so the team keeps vSphere tooling and does not convert the VMs. Rehost with MGN turns the servers into EC2 instances, so VMware tools no longer apply. Replatform and repurchase both change the application.

objective.question: A company must lift and shift 200 on-premises Linux and Windows servers to Amazon EC2 with the least operational overhead and a short cutover window. Which approach should it use?
options: Use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) with continuous block-level replication
Rebuild each server manually from AMIs and copy data with rsync
Use AWS DMS to replicate the servers
Write custom scripts to export disk images and import them with VM Import
objective.explanation: MGN is the managed rehost service. It replicates continuously and gives short, testable cutovers. Custom scripts and manual rebuilds add operational overhead, and DMS migrates databases, not whole servers.

objective.question: A company runs steady workloads on EC2, and it often changes instance families and Regions. It also runs containers on AWS Fargate and functions on AWS Lambda. It wants a commitment-based discount that covers all of these. What should it buy?
options: Compute Savings Plan
Spot Instances with a Spot Fleet
Standard Reserved Instances
EC2 Instance Savings Plan
objective.explanation: A Compute Savings Plan applies across EC2 families and Regions, and also covers Fargate and Lambda. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is locked to one family and Region. Standard RIs do not cover Fargate or Lambda, and Spot is not a commitment discount and can be interrupted.

objective.question: A security team must deploy an IAM role and an AWS Config rule to every account in the Workloads OU. New accounts are added to this OU each month, and the resources must appear in them with no manual work. What is the best solution?
options: CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment enabled, targeting the OU
A Lambda function that runs every month and calls CreateStack in each account
A nested stack in the management account
CloudFormation StackSets with self-managed permissions, updated monthly
objective.explanation: Service-managed StackSets that target an OU, with automatic deployment on, deploy to accounts that join the OU later. Self-managed permissions need manual account lists and roles. Nested stacks work only in one account, and a custom Lambda adds operational overhead.

objective.question: A CloudFormation stack contains an Amazon RDS DB instance. The team wants a final copy of the data to stay available if someone deletes the stack by mistake, and it wants to avoid paying for a running instance after deletion. What should it set on the DB resource?
options: UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
A stack policy that denies Update:*
DeletionPolicy: Delete
DeletionPolicy: Snapshot
objective.explanation: DeletionPolicy Snapshot takes a final snapshot when the resource is deleted, so the data survives without a running instance. Delete removes the data. A stack policy protects against updates, not stack deletion.

objective.question: A developer runs 'cdk deploy' for the first time in a new account and Region. The deployment fails because the assets bucket and deployment roles do not exist. What should the developer run first?
options: cdk diff
cdk init
cdk bootstrap
cdk synth
objective.explanation: cdk bootstrap creates the CDKToolkit stack, which holds the asset bucket, the ECR repository and the IAM roles CDK uses to deploy. synth and diff only produce or compare templates, and init creates a new project.

objective.question: A team deploys a Lambda function through AWS CodeDeploy. It wants 10% of traffic sent to the new version first, and the remaining 90% shifted after 5 minutes if no problems occur. It also wants automatic rollback if the error rate rises. Which configuration meets this?
options: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce with a pre-traffic hook
A weighted Route 53 record with 10% weight
CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes with CloudWatch alarms attached to the deployment group
CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute with no alarms
objective.explanation: Canary10Percent5Minutes shifts 10% of traffic and then, after 5 minutes, the rest. CloudWatch alarms on the deployment group trigger automatic rollback. Linear shifts in equal steps, AllAtOnce has no gradual shift, and Route 53 weighting does not manage Lambda alias versions or roll back automatically.

objective.question: An operations team gets paged many times during one incident, because separate CloudWatch alarms for CPU, latency and 5xx errors all fire together. It wants one page only when high latency and high 5xx errors happen at the same time, with the least operational overhead. What should it do?
options: Write a Lambda function that reads all alarms every minute and decides whether to page
Increase the evaluation periods on every alarm
Send all alarms to an SQS queue and deduplicate them
Create a CloudWatch composite alarm using AND on the latency and 5xx alarms, and send notifications only from the composite alarm
objective.explanation: Composite alarms combine alarm states with rule expressions such as AND, which reduces alarm noise with no custom code. A custom Lambda or SQS deduplication adds overhead, and longer evaluation periods only delay alerts without linking the conditions.

objective.question: A company attaches this SCP to its Workloads OU. What is the effect on IAM principals in member accounts in that OU?
options: Only the listed global services are allowed, and every other service is denied in all Regions
The policy grants full access in ap-south-1 and ap-south-2, even if IAM policies do not allow it
Actions outside ap-south-1 and ap-south-2 are denied, except the listed global services, which keep working
All actions are denied in every Region except ap-south-1 and ap-south-2, including IAM and Route 53 calls
objective.explanation: Deny with NotAction denies everything except the listed services, and the condition applies the deny only to requests outside the two approved Regions. Global services are exempt because their calls resolve to us-east-1. SCPs never grant permissions, so the last option is wrong.

objective.question: A company has one AWS Direct Connect connection in Mumbai. It must reach Transit Gateways in ap-south-1 and ap-southeast-1 over this connection. Each Transit Gateway has many VPCs attached. Which design meets this with the least complexity?
options: Create a transit VIF to a Direct Connect gateway and associate both Transit Gateways with the Direct Connect gateway
Create a private VIF to a Direct Connect gateway and attach the Direct Connect gateway to both Transit Gateways as a VPC attachment
Create a public VIF and use Site-to-Site VPN to each Transit Gateway
Create a private VIF to each VPC's virtual private gateway
objective.explanation: A transit VIF terminates on a Direct Connect gateway, and the Direct Connect gateway can be associated with Transit Gateways in different Regions. Private VIFs per VPC do not scale. A private VIF cannot connect to a Transit Gateway. A public VIF with VPN adds complexity that is not needed.

objective.question: On-premises servers must resolve records in an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone associated with a shared-services VPC. The on-premises DNS servers are connected through Direct Connect. What should the architect configure?
options: A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC, and conditional forwarders on the on-premises DNS servers that point to the endpoint IP addresses
Make the hosted zone public so on-premises servers can resolve it
An EC2 instance running BIND that copies the zone file to on premises every hour
A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule for the on-premises domain
objective.explanation: Inbound endpoints accept DNS queries from on premises and resolve them with the VPC's private hosted zones. Outbound endpoints handle the opposite direction, from AWS to on premises. A public zone exposes internal names, and a self-managed BIND copy adds operational overhead.

objective.question: A team applies this stack policy to a production CloudFormation stack. A developer then submits an update that changes the DB instance's engine version, which modifies the instance in place, and another update that changes its DBInstanceIdentifier, which requires replacement. What happens?
options: Both updates succeed because stack policies only apply during stack creation
The identifier change succeeds and CloudFormation takes a snapshot first
The engine version update succeeds and the identifier change fails
Both updates fail because the database is fully protected
objective.explanation: The policy allows all updates but denies replacement or deletion of ProdDatabase. An in-place modification is Update:Modify, so it is allowed. A change that needs replacement is blocked and the stack update fails.

objective.question: A CloudFormation stack creates an Auto Scaling group whose instances install the application with a long user data script. The stack reports CREATE_COMPLETE before the application is ready, and a dependent stack then fails its health checks. How should the team fix this?
options: Add a CreationPolicy with ResourceSignal to the Auto Scaling group and call cfn-signal at the end of the user data script
Increase the stack's timeout in the create-stack call
Add a DeletionPolicy of Retain to the Auto Scaling group
Add a DependsOn attribute from the dependent resources to the Auto Scaling group
objective.explanation: A CreationPolicy makes CloudFormation wait for success signals, sent by cfn-signal, before it marks the resource complete. If the signals do not arrive before the timeout, creation fails. DependsOn only orders resource creation, and DeletionPolicy and the stack timeout do not wait for the application to be ready.

objective.question: A platform team runs CDK Pipelines in a tooling account (111111111111). It must deploy stacks into a production account. An administrator runs this command in the production account. What does it achieve?

code.code:
cdk bootstrap aws://222222222222/ap-south-1 \
  --trust 111111111111 \
  --cloudformation-execution-policies arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess

options: It creates the bootstrap resources in the production account and lets the tooling account assume the deployment roles, while CloudFormation deploys with the given execution policy
It creates an AWS Organizations trust relationship between the two accounts
It grants the production account permission to deploy into the tooling account
It copies the tooling account's CDK stacks into the production account
objective.explanation: The --trust option lets the named account assume the bootstrap deployment roles. The --cloudformation-execution-policies option sets the permissions of the role that CloudFormation uses to create resources. Use a narrower policy than AdministratorAccess in production. Bootstrapping does not copy stacks or change Organizations.

objective.question: A company is migrating a 3 TB Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The application can tolerate only a few minutes of downtime. Which approach should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Convert the schema with AWS DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT, then use AWS DMS full load plus change data capture, and cut over once replication lag is near zero
Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate the database server to EC2
Export with Oracle Data Pump and import directly into Aurora PostgreSQL
Use AWS DMS full load only, then stop the application and run a second full load at cutover
objective.explanation: A heterogeneous migration needs schema conversion, and DMS full load with ongoing CDC keeps the target in sync, which keeps downtime short. Data Pump cannot import into PostgreSQL. A second full load means long downtime. MGN is a rehost tool and does not change the engine.

objective.question: An ECS service uses CodeDeploy blue/green with a production listener and a test listener. The team wants a Lambda function to run integration tests against the green task set through the test listener, before any production traffic is moved. In which AppSpec hook should the function run?

code.code:
version: 0.0
Resources:
  - TargetService:
      Type: AWS::ECS::Service
      Properties:
        TaskDefinition: <TASK_DEFINITION>
        LoadBalancerInfo:
          ContainerName: web
          ContainerPort: 8080
Hooks:
  - ???: arn:aws:lambda:ap-south-1:111111111111:function:IntegrationTests

options: AfterAllowTraffic
ApplicationStop
AfterAllowTestTraffic
BeforeInstall
objective.explanation: AfterAllowTestTraffic runs after the test listener routes to the green task set and before production traffic shifts, so the tests hit the new version safely. AfterAllowTraffic runs after production has already moved. BeforeInstall runs before the green task set exists. ApplicationStop is an EC2/on-premises hook.

objective.question: A company has 120 accounts in AWS Organizations. The SRE team wants to view metrics, logs and X-Ray traces from all workload accounts in one place and create alarms there, without switching roles or copying data. New accounts should be included automatically. What should it do?
options: Set up CloudWatch cross-account observability with a central monitoring account as the sink, and link source accounts through Organizations
Enable AWS CloudTrail organization trails and query them with Athena
Give the SRE team an IAM role in each account and use the CloudWatch console role switcher
Create a Kinesis Data Firehose stream in every account that forwards logs to a central S3 bucket
objective.explanation: CloudWatch cross-account observability links source accounts to a monitoring account, so you can view their metrics, logs and traces there and alarm on shared metrics. Linking through Organizations includes new accounts. Firehose only copies logs, CloudTrail covers API activity rather than metrics, and role switching is the manual work the team wants to avoid.

objective.question: A company attaches this SCP to all OUs to keep workloads in the Mumbai Region. Soon after, administrators in member accounts cannot create IAM roles or manage Route 53 hosted zones. What is the mistake?
options: SCPs cannot use Condition blocks, so the policy is treated as an unconditional deny of all actions.
The SCP must also be attached to the management account before it takes effect in member accounts.
The condition key aws:RequestedRegion does not exist, so the SCP denies every request in every Region.
The SCP denies global services such as IAM and Route 53, whose requests are handled through us-east-1. It should use NotAction to exempt global services.
objective.explanation: Requests to global services like IAM, Route 53 and CloudFront are handled in us-east-1, so a Region deny on Action '*' blocks them. AWS's example Region-restriction SCP uses NotAction to exempt these services. aws:RequestedRegion is a valid key, SCPs support conditions, and SCPs never affect the management account.

objective.question: A platform team tries to enroll an existing AWS account into AWS Control Tower. Enrollment fails. The account already has an AWS Config configuration recorder and delivery channel that a previous team created. What is the most likely fix?
options: Delete or adjust the existing AWS Config configuration recorder and delivery channel in the account's governed Regions, then retry enrollment.
Move the account into the Security OU first, because only that OU can enroll existing accounts.
Turn off AWS CloudTrail in the account, because Control Tower cannot enroll accounts that already have a trail.
Attach the FullAWSAccess SCP directly to the account and retry.
objective.explanation: Control Tower sets up its own Config recorder and delivery channel, so an existing recorder or delivery channel in governed Regions blocks enrollment. Removing or adjusting it as the documentation describes fixes the problem. The SCP, OU and CloudTrail options do not address this conflict.

objective.question: Two VPCs, A (10.1.0.0/16) and B (10.2.0.0/16), are attached to the same Transit Gateway. Both attachments are associated with the default TGW route table, and propagation is on for both. Instances in A still cannot ping instances in B. Security groups allow ICMP. What is the most likely cause?
options: The VPC subnet route tables have no route for the other VPC's CIDR pointing to the Transit Gateway attachment.
The two VPCs must be peered as well as attached to the Transit Gateway.
Propagation must be turned off for a static route to be created automatically.
Transit Gateway does not support ICMP traffic between VPC attachments.
objective.explanation: TGW route tables only control routing inside the Transit Gateway. Each VPC's subnet route tables also need a route, such as 10.2.0.0/16 or a summary route, with the TGW as the target. TGW carries ICMP, peering is not needed, and turning off propagation would remove routes.

objective.question: Put these AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) steps in the correct order for one wave of servers: (1) Launch test instances and validate; (2) Install the AWS Replication Agent on source servers; (3) Launch cutover instances; (4) Finalize cutover; (5) Mark servers ready for cutover after testing.
objective.explanation: You install the agent so that continuous replication starts, launch and validate test instances, mark the servers ready for cutover, launch cutover instances, and then finalize. Finalizing stops replication and is the last step. Testing must come before you mark a server ready.

objective.question: A company wants on-premises users to keep using an SMB file share with low-latency access to recent files. The data must be stored durably in Amazon S3, and the company wants to cut local storage. Which service fits better, and why?
options: Amazon S3 File Gateway, because it presents an SMB share on premises, caches recent data locally and stores files as objects in S3.
AWS Transfer Family, because it exposes S3 to on-premises users over SMB.
Amazon EFS mounted over Direct Connect, because EFS supports SMB clients.
AWS DataSync, because it schedules transfers from SMB shares to Amazon S3.
objective.explanation: S3 File Gateway gives users an ongoing SMB or NFS share with a local cache, and it keeps the data in S3. DataSync moves data but does not give users a share. Transfer Family supports SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2, not SMB, and EFS is NFS only.

objective.question: A data lake bucket stores millions of objects. The team cannot predict which objects will be read, and access changes month to month. It wants to cut storage cost without retrieval surprises or manual analysis. What should it use?
options: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Standard-IA for all new uploads
S3 One Zone-IA for all objects
A lifecycle rule that moves all objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days
objective.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically based on real access, with no retrieval fees for its frequent and infrequent tiers. Fixed lifecycle moves and IA classes can add retrieval charges or delays when access patterns are unknown.

objective.question: A batch-processing fleet runs on Spot Instances in an EC2 Auto Scaling group with several instance types. Jobs get interrupted too often. The team wants fewer interruptions and still wants low prices. Which allocation strategy should it use?
options: price-capacity-optimized
capacity-optimized-prioritized, with only one instance type
On-Demand only, with a Compute Savings Plan
lowest-price, with the instance pool count set to 1
objective.explanation: price-capacity-optimized picks Spot pools with the most spare capacity and then the lowest price among them, so it lowers interruption risk. AWS recommends it for most Spot workloads. lowest-price in one pool raises interruption risk, and On-Demand gives up the Spot discount.

objective.question: A network stack exports its VPC ID with Export: Name 'prod-VpcId'. An application stack imports it with Fn::ImportValue. A developer changes the network stack so that the export value would change, and the update fails. What is the cause?
options: CloudFormation does not let you change or delete an export while another stack imports it.
Fn::ImportValue works only within the same stack.
The network stack needs a DeletionPolicy of Retain on the VPC.
Exports are read-only after 24 hours.
objective.explanation: An export that another stack imports cannot be modified or removed until the importing stacks stop referencing it. To change it, first update the consumers, for example by passing the value through an SSM parameter or a new export. The other options describe rules that do not exist.

objective.question: An administrator creates a CloudFormation StackSet with self-managed permissions and deploys it to 10 accounts. Stack instances fail in 3 accounts with a permissions error about assuming a role. The other 7 succeed. What is the most likely cause?
options: Self-managed StackSets can deploy to a maximum of 7 accounts.
The failing accounts need trusted access for StackSets turned on in their own Organizations console.
The AWSCloudFormationStackSetExecutionRole is missing in the 3 failing target accounts, or its trust policy does not trust the administrator account.
The 3 accounts are not in the same Region as the administrator account.
objective.explanation: With self-managed permissions, each target account needs an execution role, by default AWSCloudFormationStackSetExecutionRole, that trusts the administration role. Accounts without it fail. Service-managed permissions with Organizations avoid this, but there is no 7-account limit.

objective.question: A developer runs 'cdk synth' on this code and gets an error. What is the cause?
options: S3_MANAGED encryption cannot be combined with BLOCK_ALL.
Bucket construct IDs cannot contain capital letters.
autoDeleteObjects works only with KMS encryption.
autoDeleteObjects needs removalPolicy set to RemovalPolicy.DESTROY. The default policy keeps the bucket, so CDK throws an error.
objective.explanation: autoDeleteObjects adds a custom resource that empties the bucket when it is deleted. That only makes sense if the bucket is destroyed, so CDK requires RemovalPolicy.DESTROY and fails synthesis without it. The other combinations are valid.

objective.question: For an AWS CodeDeploy in-place deployment on EC2, in what order do these lifecycle events run? ApplicationStart, BeforeInstall, ValidateService, AfterInstall, ApplicationStop.
options: ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService
ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, ApplicationStart, AfterInstall, ValidateService
BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStop, ApplicationStart, ValidateService
BeforeInstall, ApplicationStop, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService
objective.explanation: The order is ApplicationStop, then DownloadBundle, BeforeInstall, Install, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart and ValidateService. The old version stops before the new files are installed, and validation runs last.

objective.question: A team uses AWS Elastic Beanstalk. During deployments it must keep full capacity. If the new version fails health checks, rollback must be quick and must not depend on DNS changes reaching clients. Which deployment policy is the best fit?
options: Immutable
Blue/green with an environment CNAME swap
All at once
Rolling
objective.explanation: Immutable deployments launch new instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group while the old instances keep serving. If the new instances fail, Beanstalk terminates them, so capacity is never reduced. Blue/green CNAME swaps depend on DNS, and rolling or all-at-once deployments reduce capacity.

objective.question: A company with 80 accounts wants every high-severity Amazon GuardDuty finding from any account to open a ticket automatically through one Lambda function. It wants the least operational overhead. What should it do?
options: Designate a delegated administrator account for GuardDuty with auto-enable for the organization. Create one EventBridge rule there that matches high-severity findings and targets the Lambda function.
Export GuardDuty findings from each account to S3 and run a daily Athena query.
Use AWS Config aggregator to collect GuardDuty findings and trigger the function.
Enable GuardDuty separately in each account and deploy an EventBridge rule and Lambda function to each account with StackSets.
objective.explanation: A GuardDuty delegated administrator receives findings for all member accounts, and auto-enable covers new accounts. One EventBridge rule in that account can match on severity and call the function. The other options add per-account work, add delay, or rely on Config, which does not aggregate GuardDuty findings.

objective.question: A global application uses Amazon Aurora MySQL in ap-south-1. It needs a DR copy in another Region with an RPO of about a second and an RTO of about a minute. It also wants low-latency reads in the second Region. Which option is better here?
options: An Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in the second Region
AWS DMS continuous replication to a second Aurora cluster
Multi-AZ Aurora with replicas in three Availability Zones
Daily automated snapshots copied to the second Region
objective.explanation: Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer with typical lag under a second. It supports fast promotion of the secondary Region and serves local reads. Snapshots give hours of RPO, DMS adds lag and operational work, and Multi-AZ protects only within one Region.

objective.question: You are taking SAP-C02. You have 180 minutes for 75 questions. You have spent 5 minutes on question 12 and you are still unsure. What should you do?
options: Leave it blank and move on, because wrong answers lose marks.
Pick your best answer, flag it for review and move on. The average budget is about 2.4 minutes per question.
Skip all long questions and answer only the short ones.
Keep working until you are sure, because accuracy matters more than time.
objective.explanation: 180 / 75 is about 2.4 minutes per question. There is no penalty for guessing, and blank answers score zero, so you should always answer, flag and come back. Spending too long on one question takes time from easier ones.

objective.question: A security team must automatically remove any security group rule that opens port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 in all accounts, with the least custom code. Which solution is best?
options: Deploy the AWS Config managed rule restricted-ssh across the organization, with automatic remediation using an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook such as AWS-DisablePublicAccessForSecurityGroup.
Enable VPC Flow Logs and alert on traffic to port 22.
Use an SCP that denies ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress for everyone.
Write a Lambda function that scans all security groups every 5 minutes with cross-account roles.
objective.explanation: A managed Config rule with SSM Automation remediation detects and fixes the problem with no custom code, and you can deploy it to the whole organization. A custom Lambda adds code to maintain. A blanket SCP blocks all ingress changes, and Flow Logs only alert after traffic has happened.

subjective.question: Explain how Service Control Policies work and how they combine with IAM policies to give effective permissions.
subjective.answer: An SCP is an organisation policy attached to the root, an OU or an account. It sets the maximum permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts. It never grants anything. A user can do an action only if every SCP in the path from root to account allows it, the IAM identity or resource policy allows it, and no explicit deny exists anywhere. By default, the FullAWSAccess SCP is attached. You can use deny lists, such as denying the disabling of CloudTrail or the use of unapproved Regions, or allow lists, where you replace FullAWSAccess. SCPs do not affect the management account or service-linked roles. Because of this, I keep workloads out of the management account and use it only for billing and governance.
keyPoints: SCPs set guardrails and never grant permissions
Effective permission is the intersection of SCP and IAM, and an explicit deny always wins
Deny-list and allow-list strategies
No effect on the management account or service-linked roles

subjective.question: Design a multi-account landing zone for a mid-sized company using AWS Control Tower. Describe the OUs and accounts.
subjective.answer: I would start Control Tower in the management account and choose the home Region and governed Regions. It creates the Security OU with the Log Archive account, which holds central CloudTrail and Config logs, and the Audit account, which gives the security team cross-account access. I would add an Infrastructure OU for shared networking, such as Transit Gateway, the Direct Connect gateway and shared services. Then I would add a Workloads OU split into Prod and Non-Prod, a Sandbox OU with tight budget controls, and a Suspended OU for accounts being closed. Identity goes through IAM Identity Center with permission sets. I would enable mandatory and strongly recommended controls, add a Region deny control, and vend accounts through Account Factory. Security tools such as GuardDuty and Security Hub use the Audit account as delegated administrator.
keyPoints: Management, Log Archive and Audit accounts, with the last two in the Security OU
Separate OUs for infrastructure, prod/non-prod workloads, sandbox and suspended accounts
IAM Identity Center for central access
Controls and Region deny applied by OU
Delegated administrator for security services

subjective.question: How would you make every new account vended by Control Tower get a standard baseline, such as VPC, IAM roles and Config rules, with minimum manual work?
subjective.answer: I would use Account Factory to create accounts, so they are enrolled and governed from day one. For the baseline, I have three managed options. Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) deploys CloudFormation templates and SCPs when lifecycle events such as account creation happen. Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) does the same if the team uses Terraform. A simpler option is service-managed CloudFormation StackSets targeted at an OU with automatic deployment, so any account that joins the OU gets the stacks. Networking can be shared through AWS RAM, for example by sharing Transit Gateway attachments or subnets. I would avoid custom scripts. In exam terms, 'least operational overhead' points to these managed features.
keyPoints: Account Factory for vending
CfCT or AFT driven by lifecycle events
StackSets with automatic deployment by OU
Prefer managed options over custom scripts

subjective.question: Design hybrid connectivity between an on-premises data centre and 50 VPCs across two Regions.
subjective.answer: I would put a Transit Gateway in each Region as the hub and attach the VPCs to it, using route tables to keep prod and non-prod separate. For the main path, I would use Direct Connect with a transit VIF to a Direct Connect gateway that is associated with both Transit Gateways. This gives one private link that reaches both Regions. For backup, I would add Site-to-Site VPN attachments on the Transit Gateways. ECMP lets several tunnels add up to more bandwidth, since each tunnel is about 1.25 Gbps. BGP route preferences keep DX as the primary path. The two Transit Gateways can peer for inter-Region traffic. For DNS, I would use Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints in a shared networking account, shared through AWS RAM.
keyPoints: Transit Gateway as the regional hub
DX with transit VIF and DX gateway for multi-Region reach
VPN backup with ECMP and BGP preference
Route 53 Resolver endpoints for hybrid DNS
Central networking account shared through RAM

subjective.question: A customer says Direct Connect is private, so it is encrypted. How do you respond, and how do you make DX resilient?
subjective.answer: Private is not the same as encrypted. Direct Connect traffic travels over a dedicated path, but AWS does not encrypt it by default. If compliance needs encryption in transit, I would enable MACsec on supported dedicated connections, which gives layer-2 encryption at line rate. Another option is an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over the DX connection, often over a public or transit VIF. Application-level TLS also helps, but auditors often want network encryption. For resiliency, one connection is a single point of failure. The strongest design uses connections at two different DX locations, so a whole location can fail. If budget is tight, I would add a Site-to-Site VPN as a low-cost backup and accept the lower bandwidth during failover.
keyPoints: DX is not encrypted by default
MACsec or IPsec VPN over DX
Multiple DX locations for maximum resiliency
VPN as a cheap backup path

subjective.question: Explain the 7 Rs of migration with a short example of each.
subjective.answer: Retire means switching off apps nobody uses, such as an old reporting server. Retain means keeping an app on premises for now, perhaps because of a recent hardware refresh or a licence constraint. Rehost is lift and shift to EC2 with AWS Application Migration Service. Relocate moves VMware workloads as they are to VMware Cloud on AWS. Replatform makes small optimisations without changing the core code, such as moving a self-managed MySQL database to Amazon RDS. Repurchase means moving to a SaaS product, such as replacing an on-premises CRM. Refactor, or re-architect, redesigns the app for cloud-native services, such as breaking a monolith into Lambda and DynamoDB. In exams, the key words point to the answer: 'quickly, no code change' means rehost, and 'scalability and agility, accept effort' means refactor.
keyPoints: All seven: retire, retain, rehost, relocate, replatform, repurchase, refactor
One concrete example of each
Map scenario keywords to the strategy
Rehost uses MGN; relocate uses VMware Cloud on AWS

subjective.question: Walk through the AWS tools you would use for a large data-centre migration, from discovery to cutover.
subjective.answer: First, I assess. Migration Evaluator builds the business case, and AWS Application Discovery Service collects server inventory, utilisation and dependencies, using agents or the agentless collector. I track everything in AWS Migration Hub and group servers into applications and waves. The landing zone is ready beforehand through Control Tower. For servers, I use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN). It replicates continuously and lets me launch test instances before a short cutover. For databases, I use AWS DMS, with the Schema Conversion Tool if the engine changes, and change data capture to keep the target in sync. For large offline data, I use the Snowball family, and for file data I use DataSync. After cutover, I right-size using Compute Optimizer.
keyPoints: Assess with Migration Evaluator and Application Discovery Service
Track waves in Migration Hub
MGN for servers, DMS and SCT for databases
DataSync or Snowball for bulk data
Test launches before cutover, then right-size

subjective.question: What are the main cost optimisation levers on AWS, and in what order would you apply them?
subjective.answer: First, I get visibility. I use Cost Explorer, tagging with cost allocation tags, AWS Budgets, and Cost Anomaly Detection across the organisation. Then I remove waste, such as idle instances, unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots and unused Elastic IPs. Next, I right-size using Compute Optimizer and move to Graviton where the workload supports it. I add scheduling or Auto Scaling so non-prod resources are not running at night. Only after right-sizing do I commit, with Savings Plans or Reserved Instances for the steady baseline. I use Spot for fault-tolerant work such as batch jobs or CI. For storage, I use S3 lifecycle rules, S3 Intelligent-Tiering and gp3 volumes. For networking, I cut NAT and inter-AZ data transfer by using VPC endpoints. Committing before right-sizing locks in waste.
keyPoints: Visibility first: tags, Cost Explorer, Budgets, anomaly detection
Remove waste, then right-size
Commit with Savings Plans after right-sizing
Spot for fault-tolerant work
Storage tiering and data transfer reduction

subjective.question: Compare Compute Savings Plans, EC2 Instance Savings Plans, Reserved Instances and Spot Instances.
subjective.answer: All except Spot are commitments, usually for one or three years. A Compute Savings Plan commits to an hourly spend and applies across EC2 families, sizes, operating systems and Regions, and also to Fargate and Lambda. It is the most flexible. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives a deeper discount but is locked to one instance family in one Region, though size and OS can change. Reserved Instances are older. They still matter for services like RDS, ElastiCache and OpenSearch, which Savings Plans do not cover in the same way, and zonal RIs also reserve capacity. Spot gives the largest discount on spare capacity but can be reclaimed with a two-minute warning. I would use it for stateless, interruption-tolerant work. A common design is Savings Plans for the baseline, On-Demand for peaks and Spot for batch.
keyPoints: Compute SP: flexible across family, Region, Fargate and Lambda
EC2 Instance SP: deepest SP discount, one family and Region
RIs still matter for databases and for capacity reservation
Spot: cheapest, interruptible, for fault-tolerant work

subjective.question: How do you manage CloudFormation safely at scale across many teams and accounts?
subjective.answer: I split templates into layers, such as network, security and application. I use nested stacks for reuse and exports or SSM parameters to share values. Every change goes through a change set, so reviewers see exactly what will be replaced. Critical resources get a DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy of Retain or Snapshot, a stack policy to block risky updates, and termination protection on the stack. I run drift detection on a schedule to catch manual changes. For multi-account rollout, I use StackSets with service-managed permissions, targeting OUs with automatic deployment, and I set failure tolerance and maximum concurrent accounts so a bad change stops early. I run cfn-lint and cfn-guard in the pipeline. Templates live in Git and deploy only through CodePipeline, not from the console.
keyPoints: Change sets, stack policies, deletion policies, termination protection
Drift detection
StackSets with OU targets and failure tolerance
Linting and policy checks in the pipeline
Deploy only through a pipeline

subjective.question: What is the AWS CDK, how does it relate to CloudFormation, and what are construct levels?
subjective.answer: The CDK lets you define infrastructure in languages like TypeScript or Python. 'cdk synth' turns the code into a CloudFormation template, and 'cdk deploy' deploys it as a CloudFormation stack. So you keep CloudFormation's rollback and drift features but gain loops, types and reuse. Constructs come in three levels. L1 constructs, named Cfn-something, map one-to-one to CloudFormation resources. L2 constructs add sensible defaults and helper methods, such as bucket.grantRead(role), which writes the IAM policy for you. L3 constructs, or patterns, combine many resources, such as a load-balanced Fargate service. Each account and Region must be bootstrapped once. I use 'cdk diff' before deploying, write unit tests with the assertions module, and use CDK Pipelines for self-mutating delivery.
keyPoints: CDK synthesises to CloudFormation
L1, L2 and L3 construct levels
cdk bootstrap, synth, diff and deploy
Testing with assertions and CDK Pipelines

subjective.question: Compare all-at-once, rolling, blue/green, canary and linear deployments. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: All-at-once updates every target together. It is fast and cheap but causes downtime and has a large blast radius, so it suits dev environments. Rolling updates in batches. It needs no extra capacity, but capacity drops during deployment and rollback is slow. Rolling with an additional batch avoids the capacity drop. Blue/green builds a full new environment and switches traffic, using a load balancer target group, DNS or a Lambda alias. Rollback is instant, but you pay for double capacity for a short time. Canary sends a small share first, such as Canary10Percent5Minutes, then the rest. Linear shifts in equal steps, such as Linear10PercentEvery1Minute. Canary and linear deployments with CloudWatch alarms give automatic rollback. For production APIs on Lambda or ECS, I would use CodeDeploy canary with alarms.
keyPoints: Trade-offs: downtime, cost, blast radius and rollback speed
Rolling and rolling with an additional batch
Blue/green gives instant rollback at the cost of double capacity
Canary versus linear traffic shifting
Alarm-based automatic rollback

subjective.question: Describe an end-to-end blue/green pipeline for a containerised application on Amazon ECS.
subjective.answer: The source is a CodeCommit, GitHub or Bitbucket repository, connected through CodeStar Connections. CodePipeline triggers CodeBuild, which runs unit tests and security scans, builds the image and pushes it to Amazon ECR with image scanning. A deploy stage uses CodeDeploy with the ECS blue/green deployment type. The ALB has two target groups and a production listener, plus a test listener. CodeDeploy starts the green task set and runs hooks, such as an AfterAllowTestTraffic Lambda for smoke tests on the test listener. It then shifts production traffic using a config such as ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes. CloudWatch alarms on 5xx errors and latency are attached to the deployment group for automatic rollback. Blue tasks are kept for a set wait time before termination. I define the whole pipeline in CDK or CloudFormation and add a manual approval before production.
keyPoints: CodePipeline, CodeBuild and ECR flow
CodeDeploy ECS blue/green with two target groups and a test listener
Lifecycle hooks for smoke tests
Canary traffic shift with alarm rollback
Pipeline defined as code, with approval before prod

subjective.question: How would you design monitoring and automated incident response for a multi-account environment?
subjective.answer: I would collect signals centrally. CloudTrail runs as an organisation trail to the Log Archive account. CloudWatch cross-account observability sends metrics, logs and traces to a monitoring account. GuardDuty, Security Hub and Config use the Audit account as delegated administrator. Applications use CloudWatch metrics, structured logs, X-Ray tracing and Synthetics canaries. I would use composite alarms to reduce noise. For response, EventBridge rules match events such as a GuardDuty finding, a Config non-compliance or an alarm state change. They trigger Systems Manager Automation runbooks, for example to isolate an instance with a quarantine security group or to revoke a key. AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager handles paging, escalation and response plans. After each incident, I hold a blameless review and turn manual steps into runbooks.
keyPoints: Central logging, metrics and security findings
Composite alarms to cut noise
EventBridge plus SSM Automation for remediation
Incident Manager for engagement and escalation
Post-incident reviews feed automation

subjective.question: SAP-C02 and DOP-C02 have long scenario questions. How do you manage time and read them quickly?
subjective.answer: Both exams have 75 questions, of which 65 are scored and 10 unscored, in 180 minutes. That is about 2.4 minutes per question. I read the last sentence first to find what is asked. Then I scan the scenario for constraints: 'least operational overhead', 'most cost-effective', 'minimum downtime', 'without code changes', the RTO and RPO, and compliance words like 'encrypted'. I eliminate options that break a hard constraint, then compare the two remaining options on the qualifier. 'Least operational overhead' usually points to a managed service such as Control Tower, MGN or managed rotation, not custom scripts. If I am stuck after about 3 minutes, I mark the question for review and move on. My target is to finish the first pass with 20 to 30 minutes left. To prepare, I take timed full practice exams and aim to score above 75% before booking.
keyPoints: 75 questions in 180 minutes, about 2.4 minutes each
Read the question line first, then the constraints
Eliminate options using hard constraints and qualifiers
Flag and move on, keep review time
Timed practice above 75% as the readiness check

subjective.question: A developer in a member account has AdministratorAccess but gets AccessDenied when calling s3:PutObject on a bucket. How do you troubleshoot this systematically?
subjective.answer: I walk through the policy evaluation layers in order. First, I read the error message. Newer AccessDenied messages often name the policy type that blocked the call, for example 'explicit deny in a service control policy'. Second, I check the SCPs on the account and on every OU up to the root. I look for explicit denies, such as Region or encryption conditions, and for a missing allow if FullAWSAccess was removed. Third, I check resource control policies, if the organization uses them. Fourth, I check for a permissions boundary on the user or role, and for session policies. Fifth, I check the bucket policy and any VPC endpoint policy. A common cause is a bucket policy that denies uploads without SSE-KMS or without aws:SecureTransport. Sixth, if the bucket uses SSE-KMS, I check that the KMS key policy allows the principal. CloudTrail shows the exact request, and IAM Access Analyzer or the policy simulator help confirm the fix.
keyPoints: Read the AccessDenied message; it often names the blocking policy type
Check SCPs up the OU tree, and RCPs if the organization uses them
Check permissions boundaries and session policies
Check the bucket policy, VPC endpoint policy and KMS key policy
Use CloudTrail and the policy simulator to confirm

subjective.question: Design centralised internet egress and traffic inspection for 40 VPCs in one Region. All outbound internet traffic and traffic between VPCs must pass through a firewall.
subjective.answer: I use AWS Transit Gateway as the hub, with a dedicated inspection VPC and an egress VPC, or one combined VPC. Workload VPCs have no internet or NAT gateways. Their default route points to the Transit Gateway. On the Transit Gateway I use two route tables. The spoke route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 and the other VPC CIDRs to the inspection VPC attachment. The firewall route table sends traffic back to the spokes. In the inspection VPC, AWS Network Firewall endpoints run in each AZ. I enable appliance mode on that attachment so return traffic stays symmetric through the same AZ. After inspection, internet-bound traffic goes to NAT gateways and then to an internet gateway. I deploy across at least two AZs for resilience. Firewall policies are managed centrally, often with AWS Firewall Manager across the organization. The trade-offs are Transit Gateway data processing charges and NAT charges, but there are fewer NAT gateways and one place to audit traffic.
keyPoints: Transit Gateway hub with separate spoke and inspection route tables
AWS Network Firewall endpoints per AZ in an inspection VPC
Enable appliance mode for symmetric routing
Centralised NAT gateways for egress; no internet gateways in spoke VPCs
Firewall Manager for policy at scale; know the cost trade-offs

subjective.question: Design hybrid DNS so that on-premises servers resolve AWS private hosted zones, and 30 VPCs in many accounts resolve the corporate domain corp.example.com.
subjective.answer: I centralise DNS in a shared-services VPC in a networking account. It is connected to on premises through Direct Connect or VPN, and to the other VPCs through Transit Gateway. For on premises to AWS, I create a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint with IPs in two AZs. The on-premises DNS servers get conditional forwarders for the AWS private zones that point to those IPs. The private hosted zones are associated with the shared-services VPC. Cross-account zones are associated through an authorisation and association. For AWS to on premises, I create an outbound endpoint and a Resolver forwarding rule for corp.example.com that targets the on-premises DNS servers. I share the rule with all accounts through AWS RAM, ideally with the whole OU, and associate it with each VPC, for example through a Control Tower account baseline. Then every VPC resolves the corporate domain with no DNS servers to manage. I also allow DNS ports in security groups and firewalls, and monitor endpoint query volume.
keyPoints: Inbound endpoint for on-premises-to-AWS queries
Outbound endpoint and forwarding rule for AWS-to-on-premises queries
Share Resolver rules through AWS RAM to many accounts
Centralise in a shared-services VPC; multi-AZ endpoint IPs
Associate private hosted zones across accounts

subjective.question: You are migrating a busy MySQL database on premises to Amazon Aurora MySQL with AWS DMS. Write a cutover plan that keeps downtime to minutes and allows rollback.
subjective.answer: First, I prepare the target. I create the Aurora cluster and pre-create the schema, but without secondary indexes and triggers so the full load runs faster. I enable binary logging in row format on the source so CDC works. Next, I run a DMS task with full load plus CDC. After the full load, I add the indexes and let CDC catch up. I check row counts with DMS data validation and watch the CDCLatencySource and CDCLatencyTarget metrics. I run application tests against a copy or a read-only path. To prepare rollback, I set up reverse replication from Aurora back to the source, or keep the source unchanged and ready. At cutover, I stop writes to the source and wait for latency to reach zero. Then I run final validation, enable triggers, reset sequences and auto-increment values, and switch the DNS or connection string, using a low TTL set in advance. I watch errors closely. If problems appear, I switch back within the agreed rollback window.
keyPoints: Full load plus CDC; source binary logging must be enabled
Defer indexes and triggers until after the full load
Validate data and watch CDC latency metrics
Freeze writes, drain lag, then switch DNS with a low TTL
Keep a tested rollback path, such as reverse replication

subjective.question: A production CloudFormation stack is stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. Explain why this happens and how you recover.
subjective.answer: This state means an update failed, and then the rollback also failed. CloudFormation could not return one or more resources to their previous state. Common causes are resources changed or deleted outside CloudFormation (drift), insufficient permissions on the service role, a resource limit, or a dependency that no longer exists, such as a deleted security group or KMS key. To recover, I first read the stack events to find the exact resource and error. Then I fix the root cause if I can, for example by recreating the missing dependency or restoring permissions, and run ContinueUpdateRollback. If a resource cannot be fixed, I call ContinueUpdateRollback with resources-to-skip for those logical IDs. CloudFormation marks them as rolled back, and I later reconcile them with drift detection or a corrective update. I never delete a production stack to escape this state. To prevent it, I use change sets, stack policies and drift detection, and I block manual console changes through SCPs or permissions.
keyPoints: The update failed and then the rollback also failed
Common causes: drift, missing dependencies, role permissions, limits
Read stack events to find the failing resource
Fix the cause, then run ContinueUpdateRollback, using resources-to-skip if needed
Prevent it with change sets, drift detection and no manual changes

subjective.question: Review this CDK code for a production stack. What problems do you see, and how would you fix them?
subjective.answer: There are four problems. First, RemovalPolicy.DESTROY on a production data table means that deleting the stack, or a change that replaces the table, deletes all orders. Use RETAIN, and enable point-in-time recovery and deletion protection. Second, the hardcoded tableName causes two issues. Any change that needs replacement fails, because CloudFormation cannot create a second table with the same name. It also blocks deploying the same stack to several stages in one account. It is better to let CDK generate the name. Third, the environment variable hardcodes the name. It should use table.tableName, so CDK creates a reference and the correct dependency. Fourth, the IAM statement grants dynamodb:* on all resources, which breaks least privilege. Replace it with table.grantReadWriteData(fn), which scopes the actions to this table. I would also check for these problems automatically with cdk-nag or unit tests based on assertions, and review cdk diff before each deploy.
keyPoints: DESTROY on stateful production data is dangerous; use RETAIN, PITR and deletion protection
Hardcoded physical names block replacements and multiple stages
Use table.tableName references instead of string literals
Replace the wildcard IAM statement with grant methods
Use cdk-nag, assertion tests and cdk diff in the pipeline

subjective.question: In a blue/green deployment, both versions often share one database. How do you handle schema changes so that rollback stays safe?
subjective.answer: I use the expand and contract pattern, also called parallel change. The rule is that the schema must work with both the old and the new application versions during the switch. In the expand phase, I add new columns or tables in a way that is backward compatible. New columns are nullable or have defaults, and I never rename or drop anything. This migration runs before the green deployment, often as a separate pipeline stage. The green version writes to both the old and new structures, or I backfill the new structure with a background job. After traffic moves to green and the rollback window passes, the contract phase removes the old columns in a later release. Because blue still works against the expanded schema, rolling back is only a traffic switch, with no database restore. For risky changes I add feature flags, for example with AWS AppConfig, so new behaviour can be turned off without a deployment. Destructive migrations never run in the same release as the code switch.
keyPoints: Schema must support both old and new versions at the same time
Expand first with additive, backward-compatible changes
Backfill or dual-write during the transition
Contract, such as dropping old columns, only after the rollback window
Feature flags decouple releasing a feature from deploying code

subjective.question: A company's AWS bill shows that NAT gateway data processing and data transfer charges are growing fast. How do you investigate and reduce them?
subjective.answer: First, I find what is driving the cost. In Cost Explorer, I filter by usage type, such as NatGateway-Bytes, and by account. Then I enable VPC Flow Logs on the NAT gateway's network interfaces and query them with Athena to find the top source instances and destination IPs. Usually most of the traffic goes to AWS services. For Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, I add gateway VPC endpoints. They have no extra charge, and that traffic then bypasses the NAT gateway. For services such as ECR, CloudWatch Logs, STS or Secrets Manager, I compare interface endpoint pricing with NAT processing costs and add endpoints where they save money. Container image pulls are a common hidden cost, so I use ECR endpoints and pull-through cache. I also check for cross-AZ traffic: each AZ should route to its own NAT gateway. I look for chatty traffic between AZs, and for workloads that download large updates repeatedly. Finally, I set AWS Budgets alerts and Cost Anomaly Detection so new spikes are caught early.
keyPoints: Use Cost Explorer usage types and Flow Logs with Athena to find top talkers
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB at no extra charge
Interface endpoints where they cost less than NAT processing
Avoid cross-AZ NAT routing; use one NAT gateway per AZ
Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection to catch spikes

subjective.question: Why should you avoid running workloads and security tools in the Organizations management account, and how do delegated administrators help?
subjective.answer: The management account is the most powerful account in the organization. SCPs do not apply to it, so guardrails cannot limit its users. It can create, move and close accounts and change policies everywhere. If it is compromised, the attacker controls the whole organization. So I keep it minimal. It should hold only Organizations, Control Tower, consolidated billing and IAM Identity Center, if needed, with very few people, MFA on root, and tight monitoring. Delegated administrators let me run organization-wide services from a member account instead. For example, I register the Audit or Security Tooling account as delegated administrator for GuardDuty, Security Hub, AWS Config aggregation, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer and Firewall Manager. I can register an infrastructure account for CloudFormation StackSets. These accounts are governed by SCPs. Security teams then work without access to the management account, which reduces the blast radius and follows least privilege. I also restrict who can register delegated administrators.
keyPoints: SCPs do not apply to the management account
A compromised management account means full organization compromise
Keep the management account minimal: billing, Organizations, Control Tower, Identity Center
Delegate GuardDuty, Security Hub, Config and StackSets to member accounts
Delegated admin accounts stay under SCP guardrails

subjective.question: Your company has acquired a startup that runs 12 AWS accounts in its own AWS Organization. Leadership wants these accounts governed by your Control Tower landing zone within a month, with no workload downtime. List the steps in order and the risks at each step.
subjective.answer: First, do an inventory. List the startup's SCPs, delegated administrators, organization CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty and any services that depend on Organizations trusted access, such as RAM shares. Moving an account breaks org-scoped RAM shares and org-wide policies. Second, check that each account can stand alone: payment method, contact details and root access. Third, remove the accounts from the old organization, then send invitations from our management account and accept them. Check the current Organizations documentation, because the transfer options can change. Fourth, place them in a quarantine or Migration OU with light guardrails. Fifth, remove any conflicting Config recorders and delivery channels, then enroll the accounts in Control Tower. Sixth, test our SCPs in that OU to confirm they do not break workloads, then move each account to its final OU, such as Workloads/Prod. Finally, re-create the RAM shares and register the accounts with our security tooling. Move non-production accounts first and keep a rollback plan.
keyPoints: Inventory org-dependent features first: RAM shares, SCPs, delegated administrators, organization trails
Each account must meet standalone requirements before it leaves the old organization
Use a staging OU before applying strict SCPs
Clear Config recorder and delivery channel conflicts before Control Tower enrollment
Move non-production accounts first and validate

subjective.question: A Site-to-Site VPN shows both tunnels UP, but on-premises servers cannot reach EC2 instances in the VPC. How do you troubleshoot?
subjective.answer: A tunnel that is UP only proves IKE and IPsec are working, so I check the data path layer by layer. First, routing on the AWS side: is route propagation turned on for the virtual private gateway in the subnet route tables, or is there a static route to the on-premises CIDR? With a Transit Gateway, I check the attachment's association and propagation in the TGW route table. Second, BGP: if the VPN is dynamic, is the on-premises router advertising its prefixes, and is it receiving the VPC CIDR? With static routing, are the static prefixes on the VPN connection correct? Third, the on-premises side: does the firewall route the VPC CIDR into the tunnel, and does it allow the traffic? Fourth, the VPC: security groups must allow the on-premises source range, and NACLs must allow return traffic on ephemeral ports. Fifth, check for overlapping CIDRs and asymmetric routing across the two tunnels. VPC Flow Logs show whether packets arrive and whether they are accepted or rejected.
keyPoints: Tunnel UP does not mean routes are correct
Check route propagation or static routes, and TGW route tables
Check BGP advertisements in both directions
Security groups, NACL ephemeral ports and the on-premises firewall
Use VPC Flow Logs to find where packets stop

subjective.question: A shared-services team must expose one internal API to 200 consumer VPCs in many accounts. Some consumers have CIDRs that overlap with the provider VPC. Compare VPC peering, Transit Gateway and AWS PrivateLink for this, and pick one.
subjective.answer: VPC peering does not work here. It does not support overlapping CIDRs, it is not transitive, and 200 peerings would be hard to manage. Transit Gateway scales to many VPCs and centralises routing, but it routes whole networks. Overlapping CIDRs still break routing, and TGW gives consumers network-level access to more than the one API, which widens the attack surface. PrivateLink is the best fit. The provider puts the API behind a Network Load Balancer and publishes a VPC endpoint service. Each consumer creates an interface endpoint, which gets an ENI with an IP from the consumer's own subnet. Traffic is one-way, from consumer to service, and overlapping CIDRs do not matter because no routing between VPCs happens. The provider controls access with allowed principals and acceptance settings. The cost is per endpoint-hour and per GB, which is fine for one service. I would choose TGW only if consumers needed broad, two-way network access.
keyPoints: Peering fails because of overlap, no transitivity and too many connections
TGW routes whole networks and cannot handle overlapping CIDRs
PrivateLink exposes one service through an NLB and interface endpoints
PrivateLink is unaffected by overlapping CIDRs and is one-way
Access control through endpoint service allowed principals

subjective.question: An engineer wrote this SCP to stop anyone except a break-glass role from changing IAM in member accounts. After it was attached, Control Tower account updates and baseline deployments began to fail. Spot the mistake and fix it.
subjective.answer: The SCP exempts only BreakGlassAdmin, so it also denies IAM changes by the roles that Control Tower and other automation use. Control Tower manages member accounts through the AWSControlTowerExecution role. StackSets use their execution role, and pipelines use their own deploy roles. All of these need iam:Create* and iam:Put* to deploy baselines, so updates fail. To fix it, add the automation roles to the ArnNotLike list, for example arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution, arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*, and the pipeline deploy role pattern. Also, Control Tower's own guardrails already protect its resources, so avoid overlapping denies. A better pattern is to deny IAM changes only on protected resources, such as roles with a specific path or tag, instead of on all of IAM. Developers can still create application roles, ideally limited by a permissions boundary. Always test new SCPs in a sandbox OU before attaching them to production OUs.
keyPoints: The deny blocks AWSControlTowerExecution and automation roles
Add the service and automation role ARNs to the exemption condition
Scope denies to protected resources by path or tag where possible
Use permissions boundaries for developer-created roles
Test SCPs in a sandbox OU first

subjective.question: A company has five applications to migrate in 9 months: (a) a COTS HR system with a SaaS version available; (b) a stable Java app on Linux VMs; (c) an old reporting tool used by 3 people; (d) a mainframe billing system tied to a 2-year hardware contract; (e) a monolith that needs to scale 10x for a new product. Assign a 7R strategy to each and justify it.
subjective.answer: (a) Repurchase. Move to the vendor's SaaS version. This removes infrastructure work and fits the timeline. (b) Rehost with AWS Application Migration Service, or Replatform if the team can switch to managed pieces such as Amazon RDS or Elastic Beanstalk with little code change. Rehost is the fastest and lowest-risk path. (c) Retire, after confirming with the users and keeping the data if compliance requires it. Each retired app cuts licence and run cost. (d) Retain for now. The hardware contract and risk make moving it in 9 months a poor choice. Plan a later Refactor or a mainframe modernisation project, and connect it to AWS through hybrid networking. (e) Refactor. Break out the parts that need to scale into containers or serverless services. Rehosting a monolith will not give 10x elastic scale. In the meantime it could be rehosted first and refactored after, which lowers schedule risk. I would plan the waves by dependency mapping from discovery data, not by app size.
keyPoints: Repurchase when a SaaS option exists
Rehost or replatform stable apps for speed
Retire apps that are not used, and Retain apps blocked by contracts or risk
Refactor only where a business need such as scale justifies it
Plan waves using discovery and dependency data

subjective.question: For blue/green deployments on EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer, compare shifting traffic with Route 53 weighted records versus ALB weighted target groups. Which is better for fast rollback, and why?
subjective.answer: With Route 53 weighted records, blue and green usually sit behind separate load balancers, and you change record weights. This works across Regions and stacks, but clients and resolvers cache DNS for the TTL. Some clients ignore TTLs, so both the cutover and the rollback are slow and uneven. You also pay for and run two load balancers. With ALB weighted target groups, one listener rule forwards to both target groups with weights, such as 90/10. Changing the weights takes effect at the load balancer straight away, with no DNS caching, so rollback is close to instant. You can also turn on target group stickiness so that a user stays on one version during a canary. For fast, predictable rollback within one Region, ALB weighted target groups are better. Route 53 weighting suits cross-Region moves or cases where blue and green must be fully separate stacks. Either way, keep blue running until green is proven.
keyPoints: DNS weighting depends on TTLs and client caching, so rollback is slow
ALB weighted target groups change at the load balancer, almost instantly
Stickiness keeps a user on one version
Route 53 suits cross-Region or fully separate stacks
Keep blue running until green is validated

subjective.question: An ECS blue/green deployment through CodeDeploy keeps failing and rolling back. The deployment events show that green tasks start, then the deployment fails before any traffic is shifted. What are the likely causes and how do you find the real one?
subjective.answer: Failure before traffic shifts means either the green tasks never become healthy or a hook fails. First, check the ECS service events and stopped-task reasons. Common reasons are image pull errors, such as a missing ECR permission on the task execution role or no route to ECR from private subnets, missing secrets, out-of-memory errors, or a container exiting. Second, check the green target group health checks. The health check path, port or success codes may not match the new version, or the security group may not allow traffic from the ALB to the task port. Third, check the AppSpec hooks. If a BeforeAllowTraffic or AfterAllowTestTraffic Lambda fails, or never calls PutLifecycleEventHookExecutionStatus, CodeDeploy fails the deployment. Check the Lambda's logs and its IAM permission for that call. Fourth, check that the test listener and target groups in the deployment group match the ALB. CloudWatch Logs for the container usually show the root cause quickly.
keyPoints: Check stopped-task reasons: image pull, secrets, out of memory, exits
Check green target group health checks and security groups
Hook Lambdas must report status with PutLifecycleEventHookExecutionStatus
Verify listener and target group configuration in the deployment group
Use container logs to confirm the root cause

subjective.question: A company's dev and test accounts cost almost as much as production. Those environments run 24x7 but are used only during Indian business hours. Design a plan to cut this cost with governance, not one-off clean-ups.
subjective.answer: First, get visibility. Enforce cost allocation tags such as env, team and owner with tag policies, activate them in Billing, and use Cost Explorer or Data Exports to see spend by team. Second, schedule resources. Stop EC2 and RDS outside business hours with the Instance Scheduler on AWS solution or Systems Manager Automation. Running about 12 hours on weekdays instead of 24x7 cuts compute hours by more than half. Scale ECS services and Auto Scaling groups to zero at night.
